name: Connecticut Mirror
title: ConnCAT founder Clemons steps down to focus on sister organization ConnCORP
description: The shared goal of ConnCAT and ConnCORP is to promote economic empowerment and community development in New Haven’s Black communities.
text:
When Erik Clemons looked around New Haven more than 14 years ago, it sparked an idea: an organization dedicated to workforce development and job training in the city’s historically Black communities. 
The idea led to the creation of the Connecticut Center for Arts and Technology, or ConnCAT. Modeled after the Manchester Bidwell Corporation in Pittsburgh and founded in the early 2010s, ConnCAT uses job training to spur economic empowerment, launching a variety of programs and projects to further build self-reliance and skills in New Haven’s Dixwell-Newhallville communities.
Now, after more than a decade at the helm, Clemons is stepping down.  
Last week, Clemons announced that he would be leaving the organization he started. The founder and longtime CEO will direct his attention to ConnCORP, a sister organization. (ConnCORP started out as a for-profit focused on economic development and was reorganized into a nonprofit in 2021.) 
Clemons, who started both organizations, had been serving as CEO of both ConnCAT and ConnCORP.
ConnCAT will be led in the interim by Malcolm Ellis, a current member of the ConnCORP board of directors. A search for a permanent CEO is expected to begin in the near future. 
“ConnCAT is in the strongest position it’s ever been in, and that’s a credit to our staff, our students, and this community,” Clemons said in a statement. “The work ahead is bigger: continuing to build economic opportunity across New Haven and making sure the doors we’ve opened stay open for the next generation.”

The newly constructed ConnCAT building on Dixwell Avenue in New Haven, June 18, 2026.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror
The exit comes as ConnCAT and ConnCORP are both growing. In June, ConnCAT opened a new 65,000 square foot $65M headquarters in the heart of Dixwell. The center includes space for ConnCAT’s various job training and youth development programs, including a recording studio, computer lab, and work spaces for its culinary, phlebotomy and bioscience programs. 

ConnCORP, meanwhile, is spearheading First HAVEN, a broader $200 million redevelopment project in Dixwell. When completed, the roughly 8-acre project will encompass a mixed-use development including retail and grocery space, apartments, a performing arts center and the recently completed workforce development hub. 
The shared goal of both ConnCAT and ConnCORP, Clemons said, will continue to revolve around promoting economic empowerment and community development, supporting New Haven’s Black communities and the infrastructure of the neighborhoods they live in. 
“We want to ensure that economic development and economic infrastructure comes to Dixwell Avenue, and to ensure that ConnCORP, which is now a national model, continues to fly high,” Clemons said in an interview.
A heightened focus on economic and community development
Clemons previously stepped away from ConnCAT in 2021, but later returned to his role as CEO following an unsuccessful leadership transition. 

ConnCAT&ConnCORP board chairman Carlton Highsmith (second from left) and CEO Erik Clemons (center left) celebrate after the ribbon cutting for the new ConnCAT headquarters on June 19, 2026.  Credit: Courtesy of ConnCORP/The Narrative Project

His second turn as ConnCAT CEO was never meant to be permanent, and the organization has been preparing for the recently announced transition.
This time, he said, the organization is in a much stronger position. According to ConnCAT’s 2024-25 annual report, hundreds of students have graduated from the organization’s job training programs. It also supports young people in the city through afterschool programming. And last year, ConnCAT and ConnCORP, with the support of other partners formally launched the Wealth Accelerator, which aims to test the state’s baby bonds program through a pilot that includes direct financial assistance and education programming for a group of local residents. 
At ConnCORP, Clemons will be continuing the organization’s economic development work with an eye to tackling some of the biggest challenges facing Black communities in Connecticut. That includes entrepreneurship support for small business owners, assessing the state of Connecticut’s Black businesses and creating new programs for financial literacy. 
ConnCORP is also involved in the state’s recently announced NSF quantum engine, with Clemons working as a co-principal investigator on the proposal for federal funding. 
The ongoing First HAVEN development is looking to bring jobs, housing and community recreational programming to Dixwell. The ConnCAT center construction was the first phase of the project, with attention now shifting to apartments and housing construction that centers the community. 
Clemons also said ConnCORP intends to do more real estate work in the future.
ConnCORP CEO Erik Clemons tours the construction site of the future ConnCAT Place at Dixwell in February 2024 with staff members Jahkeeva Morgan, Elaine Roper and Jeneave Dacres. Credit: Courtesy of / ConnCORP
As ConnCAT searches for a new leader, Clemons said he hopes the board will focus on finding a strong fundraiser who is deeply invested in building hope and opportunity in the community.
Ellis, the interim CEO and board member, said in the coming months he will prioritize building on the foundation the organization already has, while “keeping our programming and community partnerships moving forward without interruption.” 
“My immediate priority is continuity, making sure ConnCAT’s programs and the people we serve don’t feel any disruption,” he said in an emailed statement. Ellis will return to his position on the ConnCORP board after a permanent CEO is found, and he’ll become chair of the board after its current leader, Carlton Highsmith, retires at the end of the year.
ConnCAT and ConnCORP leaders say they hope their shared work will continue to expand the range of opportunities accessible to the people who have often been left out of New Haven’s growth. 
“Our job is to fight with folks who are continuing to fight for themselves,” Clemons said.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Trump-backed challenger jumps ahead of Republican senator in Indiana recount
description: The Indiana Recount Commission on Monday flipped a Republican primary race in favor of a President Donald Trump-endorsed challenger over a state senator who opposed Indiana congressional redistricting.
text:
Republican state Senate candidate Paula Copenhaver speaks with her attorneys during an Indiana Recount Commission meeting on Monday, Aug. 10, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The Indiana Recount Commission on Monday flipped a Republican primary race in favor of a President Donald Trump-endorsed challenger over a state senator who opposed Indiana congressional redistricting.
The commission’s decisions on challenged ballots turned what had been a three-vote lead for Sen. Spencer Deery of West Lafayette into a three-vote margin for challenger Paula Copenhaver.
The new certified totals from the May primary now give Copenhaver 6,332 votes to Deery’s 6,329.
The commission threw out eight votes for Deery and two for Copenhaver — all largely for technical reasons over missing signatures or initials from county election officials on absentee ballots.
Deery’s attorney said she planned a quick appeal to the state Court of Appeals.
Voter subpoenas denied in recount of narrow Indiana Senate Republican primary

“This is unprecedented,” attorney Samantha DeWester said after the commission’s vote. “Ballots don’t get tossed for a signature missing from a clerk. It’s now going to set the tone going forward for people that are losers of elections that want to overturn them on technicality stuff. I mean, they just disenfranchised a bunch of voters.”
The Deery-Copenhaver race is the last one undecided from the Republican primary in which Trump-endorsed challengers defeated six of the seven other incumbent senators targeted by the president in retaliation for their votes against redistricting.
Copenhaver, the Fountain County Republican chair and staffer to Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith, said she was confident her primary victory would stand.
“I think there was a mandate throughout the whole state regarding the redistricting, and what I have found is that a lot of people are afraid to vocalize their position,” Copenhaver said. “They don’t speak up for fear of retribution. I’m not afraid.”
The Deery-Copenhaver winner will face Democratic West Lafayette City Councilman David Sanders and independent candidate Joshua Brant in the November election for the heavily Republican district, which spans all or parts of six counties in the area between Lafayette and Terre Haute.
This story will be updated.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NCGOP to select new NC-11 candidate after US Rep Edwards’ withdrawal
description: The meeting takes place less than a week after Edwards dropped out early Wednesday morning.
text:
ASHEVILLE, NORTH CAROLINA - MARCH 13: A North Carolina constituent points at Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-NC) before a congressional town hall meeting on March 13, 2025 in Asheville, North Carolina.   The event comes as Republicans have faced protestors at town halls critical of the Trump administration slashing federal jobs. (Photo: Sean Rayford/Getty Images)The North Carolina Republican Party’s 11th Congressional District Executive Committee is meeting Monday night to decide on a replacement candidate after incumbent U.S. Rep. Chuck Edwards withdrew following a U.S. House Ethics report.
The meeting, scheduled to begin at 6:30 p.m., takes place less than a week after Edwards dropped out early Wednesday morning. Last Monday, the U.S. House Ethics Committee recommended his censure for inappropriate conduct toward two young women who worked in his office. 
Several Republican state lawmakers from the area initially indicated interest in the seat,  but over the past few days, most of them have announced they’ll seek reelection to their current districts instead. State Sens. Kevin Corbin, R-Macon, and Tim Moffitt, R-Henderson, as well as state Rep. Jake Johnson, R-Polk, all issued statements saying they’re not interested in the seat. 
That leaves state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom, a Republican from Henderson County, as the only state lawmaker in the running. Balkcom has represented District 117 in the state House since 2023. She initially endorsed Moffitt — her predecessor in the 117th — before he decided against running. 
In a statement Sunday on social media, Balkcom said she hadn’t “planned to go to Washington,” but has learned that “when your community needs you, you don’t sit on the sidelines; you step up.”
“After much prayer, reflection, and conversations with my family, I’m in,” she said. “We must hold this seat, preserve our mountain values, work with President Trump’s Administration to continue rebuilding Western North Carolina, and make sure Washington never forgets the people who call these mountains home.”
Edwards’ abrupt withdrawal leaves western NC Republicans scrambling

If NCGOP selects Balkcom, she could continue to serve in the state House while she campaigns for the congressional seat. Henderson County Republicans would need to find a replacement candidate to run for her District 117 seat.
Three of the other four candidates known to be seeking the seat have previously run for public office, some against Edwards himself. None appear to have won elections.
Ken McKim ran for the state Senate in 2006, and for North Carolina’s 14th Congressional District in 2022. 
Kristie Sluder sought the District 49 seat in the state Senate in 2024, losing to incumbent Democrat Julie Mayfield. Her website from that campaign describes her top goals as rebuilding the nuclear family, prioritizing public safety, and protecting individual rights. Before that, she sought the Republican nomination for NC-11 in 2022, winning 1.5% of the vote. 
Matthew Burril also ran for NC-11 in 2022, winning 9.5% of the vote in the Republican primary. He came in third after Edwards and incumbent Rep. Madison Cawthorn. 
Chad Nesbitt is a Republican activist and the president of Skyline News in Asheville, as well as the stepson of Martin Nesbitt, a Democratic state lawmaker who died in 2014. 
The replacement will face off against Democrat Jamie Ager, a fourth-generation farmer from a political family, on the ballot in November. They’ll have less than three months to launch a campaign and overcome Ager’s $2 million fundraising advantage. 
“No matter who we face in November, I’m confident we can win this race and deliver what I’ve been talking about since day one: Hurricane Helene recovery, lower costs, and an end to the corruption in Washington,” Ager said last Wednesday in a statement.
Ager’s grandfather previously represented the 11th district from 1983 to 1985 and 1987 to 1991. His brother Eric Ager serves in the North Carolina House.
Even before the March primary election, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee pledged resources and fundraising support to Ager in February, adding him to its “Red to Blue” program. Election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball shifted its assessment of the district from “Leans Republican” to “Toss-up” at the end of July.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Nessel and environmental groups file initial arguments in appeal of DTE Saline data center contract
description: Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel, alongside several environmental advocacy groups, is continuing to push for scrutiny as they demand the Michigan Court of Appeals overturn a set of energy contracts for a controversial data center in Saline Township.  On Friday, Nessel announced she had filed a brief challenging the Michigan Public Service Commission’s d[...]
text:
Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel holds up a sign showcasing redactions in a DTE Energy to supply energy to a data center planned in Saline Township. Dec. 16, 2025 | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan AdvanceMichigan Attorney General Dana Nessel, alongside several environmental advocacy groups, is continuing to push for scrutiny as they demand the Michigan Court of Appeals overturn a set of energy contracts for a controversial data center in Saline Township. 
On Friday, Nessel announced she had filed a brief challenging the Michigan Public Service Commission’s decision to grant conditional approval to two contracts permitting DTE Energy to provide 1.4 gigawatts of energy to the Stargate data center under development by OpenAI, Oracle and Related Digital.
Since the contracts first came under the regulatory body’s consideration, Nessel has lobbied for a contested case proceeding, which would allow her office and other interested parties to examine the contracts and file testimony with the commission. However, the commission gave the contracts ex parte approval, advancing the contracts without outside input. 
In her appeal, the attorney general aims to invalidate the contracts’ approval and have the matter placed back before the commission as a contested case, arguing the commission failed to make several key considerations when reviewing the contracts.
Construction underway on Related Digital’s hyperscale data center in Saline Township, Michigan. June 20, 2026. | Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance
“Despite the enormity of this project, DTE’s application omitted or glossed over several categories of investment costs, declined to provide modelling as normally used to evaluate large investment proposals, and presented extensively redacted contracts for which key terms were left undisclosed and unexplained,” Nessel’s brief reads. “DTE sought fast-tracked approval by deadlines unconfirmable from redacted sections of the contracts. What’s more, it insisted that no other interested parties – namely the Attorney General as the State’s utility ratepayer advocate – should have the opportunity to review further or even ask questions to ensure against cost increases for Michiganders, deviating from the Commission’s default review procedures.”
In a statement, Matt Helms, the public information officer for the Michigan Public Service Commission noted that Nessel’s filing was simply the latest step following her decision to pursue an appeal in April, and that there was nothing in the attorney general’s arguments that the commission hadn’t already reviewed and rejected when considering the case last year. 
“The Commission’s conditional approval of the power supply arrangements between DTE Electric and the Oracle-backed data center project, after thorough review of the unredacted contracts by the Commission, is fully consistent with decades of well-established legal precedent governing MPSC proceedings,” Helms said. “The ultimate approval included some of the strongest consumer protection requirements in the country – protections that would not be available under existing rate schedules without the Commission’s approval – and is projected to result in $300 million in annual savings for DTE’s other customers.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In a separate brief filed Friday, Earthjustice, the Sierra Club, Michigan Environmental Council and the Natural Resources Defense Council similarly argued that the contracts should be overturned.
“The secretive and rushed approval of DTE’s deal for an Oracle AI data center robbed the people of Michigan of their right to evaluate its details and impacts through a contested hearing process, even as it exposed customers to nearly half a billion dollars in up-front costs,” Jacob Elkin, an attorney for Earthjustice, said in a statement. “This appeal is an important part of the fight to ensure that any such deals are reviewed in transparent, public processes, and to protect ratepayers from the unprecedented costs of these AI data centers. Anything less is a violation of the people’s rights under Michigan law.”
Danny Wimmer, Nessel’s press secretary, told Michigan Advance that the attorney general’s office and the environmental groups filed as separate appellants, though the Court of Appeals had consolidated their appeals into one docket. 
DTE maintains its contracts – and the process used to approve them – are all above board. 
“We’re reviewing the appeal but we’re confident – and the MPSC agreed – that our energy service contracts with Oracle offer some of the best customer protections in the country,” DTE Director of Corporate Communications Jill Wilmot told Michigan Advance in a statement Friday. “When submitting our contracts for approval, we followed the established regulatory process, which gives the Commission the authority to approve the contracts without a hearing.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Professor’s varied lawsuits against University of Kentucky pending in state and federal courts
description: FRANKFORT — Cases from a University of Kentucky law professor who was removed from his teaching duties more than a year ago now span state and federal court.  Professor Ramsi Woodcock filed a federal lawsuit last month against incoming law dean Judge Gregory VanTatenhove, UK President Eli Capilouto, Provost Robert DiPaola and the university, over Van […]
text:
Ramsi Woodcock has been reassigned from teaching and banned from entering the University of Kentucky College of Law, where he is an assistant professor.FRANKFORT — Cases from a University of Kentucky law professor who was removed from his teaching duties more than a year ago now span state and federal court. 
Professor Ramsi Woodcock filed a federal lawsuit last month against incoming law dean Judge Gregory VanTatenhove, UK President Eli Capilouto, Provost Robert DiPaola and the university, over Van Tatenhove’s appointment. However, Woodcock withdrew the matter and refiled it in Franklin Circuit Court last week. 
UK had announced Van Tatenhove, a federal judge who was appointed to the bench by Republican President George W. Bush, as the next dean of the College of Law earlier this year. However, the choice has been met with criticism, including from Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear, who had concerns over the procedures used to appoint the judge as dean and possible politicization of the law school. 
Woodcock’s attorneys argue that the matter can be reviewed in state court based on state contract laws and by appointing Van Tatenhove, who has been criticized for not having enough legal scholarship, the action is a violation of Woodcock’s employment contract with UK, according to the complaint. The contact says that the university must comply with “accreditation requirements” and some have argued that Van Tatenhove’s appointment could risk UK’s American Bar Association accreditation. 
Franklin Circuit Judge Phillip Shepherd has been assigned the case and a hearing was held Monday morning largely to review the first motions filed in the case, including for discovery and another hearing in the future. 
Meanwhile, Woodcock filed a lawsuit in state court similar to another pending federal lawsuit where he is seeking to have his teaching duties restored and end an investigation into his criticism of Israel and support of Palestine, such as circulating an online petition calling for military action against Israel. Last summer, Capilouto shared a public message that did not name Woodcock directly, but indicated the university was aware of the petition and called his views “if accurately attributed … repugnant.”
The state lawsuit was filed in Fayette Court but Woodcock’s attorneys requested to move the matter to Franklin Circuit. The U.S. Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals heard oral arguments in the federal lawsuit on July 28.

title: Search is on for 2026 most popular item manufactured in Nebraska
description: LINCOLN — The fifth annual “Coolest Thing Made in Nebraska” competition has started, with nominations to be accepted through August followed by public voting in September. The contest — designed as an image-booster for the state’s manufacturing industry — has grown in popularity, with some 40,000 votes cast last year over multiple rounds of a […]
text:
The 2026 "Coolest Thing Made in Nebraska" contest is underway, with nomination phase currently ongoing and public voting to begin in September. (Courtesy of Nebraska Chamber of Commerce and Industry)LINCOLN — The fifth annual “Coolest Thing Made in Nebraska” competition has started, with nominations to be accepted through August followed by public voting in September.
The contest — designed as an image-booster for the state’s manufacturing industry — has grown in popularity, with some 40,000 votes cast last year over multiple rounds of a bracket-style tournament. Many Nebraskans follow the annual competition started in 2022 and learn about products made in their state. 
A hope is that it also sparks more interest in manufacturing jobs. One chamber leader once said a sign of success would be to hear a student say, “Holy cow, I had no idea I could make something like this in my own backyard, in this area, and have this really unique and interesting career.”
Sixteen products will be chosen from the pool of statewide nomination entries by a panel of business and nonprofit leaders. Members of the public will vote for their favorite product to advance it to the next round. The champion will be announced Oct. 29 when the Nebraska Chamber of Commerce and Industry holds its manufacturing summit in La Vista.
Last year’s winner was a combine series made at the Grand Island-based CNH Industrial plant, of parent company Case IH. (Photo courtesy of Nebraska Chamber and Case IH)
The winner will join the ranks of other “coolest” Nebraska-made products: a Grand Island-produced combine series by Case IH (2025), Valley Irrigation’s center pivot irrigation machine (2024), Rocket Mobility’s all-terrain tracked wheelchair made in Columbus (2023) and Kawasaki’s subway car built in Lincoln to run on the rail tracks of New York City (2022).
According to contest rules, the company that makes the product does not have to be headquartered in the state, but the product must be manufactured in a Nebraska-based facility.
“Nebraska manufacturers are second to none in the U.S., creating innovative products that strengthen our economy and local communities every day,” said state chamber President and CEO Joseph Young. 
The Coolest Thing contest leads into National Manufacturing Month in October and celebrates one of the state’s largest industries, which contest organizers say employs more than 100,000 Nebraskans.
“From innovative products to quality jobs, Nebraska manufacturers strengthen our economy and communities across the state,” said Marc Wisdom, president of Pinnacle Bank, a partner in sponsoring the contest with the chamber and Nebraska Manufacturing Alliance.
Registration for the October manufacturing summit is open to the public and has an entry fee.

description: A Des Moines therapist accused of business-related theft, fraud and forgery will retain her license to practice in Iowa. In January 2026, the Iowa Board of Behavioral Health Professionals charged state-licensed marital and family therapist Michelle Raye Stewart-Sandusky, 38, of Baxter with being convicted of an offense that directly relates to the duties and[...]
text:
The Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing administers the state's Board of Nursing and Board of Behavioral Health Professionals as well as other licensing boards. (Main photo by Getty Images; logo courtesy State of Iowa)A Des Moines therapist accused of business-related theft, fraud and forgery will retain her license to practice in Iowa.
In January 2026, the Iowa Board of Behavioral Health Professionals charged state-licensed marital and family therapist Michelle Raye Stewart-Sandusky, 38, of Baxter with being convicted of an offense that directly relates to the duties and responsibilities of the profession.
Recently, the board agreed to a settlement that calls for Stewart-Sandusky to retain her license subject to 36 months of probationary status that will include monitoring of her practice. As part of the settlement, Stewart-Sandusky will also be required to complete a one-day course on ethics and professionalism.

Court records indicate that in April 2024, Johnston police charged Stewart-Sandusky with felony first-degree theft, alleging she had written bad checks totaling $86,800. One area bank incurred financial losses totaling $34,334 as a result of the alleged scheme, according to police.
The police records indicate the theft involved checks written by Stewart-Sandusky on a Community State Bank account in the name of SS Therapy and Consulting, which she controlled, and a Bank of Iowa account in the name of Central Iowa Mental Health Organization, which she also controlled.
In October 2024, police charged Stewart-Sandusky with forgery and insurance fraud for allegedly forging a financial document in a bank employee’s name in order to have her group healthcare insurance reinstated after it was canceled due to failure to pay the premiums.
According to court records, the initial theft case was resolved in December 2024 plea of guilty to a reduced charge of third-degree theft, which resulted in a suspended prison sentence of two years. In April 2025, the second criminal case was resolved when Stewart-Sandusky pleaded guilty to a charge of insurance fraud and was fined $1,025. Court records show that as part of a plea deal, the forgery charge was dismissed.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Stewart-Sandusky at Therapy Group Inc., where she is the clinical supervisor. The business provides family counseling in Burlington, Des Moines and other areas of Iowa.

name: WyoFile
title: Despite headwinds, University of Wyoming’s new president is bullish on the future
description:
Shane Reeves arrives as the state’s only four-year university faces challenges like a $15 million budget shortfall. Still, the Rock Springs native and retired Army general is optimistic.  
The post Despite headwinds, University of Wyoming’s new president is bullish on the future appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
A complex mix of challenges, including troubling enrollment trends, faltering public trust in higher education and a $15 million budget shortfall, is bringing brand new headwinds to Wyoming’s sole undergraduate and graduate university. 
Despite that, the University of Wyoming’s new president is bullish on its future. 
“I think it’s on the ascent,” Shane Reeves said. “I absolutely think it has a lot of momentum behind it, and accelerating what already exists is going to be part of my job. And I’m really honored to have the opportunity to do it.”
The Rock Springs native retired from a 30-year Army career to take the helm at UW in July. Reeves returned to Wyoming from the U.S. Military Academy, where he served as the dean of the academic board. The father of three holds a juris doctor and is a prolific scholar. He was awarded a Bronze Star for combat service in Iraq. 
He replaced Ed Seidel, whose departure was announced in 2025. Seidel had led the university since 2020, overseeing higher education through the disruptions of COVID-19. When Seidel was hired, he represented UW’s fifth president in just over six years. 
The university’s board of trustees selected Reeves in April. He edged out roughly 100 candidates, including fellow finalist Kelly Crane, who has served as dean of UW’s College of Agriculture, Life Sciences, and Natural Resources since 2024. Reeve’s four-year contract comes with an annual base salary of $500,000.
The Wyoming Union welcomes visitors to the University of Wyoming on Feb. 14, 2015, in Laramie. (Ryan Dorgan)
After taking the post July 1, one of his first actions was a proposal to revamp the leadership structure, which trustees approved. It creates a new position of executive vice president, which Reeves tapped former West Point colleague Kraig Sheetz to fill. Six administrators who previously reported to the president will now report to Sheetz. 
Reeves operates from a philosophy of focusing on the future and not getting mired in the past, he told WyoFile. In that sense, he is interested in exploiting what he sees as significant growth potential for UW. 
“My message is: I want us all to have a relentless pursuit of excellence in all parts of the institution, with a particular focus on growth,” he said. 
President Reeves sat down with WyoFile for a wide-ranging interview to discuss everything from growing the university’s enrollment to the role of free speech in college classrooms to the ways AI can be harnessed in post-secondary education. 
The conversation has been edited for length and clarity. 
WyoFile: You’re about a month into the new job. How’s it been so far?
Shane Reeves: Great. It’s been a bit of a whirlwind. I’ve been doing a big listening and learning tour, both internally and externally. I have started to work my way around the campus to talk to different parts of the enterprise to see what their concerns are, their interests, things they’re thinking through, but mostly focusing on what their perspective is on how we can grow and leverage the university to be successful in the future. And similarly, I’ve had some opportunities to get around the state. 
WyoFile: Regarding the campus discussions, are those with heads of departments?
Reeves: Yes. It might be the deans and whoever they want to bring to about a 90-minute to two-hour session. It’s really been a free-flowing conversation. They lay out some of the basics, like their organization, their structure, maybe their enrollment. I wanted them to tell me some of their challenges. I’ve asked them all to give me an idea of their vision for the university to grow, and then maybe three or four imperatives the institution should think about. But I’m also interested in talking to the faculty senate, the staff senate, the students, the [student government], the vice presidents, the vice provost, just trying to get out and hear it all.
WyoFile: What are some of the themes that are emerging?
Reeves: Well, the thing I’m taking away is excitement. That, and there’s some trepidation in terms of some recognized concerns about higher education in the United States. Some of those challenges are not insignificant. You have what’s called the birth dearth or the enrollment cliff, and that is of particular importance in the state of Wyoming, where we have almost an existential crisis with the number of young people in the state, and so you’re trying to grow the institution while you’re facing demographic headwinds. 
You also have some significant challenges in higher education when it comes to artificial intelligence and how AI is changing the model. You know, for 1,000 years or more, the university system has basically been the same. That dynamic is shifting quickly because AI has made it that information is easy to access and it’s cheap, and so it’s not as much about the transmission of information, but it’s how are you going to apply that information to be competitive in a quickly shifting global economic environment. 
Brayton Tolman, a UW mechanical engineering student from Torrington, uses a robotic arm June 16 at the Innovation Wyrkshop, the university makerspace with more than $1.4 million of 3D printers and other equipment. The space opened in 2019 as part of the new Engineering Education and Research Building. (Daniel Bendtsen)
And then there’s some cynicism about the value of education, particularly higher education. So there’s some of the concerns you hear. On the other hand, the University of Wyoming has great potential. It has a monopoly on higher education in the state of Wyoming. In a state of roughly 600,000 people, over 60,000 are alum, which means there’s a lot of passion and excitement and pride in the university. And there’s been some great efforts over the last few years to put the University of Wyoming on a really interesting trajectory. The accomplishment of becoming an R1 Research Institution is not insignificant. There’s only 187 in the entire country, and Wyoming has one of those, and that has the potential to do amazing things for the state of Wyoming.
WyoFile: University leaders announced a $15 million budget shortfall in May. Do you have a plan for addressing the shortfall?
Reeves: We do. There’s been a really robust and rigorous conversation on the shortfall, and that conversation has been taking place since before I arrived. But I do think it’s our responsibility as the institution to look at everything we’re doing. There’s nothing wrong with looking at what you’re doing, figure out where there’s redundancies, create efficiencies, try to figure out a way to address that. I think we’ll be able to respond to that deficit in a way that makes sense without diminishing the excellence.
One of the great powers of this new [leadership] structure is you can let the team work through this at the granular level. The first step and the way we’re pursuing this is you have this working group. They’re really getting in there; they’ve rolled up their sleeves and they’re talking to each other and they’ll come up with, here are the things to look at. And then when the time comes, we’ll sit down and we’ll make the hard decisions on where we’ll either reprioritize or find those efficiencies.
WyoFile: Concerns about First Amendment rights and free speech on college campuses have emerged nationally. Do you think that’s applicable to UW?
Reeves: It’s absolutely applicable. But I think that the university has done some really amazing work. President Seidel started an initiative on free inquiry, free expression and constructive dialogue. I think it was exactly right.
Intellectual discourse is a very traditional Wyoming value, right? We can talk about anything, and we can disagree and at the end of the day, we’re still neighbors. As a son of the state of Wyoming, I was brought up with a healthy level of cynicism from being told what to think or what to believe. I think that this effort to have real discussion, real discourse, to have students engaged in ideas is a real commitment to the free marketplace of ideas that is the very purpose of an institution of higher education. 
You go to college to obviously gain the ability to be employed, right? But you also come to college to become a better person, to become more sophisticated in your thinking, to engage in ideas and debate those ideas. I think this is something the University of Wyoming has a real opportunity to lead this nation in. 
This graph was included in a 2026 report called Blueprint for Reform Wyoming, which concluded that UW has administrative bloat. (James G. Martin Center)
WyoFile: In July, a report called Blueprint for Reform Wyoming concluded UW has administrative bloat and recommended eliminating low-enrollment programs, shrinking administrative functions and downsizing athletic activities. Are you aware of this report? 
Reeves: I’ve seen the report. I haven’t done enough assessment to be able to address all those things yet. I will say it may not take into account some of the unique aspects of being at the University of Wyoming. For example, almost every university in the country will now outsource, say, concessions. But why does the University of Wyoming not do that? Well, because there isn’t anybody in the vicinity of Laramie that you could outsource to, right? So let’s put it completely in context.
I do think it is important for any institution to consistently be looking at yourselves and how you can get better. Especially in big organizations, you do have situations where it’s time to sunset things, and you do need to grow things. 
You mentioned athletics. The front porch of an institution is athletics. And so much of the pride of this state runs through the Cowboys and Cowgirls. So much of the brand recognition for this state is through the emblem that you see at UW. If you want to grow, athletics really matter. A dynamic campus culture is also important. I’m stereotyping, but young people are connected but more isolated than ever. They want experience, they want to engage, they want social connection. They want a traditional campus environment where they’re walking around, they’re drinking coffee, they’re playing frisbee, they’re going to class. So a dynamic campus culture is a really important part of where my brain is. But also, unleashing innovation through some of the research efforts. And we really need to be a little bit more nimble and flexible when it comes to admissions and meeting students where they’re at and looking at non-traditional students.
University of Wyoming ROTC cadets run to the Colorado-Wyoming line to hand the Border War football game ball off to Colorado State University cadets who will run it to Fort Collins on Nov. 14, 2024. (Tennessee Watson/WyoFile)
WyoFile: Any other thoughts?
Reeves: At the end of the day, it’s important for the state of Wyoming that the University of Wyoming is a dynamic and growing and interesting institution. It’s already indispensable to our state, but I think it can be an institution of national importance.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ Supreme Court sides with Seaside Park in eminent domain case
description: New Jersey law does not require municipalities say in ordinances why they need land they seek to claim through eminent domain.
text:
New Jersey Supreme Court Justice Michael Noriega wrote Monday’s majority opinion backing Seaside Park in its attempt to seize a motel via eminent domain. (Photo by Mary Iuvone/New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey law does not require municipalities to say why they need land they seek to claim through eminent domain, the state’s Supreme Court said in a divided ruling Monday.
In a 6 to 1 decision, the justices ruled that towns are not required to state the public use that prompts them to claim property through eminent domain, resolving Seaside Park’s yearslong quest to claim the Desert Palm Inn, a motel it moved to condemn in April 2022.
“No law requires a municipality to articulate the intended public use in the ordinance itself,” Justice Michael Noriega wrote for the majority.
Shree Jyoti, the firm that owned the motel, had argued it could not be seized by eminent domain because Seaside Park did not specify why it needed the property when it passed an ordinance to take it. The borough said only that it would be put toward a public use.
Though town officials in legal filings later said they would turn the property into a parking lot — and yet later, a well — neither New Jersey’s Eminent Domain Act nor its Local Lands and Buildings Law require it to state the taking’s purpose in ordinance. They only require the municipality to pass an ordinance, the court ruled.
“The statute does not set forth any requirements for the ordinance beyond the need for its adoption — it is silent as to the contents of the ordinance,” Noriega wrote.
In his dissent, Justice John Hoffman said he would have blocked the acquisition because Seaside Park had violated the square corners doctrine, a judicial construction that effectively says government agencies must be forthright when dealing with the public.
In this case, forthrightness would have meant disclosing the proposed public use for the property as early as possible, wrote Hoffman, who agreed that state law does not require towns to state a public use in an ordinance approving an eminent domain seizure.
Seaside Park knew its plans for the property at least at least a month before it moved to claim it, according to court records, but declined to disclose that purpose to the motel’s owner upon request.
It only revealed the purpose the second time it sued to claim the property, some five months after the borough approved the ordinance to seize it. The borough’s first suit was dismissed because it did not state a public use, and this appeal flowed from the second.
“I cannot join an opinion that overlooks the Borough’s intentional lack of candid engagement,” Hoffman wrote. “By excusing such conduct, the majority degrades the ‘square corners’ doctrine that asks our public leaders to operate with a baseline level of honesty and integrity.”
The majority’s opinion did chide Seaside Park for its lack of candor, acknowledging “the borough has spent the last four years involved in a matter that likely could have been resolved by simply disclosing the intended public use at the earliest reasonable point.”
The court’s decision here is incongruous with a recent ruling that blocked Jackson’s use of eminent domain to claim land it attempted to swap with a developer for a different parcel, Hoffman noted. There, the court found Jackson failed to be forthright because its statements that the seized lands would be used for open space were false.
“If a municipality can be found to have failed to ‘turn square corners’ by offering a pretextual public purpose, it is unclear how, exactly, it can satisfy its obligation to act ‘forthrightly’ by refusing to disclose its known public purpose for the property in question when asked,” Hoffman wrote.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: In an uncertain job market, top economists offer advice for incoming NC college students
description: It’s move-in week for college students across North Carolina. And once students have gotten settled into their dorms, their attention will turn to getting the classes needed to fulfill their chosen major. But which career paths are a safe bet in 2026? U.S. employers cut 23,000 jobs in July. Job creation for May and June […]
text:
Students walking between classes on the University of North Carolina campus at Chapel Hill. (Photo: Getty Images/Will and Deni McIntyre It’s move-in week for college students across North Carolina. And once students have gotten settled into their dorms, their attention will turn to getting the classes needed to fulfill their chosen major. But which career paths are a safe bet in 2026?
U.S. employers cut 23,000 jobs in July. Job creation for May and June was also revised downwards, showing a combined loss of 103,000 positions.
A report by outplacement and executive coaching firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas found artificial intelligence remains the top reason for job cuts, accounting for almost 11,000 of the announced cuts last month. It’s the fifth straight month AI has been the leading explanation that employers have provided for eliminating jobs.
Gerald Cohen, chief economist at the Kenan Institute of Private Enterprise (Photo: Kenan-Flagler Business School)
“AI is shifting the labor market, it is not dismantling it,” writes Andy Challenger, chief revenue officer for Challenger, Gray & Christmas, in their latest report.
Technology, financial firms, and the government sector accounted for the most job losses in July.
Gerald Cohen, chief economist with the Kenan Institute of Private Enterprise, calls the latest employment data worrying.
Cohen said economists are actively debating whether AI is going to create massive job losses in certain fields – careers one would want to avoid – or if it will create new career pathways.
Careers projected to see major disruptions in the near future include marketing and public relations, customer service, technical writing, journalism and web development.
Cohen says ultimately, it may come down to how a person uses artificial intelligence to their advantage.
“If you’re a critical thinker, learn how to use AI and learn how to leverage it, [choose] whatever field that’s going to inspire you,” Cohen said in a call with reporters.
North Carolina State University economist Dr. Mike Walden said two or three years ago, he would absolutely have recommended a young person heading to college pursue a degree in technology. It’s a less safe bet these days.
NC State University economist Mike Walden (Photo: NC State University)
“Now that’s up in the air because of AI,” said Walden. “AI is a technology that can replace people.”
Walden believes that while it’s unclear to what extent that may happen, AI is more likely to change certain jobs than to eliminate them.
“There’s a part of decision making that only humans can do,” Walden said.
Walden told NC Newsline the uncertainty AI creates may help promote social sciences.
“Social sciences are fields where you rely on human interaction, being able to assess other people, being able to work with other people,” explained Walden. “That’s actually something that I would tell students going to college, and say, certainly look at technology, but don’t forget the social sciences. I think that may very well have a rebirth in the new economy that has AI.”
Walden said skilled trades are another area where AI can’t easily replace humans.
“I’m also a big promoter of skilled fields that maybe require just community college,” said Walden. “We need entrepreneurs, we need plumbers, we need electricians. That’s not what a lot of people think about when they go to college, but prospects for those jobs, I think, are very, very good.”
The good, the bad and the unknown: The future of AI in North Carolina

For those newly graduated or early career professionals who are still struggling to land a job, Cohen says it may not be AI’s fault.
“One of the reasons why the unemployment rate for folks with bachelor’s has been rising faster than the unemployment rate with folks without a bachelor’s degree is not because of AI, but because of the impact of remote work and the fact that it’s harder to gain [certain] skills from remote work, and it’s harder to learn from other workers when you’re remote,” said Cohen.
Cohen said he’s a big proponent of flexibility, but the truth is many employers are still grappling with managing and growing employees who aren’t on-site as the workplace continues to change.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Congressional Democrats launch probe of efforts to deport US military members and their families
authors: Jack Brook and Safiya Riddle, Associated Press
description: Army Staff Sgt. Alexis Jaramillo poses with a photo of his wife, Maisa Lopes Eliaser, a Brazilian national who is being detained by ICE, before visiting her at the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center in Basile, La., Sunday, Aug. 2, 2026.
text:
Congressional Democrats said they are investigating the Trump administration’s efforts to deport military service members and their families after The Associated Press found more than 50 active-duty troops’ spouses and parents have been detained by immigration authorities.
In a letter sent Sunday evening to the Department of Homeland Security, the Defense Department and the Department of Veterans Affairs, the Democrats said they will investigate whether the Pentagon and DHS are coordinating to deport military service members and their families.
Army Staff Sgt. Alexis Jaramillo shows photos of his wife, Maisa Lopes Eliaser, a Brazilian national who is detained by ICE, near the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center where she is currently held, in Basile, La., Sunday, Aug. 2, 2026.  Credit: AP Photo/Joseph Vidrine
“These efforts imperil military readiness, weaken service members’ morale, and betray America’s promises to the people who put their lives on the line for our nation,” according to the letter, which was signed by more than 60 lawmakers and provided to the AP.
The Pentagon declined to comment, stating it would “reply directly to the authors of the letter.”
DHS told the AP that it values service members’ contributions and “U.S. military service alone does not automatically grant lawful immigration status, or exempt aliens from the consequences of violating U.S. immigration laws.”
The VA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In their letter, the Democrats provided an extensive list of questions to the agencies. They said the apparent collaboration between DHS and the military to deport troops’ families “raises both ethical and legal concerns.”
“Donald Trump is breaking our country’s promises to service members by tearing apart dozens of military families who were promised immigration protections,” Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren said. “That’s just plain cruel, and it’s hurting our military readiness and morale.”
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., walks through the Capitol during votes in Washington, Thursday, July 16, 2026.   Credit: AP Photo/Allison Robbert
Warren’s office is leading the probe alongside Connecticut Sen. Richard Blumenthal, Illinois Sen. Tammy Duckworth and several House Democrats.
The AP investigation found President Donald Trump’s administration has rolled back protections for military families and departed from longstanding bipartisan consensus to carry out its mass deportation agenda. Service members have been forced to take leave of their duties, including delaying deployment, to care for their children after their spouses were detained.
The lawmakers pressed the administration on why military recruiters are still promoting immigration protections.
Citing the AP’s reporting, the lawmakers urged the Trump administration to restore policies that had previously shielded military service members’ families from immigration enforcement while allowing them to adjust their legal status.
“This report is appalling and shows the unbelievable cruelty at the center of the Trump immigration agenda,” said Blumenthal, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Committee on Veterans’ Affairs. “We will be demanding answers and accountability.”
The Republican chairs of the armed services and veterans’ affairs committees, Mississippi Sen. Roger Wicker and Kansas Sen. Jerry Moran, did not respond to requests for comment.
Sen. Roger Wicker, R-Miss., chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, walks to a closed-door briefing on the Iran war at the Capitol, March 10, 2026, in Washington. Credit: AP Photo/Jose Luis Magana
Last week, Trump established the Military Spouse Commission, chaired by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s wife, Jennifer Rauchet, to develop policies and recommendations for improving life for troops’ spouses.
“Military spouses are intrinsically linked to the good order, readiness, and retention of our military,” Trump stated in a letter published in the Federal Register on Aug. 6. “Their support and contributions to our Armed Forces are crucial to mission success.”
The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
The Defense Department said in a December letter to Democratic lawmakers, obtained by the AP, that it had not implemented any recent policy changes for noncitizen family members in the military and has not conducted analysis on how deportations impact troop readiness and morale.
Danitza James, president of Repatriate Our Patriots, an organization providing support to military families and veterans facing deportation, said troops are being betrayed.
“Our military service members are the ones that sign on the dotted line to go and defend our country and maybe not come back,” James said. “They trust our government to take care of their families, and they’re not doing that.”
___
Brook is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Veteran Republican lawmakers lose Tennessee House races
description: Two veteran Republican Tennessee lawmakers from East Tennessee lost re-election bids while a first-term Democratic state House legislator from Memphis fell in last week’s primary election. Rep. John Crawford, a 10-year legislator and chairman of the State and Local Government Committee from Sullivan County, was defeated by Jessica Means by a vote count of 4,[...]
text:
Rep. Dennis Powers, a Jacksboro Republican, lost the Republican primary on Aug. 6, 2026.  (Photo: John Partipilo/ Tennessee Lookout)Two veteran Republican Tennessee lawmakers from East Tennessee lost re-election bids while a first-term Democratic state House legislator from Memphis fell in last week’s primary election.
Rep. John Crawford, a 10-year legislator and chairman of the State and Local Government Committee from Sullivan County, was defeated by Jessica Means by a vote count of 4,021, 61%, to 2,574, 39%, in the House District 1 race, according to the Secretary of State’s unofficial count.
Means, a homeschool parent, captured the primary despite political attack ads claiming Democrats funded her campaign and accusing her of backing “higher taxes and open borders,” all of which she said was false, according to a news report. Means faces no Democratic opponent in November’s general election.
Rep. Dennis Powers, a 14-year legislator and chairman of the Private Acts Committee from Jacksboro, fell to Noah Smith, an airline pilot, by a wide margin, 8,034, 67%, to 3,963, 33%, in the House 36th District race. Smith has no opposition in the Democratic camp this fall.
Rep. Gabby Salinas, a former researcher at St. Jude Children’s Hospital, lost to Memphis entrepreneur Telisa Franklin 4,593, 55%, to 3,725, 45, after one term representing the 96th House District. Salinas, who barely lost to former state Sen. Brian Kelsey in 2018, was among a group of lawmakers who sued the state to prevent the Tennessee National Guard from being deployed as part of the Memphis Safe Task Force. The Supreme Court ruled that she and other plaintiffs didn’t have standing to file the suit.
First term state Rep.Gabby Salinas of Memphis lost a rematch with entrepreneur Telisa Franklin in the August 6 Democratic primary. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Franklin publishes “I Love My Community” magazine and operates CEO Academy for aspiring business people.
Republican Rep. Todd Warner of Chapel Hill was beaten soundly by state Sen. Brent Taylor in the Republican primary for a congressional seat but narrowly defeated Vincent Cuevas in the District 92 GOP primary. Warner, who collected 4,430 votes, 52%, to Cuevas’ 4,062, 48%, survived attacks connected to a quarry/lake operation on his Marshall County farm that ran into neighbors’ complaints.
In a tight Democratic primary for the House District 59 seat being vacated by Rep. Caleb Hemmer, retired Tennessee Highway Patrol Lt. Col. Mark Proctor squeaked by attorney and businesswoman Angie Lawless. Proctor collected 2,475 votes, 31.9%, to Lawless’ 2,397, 30.8%, Beth West’s 1,755, 22.6%, and Rick Ewing’s 1,135, 14.62%.
Proctor, who will face Republican Bill Hancock in the November general election, received a boost from the LGBTQ Victory Fund Federal PAC, which sent out mailers hammering Lawless for asking a federal judge to give a light sentence to former House aide Cade Cothren in his corruption trial. Cothren and former ex-House Speaker Glen Casada were convicted on multiple counts of honest services fraud and conspiracy in connection with a secretive political services firm but were pardoned by President Donald Trump.
Republican state Rep. Michele Reneau of Signal Mountain bested attorney Tony Hullender by 17 percentage points, 6,030 to 4,313, even though the Tennessee Chamber of Commerce endorsed the challenger. Reneau aligned herself with Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Healthy Again campaign. 
Reneau, who upset former House finance chair Patsy Hazlewood two years ago, passed legislation this year prohibiting certain dyes in school food programs but failed to pass a bill prohibiting public utilities from adding fluoride to water systems. She faces Democrat Paige Quirin in November.
In House District 80, where longtime Democratic Rep. Johnny Shaw is leaving the legislature, Andrea Bond Johnson won the nomination with nearly 50% over Bethany Miller and Shelia Godwin. She will go up against Republican Julian McTizic, mayor of Bolivar, in the November election.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi officials urge regular upkeep at high-hazard dams
authors: Morgan Gill, Roy Howard Community Journalism Center and Bibhas Pantha, RhCJC News
description: Lake Serene North Dam in Lamar County is classified as a high-hazard dam and is rated in fair condition. An emergency action plan has been prepared for the dam. State officials say aging infrastructure and downstream development continue to increase dam safety concerns across Mississippi.
text:
LAKE SERENE — As hurricane season enters its busiest stretch, state officials say routine inspections and maintenance by private dam owners are critical to reducing the risk of failures at Mississippi’s high-hazard dams. 
A high-hazard designation reflects the potential consequences of a dam failure — not the likelihood that one will occur. Mississippi has more than 6,800 dams, including 351 classified as high hazard.  
According to the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality’s 2025 annual report, Mississippi has 6,871 dams. Of those, 351 are classified as high hazard, 52 as significant hazard, 5,077 as low hazard and 1,391 remain unclassified. Credit: Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality
Matthew Iburg, with the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality’s Dam Safety Division, said 52 high-hazard dams are classified as being in unsatisfactory condition. Most have already been intentionally breached or placed under lake-level restrictions to reduce risk while repairs are completed. 
MDEQ Executive Director Chris Wells said each of the agency’s regional project managers is responsible for an average of 1,380 dams. 
“This is much higher than the national average of approximately 280 dams per employee as obtained from the Association of State Dam Safety Officials,” Wells said. 
Because MDEQ cannot inspect every dam frequently, he said owners’ routine inspections and maintenance are essential to identifying problems before they become emergencies. 
Owners of high- and significant-hazard dams are required to complete annual inspections and obtain a formal inspection from a Mississippi-licensed professional engineer every five years, Iburg said. MDEQ compares its findings with owner reports and provides guidance to help owners recognize potential problems. 
“They’re following a checklist, but they may not know what all the terminology is,” Iburg said. “We try to give them as much information as possible, so they understand what they’re looking for.” 
Inspectors routinely look for seepage, cracks, overgrown vegetation, animal burrows and spillway deficiencies that can weaken a dam. While many of Mississippi’s dams are decades old, Iburg said age alone is not the greatest concern. 
“Our dams are aging infrastructure,” he said. “The main reason for them becoming more hazardous is lack of maintenance.” 
That inspection process plays out every month at Lake Serene in Lamar County, where the homeowners association maintains five lakes, including two dams classified as high hazard. 
Jonathan Williams, president of the Lake Serene Homeowners Association, said the group conducts monthly inspections, documents potential problems and works with MDEQ before repairs begin. 
“Sometimes we find weak spots or spots that just need a little bit of attention,” Williams said. “Before we do any maintenance, we have to involve them.” 
A map highlights dam locations across southern Mississippi, including Greene, Lamar, Forrest and surrounding counties. Credit: National Inventory of Dams
Williams said the association submits reports describing proposed repairs and, if needed, MDEQ brings in outside engineers to evaluate the structure. 
Despite having two dams with a high-hazard classification, Williams said residents should not assume the dams are likely to fail. 
“It is very, very unlikely, if everyone is doing what they’re supposed to do, of a dam failure to that magnitude,” he said. 
Residents can use MDEQ’s online dam map to locate nearby dams and view flood maps showing areas that could be affected if a dam were to fail. 
Iburg said residents living downstream from high-hazard dams should stay informed during severe weather, monitor emergency alerts and know their evacuation routes. Every high-hazard dam is required to have an emergency action plan identifying areas that could be affected by a failure and outlining notification procedures for emergency responders and public officials.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Popular DROP program could be dropped for new public employees
description: Put this on the radar for 2027 legislative session: A business-backed advocacy group is recommending sweeping changes to a popular retirement option for Florida state workers that has been used to keep experienced employees on the job longer. Florida TaxWatch issued a report last week looking at what is called the Deferred Retirement Option Program […]
text:
Jeff Kottkamp, Florida TaxWatch executive vice president and general counsel, presents the annual budget turkey report on May 15, 2024. (Photo by Jackie Llanos/Florida Phoenix)Put this on the radar for 2027 legislative session: A business-backed advocacy group is recommending sweeping changes to a popular retirement option for Florida state workers that has been used to keep experienced employees on the job longer.
Florida TaxWatch issued a report last week looking at what is called the Deferred Retirement Option Program — a popular option for public employees who have maxed out their traditional retirement benefits but don’t want to quit their jobs.
Those who enroll in DROP can get a lump sum payment when they finally retire. The program — with nearly 31,000 people participating — does require those who join to retire within a few years, although legislators in 2023 extended the period to eight years for most employees and up to 10 years for some.



Quotation







Employer contributions to the Florida Retirement System are funded by state appropriations, school district budgets, county and municipal tax revenues, and university operating funds. When contribution rates rise, those increases translate into higher public expenditures, which can require higher taxes and fees or cuts to services.


– Florida TaxWatch President and CEO Jeff Kottkamp


But TaxWatch, best known for its annual review of what it considers wasteful budget projects called “turkeys,’ is questioning the cost of these most recent changes. The organization is recommending DROP either be closed off to public employees at some future date or limited to certain workers when there is a documented shortage such as teachers, law enforcement officers, or firefighters.
“Employer contributions to the Florida Retirement System are funded by state appropriations, school district budgets, county and municipal tax revenues, and university operating funds,” said Florida TaxWatch President and CEO Jeff Kottkamp. “When contribution rates rise, those increases translate into higher public expenditures, which can require higher taxes and fees or cuts to services.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Any push to restrain retirement benefits for public workers is likely to prove contentious even in a Republican-controlled Legislature.
Sen. Ed Hooper via Florida Senate
Since Republicans assumed control of state government, there have been multiple efforts to privatize or limit participation in Florida’s retirement programs for public employees. Over the years, the Florida Retirement System has been broadened to allow workers to choose a traditional pension plan or an “investment plan” that functions like private sector 401(k) retirement accounts.
But attempts to close off the traditional pension plan have witnessed fierce resistance. In 2011, it was then-Gov. Rick Scott who pushed to require public employees, including teachers, to start contributing to their pension plans. That sweeping legislation also made a whole slate of changes to retirement programs, including greatly reducing the amount of money guaranteed under DROP.
Legislators, however, have considered or even passed bills in recent years to expand retirement benefits. 
The 2023 bill (SB 7024) increased the guaranteed interest rate payments in the DROP program. This past year, the Legislature — at the prodding of outgoing Sen. Ed Hooper, the Senate budget chair — restored cost-of-living adjustments to retired special-risk employees including firefighters and law enforcement officers.

name: Alaska Beacon

The Alaska Public Offices Commission approved the final consent agreement July 28. Under the terms of the agreement, Stutes will pay a penalty of $2,643.50 and […]
text:
Then-Speaker of the House Louise Stutes, R-Kodiak, listens to a speech on Wednesday, May 18, 2022, during final debates on Alaska's state budget. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)Rep. Louise Stutes, R-Kodiak, will pay more than $2,000 to settle a series of campaign finance complaints filed by a former chair of the Alaska Republican Party in 2025.
The Alaska Public Offices Commission approved the final consent agreement July 28. Under the terms of the agreement, Stutes will pay a penalty of $2,643.50 and repay her campaign $13,869.44 to settle complaints regarding improper campaign finance reporting and improper campaign spending in the 2020, 2022 and 2024 elections.
Investigating the complaint by Randy Ruderich against Stutes, the commission said the Kodiak legislator responded promptly to requests for information, and that there was “nothing to indicate” that serious violations identified by Ruderich were “intentional or provided a personal benefit to the candidate.”
Stutes, who has represented Kodiak, Cordova and parts of the Gulf of Alaska coast since 2015, is running for state Senate this year, seeking to replace Sen. Gary Stevens, R-Kodiak. Two other Republicans are also running for the seat.
By phone, Stutes said Ruderich informed her about the complaint before he sent it to APOC, and she ended up being the one informing regulators about the issue. 
The issues were the result of innocent mistakes, and she’s actually grateful to Ruderich for pointing them out, she said. She’s no longer trying to keep her own campaign accounts and has hired a professional.
“What gave me the most satisfaction of all this was saying to Randy Ruderich, ‘I really appreciate you calling this to my attention because if you didn’t, I’d still be making those mistakes, and then it would be a great big mess.’”

title: Dordt University students study potential air quality impact on student success
description: Student researchers at Dordt University are working to uncover the intricacies of how air quality can impact student performance across the U.S. Daniel Garcia and Cameron Grimes, both incoming juniors at the Sioux Center private university, with support from faculty, have spent the summer combing public education and pollution data to explore how different p[...]
text:
Dordt University students Cameron Grimes, left, and Daniel Garcia spent this summer studying air quality in relation to schools. (Photo courtesy of Dordt University) Student researchers at Dordt University are working to uncover the intricacies of how air quality can impact student performance across the U.S.
Daniel Garcia and Cameron Grimes, both incoming juniors at the Sioux Center private university, with support from faculty, have spent the summer combing public education and pollution data to explore how different pollutants can influence test scores. While they’re still analyzing results, the pair said they’ve already seen interesting results about pollution and where schools tend to be built.
Associate economics professor Joshua Hollinger said the “question of air pollution and test scores” came from conversations with assistant professor of engineering Jonathan Gingrich, as well as the idea to include undergraduate students in the research.
“It’s one of those things that I think you learn by doing a lot,” Hollinger said. “It helps when you have good students that are willing just to try to figure things out.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Grimes, an economics major, analyzed a dataset from Stanford with test scores spanning the decade from 2009 to 2019 and other demographic data, as well as previous literature on this topic. Garcia, who’s studying for his bachelor’s degree in data science and computer science, focused on a database from the Center for Air, Climate and Energy Solutions to examine different pollutants.
An overarching goal of the project is to “quantify differences in pollution across districts across the country,” Hollinger said, and to “line that up with different disparities between groups.” Previous literature suggests that air pollution does have a negative impact on test scores and that groups like minority students and low-income students are more likely to go to school in areas with worse pollution.
“What we’re kind of trying to do with this is pull together all the data to describe this at a national level, and then try to eventually get at the question like how much of the differences in test scores that we see across more and less advantaged groups, how much of that might be potentially explained by different exposure to pollutants,” Hollinger said.
Using both fixed regression and two-way fixed effects models, Grimes said, the group found that across time, if a school district’s nitrogen dioxide levels increase then its test scores go down. However, the data seemed to show that school districts with higher nitrogen oxide levels in general test slightly higher, Hollinger said, which could be due to other variables.
One finding they didn’t expect to run into was just how many schools are located close to major roadways. Garcia said the team mapped out highways then plotted where schools sat in relation, and found that “a very high percentage of schools” sit within 250 meters of a highway — nearly 20%, Gingrich said in a news release.
A study from Florida correlates proximity to highways, as well as the wind’s direction, with test scores and sick days, Grimes said. That study found evidence of worse school attendance in schools located downwind of a highway.
While the work the Dordt researchers are completing won’t necessarily point to causal relationships between the factors they’ve focused on, Hollinger said the eventual goal is to “tie things more to some of the more causal research.” As for the students, their work right now is pointed at finishing their data analysis and getting a report completed and hopefully published.
“The overall goal is a journal published outside of Dordt,” Grimes said. “But we’re still trying to figure out again, like what are we truly understanding from the data, what does the data actually tell us, what does this differ from other research that’s done, and then where would this best fit for the wider public?”
Each of the researchers said they want to bring more awareness to this topic, and Hollinger said the bigger reason to study negative impacts from pollution is to “help us kind of weigh the costs and benefits of how we might mitigate that, especially when certain groups are much more negatively affected than others for historical reasons.” Examples he said included redlining and how cities were constructed with major roads going through certain areas.
“Personally, I had never heard that there was any sort of relationship between education and air pollution,” Garcia said. “So I guess … just adding that awareness to people, so that they’re conscious of where they go to school, or where they can build a school.”
As most students live near their schools as well, Hollinger said, an aspect of this issue they couldn’t show in the data but one that could provide more evidence to the need for fixing air quality more than just school location.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont Psychiatric Care Hospital cuts staff and beds despite pushback
description:
The Department of Mental Health says the cuts are due to declining census, though demand for psychiatric care is high in Vermont.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Psychiatric Care Hospital cuts staff and beds despite pushback.
text:
The Vermont Psychiatric Care Hospital in Berlin in Sept.2023. File photo by Natalie Williams/VTDigger

Vermont Psychiatric Care Hospital has cut three staff members and four of its patient beds, a decision that has inspired pushback from staff and some lawmakers.
The state-run hospital in Berlin is one of Vermont’s main facilities for acute inpatient mental health care.
The Vermont Department of Mental Health, which runs the facility and confirmed the job cuts, said that a declining patient census at VPCH over the last five years led them to bring the four beds offline and cut the three positions to align with what’s necessary. As a result, the hospital now has 21 beds.
The three staff members whose jobs ended in recent weeks were recovery services specialists, a broad support role on a patient’s treatment team that is not considered a direct care position. Only one of the four-people employed at VPCH in this position remains.
“The goal was to eliminate vacant positions whenever possible and focus on positions assigned to the unoccupied unit,” Matt Kostik, a spokesperson for the Vermont Department of Health, wrote in a written statement to VTDigger.
He said the hospital’s annual census data shared with VTDigger showed that “the system’s need for the highest acuity beds was being met,” though the state continued to staff the hospital for 25 beds — with a unit left empty. 
Yet data obtained by VTDigger complicates that claim. There is no period when the hospital opened all 25 beds, which Kostik said is due to them “not being used.” Still, the hospital’s census data show climbing demand at VPCH, with open beds at capacity. In 2022 and 2023, the hospital had a daily occupancy average of 16. By 2024 and 2025, that average climbed up to 20 — with four beds closed.
Two weeks ago, Kristen Schieman, an emergency department nurse at Central Vermont Medical Center, told VTDigger that patients can be forced to board in the emergency department for days on end, waiting for an inpatient bed such as those at the psychiatric hospital to open up. Vermont Psychiatric Care Hospital is one of six in the state that provides this type of inpatient psychiatric care.
A 2025 point-in-time snapshot report from the Vermont Association of Hospitals and Health Services found that, for the week of May 5, 2025, 20 patients across 10 Vermont hospitals were waiting in the emergency department for inpatient psychiatric care — eight of those patients were waiting for over 24 hours. 
“Is there a need? I would say absolutely,” Kathleen Kilbourne, a spokesperson for Vermont’s chapter of the National Alliance on Mental Illness, said of inpatient psychiatric care. She said she had understood the need for temporary bed closures at the hospital to be a response to a shortage of staff.
The department’s rationale struck Sen. Andrew Perchlik, D/P-Washington, as hard to believe given how much demand there is for inpatient mental health care in the state, he told VTDigger. The department had testified to the Senate Appropriations Committee, which Perchlik chairs, in March that it intended to balance its budget by eliminating only vacant positions, Perchlik said. The department has nearly 60 empty positions — 46 of them in the Vermont Psychiatric Care Hospital, according to data from the department. The hospital has an already high rate of annual staff turnover, at nearly 30%, per the same DMH data.
In a July 16 letter, Perchlik wrote to Mental Health Commissioner Emily Hawes urging her to stick to the plan she’d testified to or request a budget increase in order to fund the fired specialists. 
“Legislative oversight requires that the executive be forthright in their budgetary and policy plans,” he wrote. He requested that the department rescind the staffing reductions.
As of last week, the Department of Mental Health has not. 
“It’s troubling that the commissioner unequivocally and clearly said that these are going to be vacant positions,” said Steve Howard, the executive director of the Vermont State Employees’ Association, the union that represents the psych hospital staff. 
He and staff worry about the impact the cuts will have on patient care and remaining employees. More than 60 staff at VPCH have signed a petition urging the department to reconsider the firings. 
“These folks play a vital role in direct care, emotional support, in advocacy, in clinical observation and input. They play a unique role in helping people get better,” Howard said. “That’s going to shift to already-overburdened staff that are working there.”
