title: Idaho public housing authorities approach proposed work requirements with caution
description: Only one of Idaho’s public housing authorities has signed on to a U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development coalition to consider adding work requirements to its subsidized housing programs. Other authority leaders say they remain skeptical about the benefits of a work requirement.  Feds encourage public housing authorities to impose work rules, time[...]
text:
Many of Idaho's public housing authorities are still weighing the benefits of a proposed work requirement. (Abigail Gerstein/Idaho Capital Sun)Only one of Idaho’s public housing authorities has signed on to a U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development coalition to consider adding work requirements to its subsidized housing programs. Other authority leaders say they remain skeptical about the benefits of a work requirement. 
Feds encourage public housing authorities to impose work rules, time limits

The Work and Dignity Coalition was announced by HUD earlier this year in tandem with a proposed rule to allow independent housing authorities to enforce “work requirements, time limits, and supportive service frameworks for able-bodied, non-elderly adults receiving assistance.”
“Housing assistance was never meant to trap work-able individuals on government support their entire lives,” U.S. Secretary of Housing and Urban Development Scott Turner said in a press release. “Rather it should be a temporary foundation to launch into a life of self-sufficiency. Getting a paycheck is empowering, getting a welfare check is not.”
The proposed rule and the coalition signal a change in HUD’s approach to public housing assistance, focusing on proving self sufficiency.
 How would HUD’s proposal affect Idahoans?

While the leadership of many of Idaho’s housing authorities align with these goals, slashed operating budgets, increased administrative burden, and concerns around efficacy leave them circumspect about joining the coalition.
Sunny Shaw leads four different Idaho housing authorities, overseeing the work of Twin Falls, American Falls, Jerome and Buhl. Many of the programs she manages, which overwhelmingly serve disabled and elderly populations, would not see changes from a work requirement rule, she said. 
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“There’s 196 households that we serve in Twin Falls. 82% of those are elderly disabled, so that eliminates them. I have 34 households that are able-bodied by definition, and 83% of those are working. So it’s such a minor amount,” Shaw said. “I don’t generally see a population who is just choosing to be able-bodied and not working.”
One Idaho housing authority, however, sees opportunities to combat fraud in the system. In Pocatello, Housing Alliance and Community Partnerships joined the Work and Dignity Coalition this May. 
With a work requirement as part of the system, Executive Director Jared Magnum said, the government could have a better understanding of enrollees’ income. 
“If someone’s working under the table or they’re doing something on the side, it’s just unreported — that happens a lot,” Magnum said. “With the work requirements, it has to be a W-2 job, something the government’s going to be able to track.”
Magnum also praised the coalition’s consideration of time limits on housing vouchers, which provide government assistance to pay for housing in the private market.
“Someone could be on the voucher for 20 years, or 30 years, or 40 years, as long as they otherwise qualify,” Magnum said. “If you were doing two-year vouchers, you would probably be able to help a lot more people, because the only time that a new voucher is going to come available is if someone passes away or they lose the voucher. ”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Other Idaho housing authority officials are still weighing their options

The Southwestern Idaho Cooperative Housing Authority and Boise City/Ada County Housing Authorities have not made final decisions on joining the work and dignity coalition. 
Elisa Velasco, executive director of Southwestern Idaho Cooperative Housing Authority, expressed concern about extra work her staff might have to take on, without extra funding, should a work requirement be instated. 
Idaho leads the nation in housing growth. The data shows it’s still not enough.

“They’re only funding us at 86% of what we’re entitled to right now. So we’re not being paid anymore to do this,” Velasco said.
“So many of the targets set by this program are laudable and worthwhile, there remain some concerns,” said Deanna Watson, executive director at Boise City/Ada County Housing Authorities. “Too often employment does not pay a living wage, does not include benefits or paid time off so the loss and risks of losing assistance in a trade for precarious working conditions.”
Idaho’s largest housing authority, the Idaho Housing and Finance Association, has not joined the coalition. 
“Idaho Housing won’t make a decision about what, if anything, changes until the final rule is published,” IHFA spokesperson Jason Lantz said. 
In Pocatello, Magnum remains optimistic about the possibility of improving the public housing system. 
“It’s a monster to try to tackle something that big, and I applaud HUD for at least trying to do something,” he said.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: A voter guide to Alabama’s special primary elections
description: Voters in Alabama’s 1st, 2nd, 6th and 7th Congressional Districts will go to the polls Tuesday to vote in the state’s special primary election. Following a special session held by the Alabama Legislature, Gov. Kay Ivey called for a special primary election in those districts after a U.S. Supreme Court order allowed the state to […]
text:
A sign saying "Vote Here" is seen at the Dean Road Recreation Center in Auburn, Alabama, on May 19, 2026. Voters in Alabama's 1st, 2nd, 6th and 7th Congressional Districts will vote in special primaries on Tuesday. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector) 


 Key Points

Voters in Alabama will choose Republican and Democratic nominees in the Aug. 11 special primary election for the state’s 1st, 2nd, 6th and 7th congressional districts.
There is no runoff election meaning the candidate with the most votes will be the nominee on the ballot in the November general election. 
Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Tuesday.




Voters in Alabama’s 1st, 2nd, 6th and 7th Congressional Districts will go to the polls Tuesday to vote in the state’s special primary election.
Following a special session held by the Alabama Legislature, Gov. Kay Ivey called for a special primary election in those districts after a U.S. Supreme Court order allowed the state to use a 2023 Legislature-approved map instead of a court ordered one. The 2023 map, previously struck down for being racially discriminatory, had led to two Black representatives being elected at the same time, first in Alabama’s history.
Democratic candidates have been largely decided in every race except for 6th Congressional District.
Sample ballots for counties having an election can be found on the Alabama Secretary of State’s website. Alabama has open primaries meaning voters will be allowed to pull either a Republican or Democratic ballot at their polling location.
There will be no runoff in the election, meaning the candidate who gets the most votes on Tuesday will be the nominee.
Alabama’s 1st Congressional District
Voters who pull a Republican ballot in south Alabama centered around Mobile will choose between Jerry Carl, John Mills and Austin Sidwell. The redrawn district covers all of Mobile, Baldwin and Escambia counties and part of Covington County.
The seat is currently held by U.S. Rep. Barry Moore, R-Enterprise, who is the Republican nominee for the U.S. Senate seat being vacated by U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville, who is running for governor.
Carl was elected to serve as U.S. Rep. for Alabama’s 1st Congressional District in 2020 and he lost re-election to Moore in 2024 according to election results. He said last month he wants to preserve an underwater petrified forest by turning it into a national park to prevent companies from harvesting the timber and said voters should choose him because of his experience in Congress.
Three Republican candidates in AL-01 face fears of low turnout in August special primary

Mills said last month he was running in the special election because he didn’t like any of the candidates running to replace Moore. If elected, Mills said he would ensure election integrity, border security and “stop reckless spending.”
Sidwell told the Reflector last month he wants to control government spending and address issues with Social Security.
The winner of the election will face Democratic nominee Clyde Jones in November. No other Democratic candidate qualified for the race.
Campaign finances: According to Federal Elections Commission filings through July 22, Carl has raised $1.2 million and spent $865,000; Sidwell has raised $199,000 and spent $194,000; Mills has raised $18,000 and spent $15,000.
Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District
Voters in Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District, centered on the Wiregrass in southeastern Alabama, will choose between Republican candidates Hampton Harris, Christian Horn, Rhett Marques, David Matthews, Joshua McKee and James Richardson. The district covers the southeastern part of the state including Geneva, Houston, Montgomery and Macon counties and a portion of Covington County.
Horn said in a recent interview that his top priority is affordability.
“People want to be able to have policies that are going to be able to give them an opportunity to save money at home, to be able for seniors to be able to not have to make the choice between food and their pharmaceuticals,” he said.
Marques, a state representative, has touted his endorsement from President Donald Trump, mentioning it six times during a Republican Republican candidate forum in Eufaula last week. Marques said afterward that he wanted to run to “help President Trump pass his agenda and help the state move forward.”
One week before primary, AL-02 GOP candidates pitch platforms at Barbour County forum

According to his website, Marques wants to strengthen rural areas through investments in broadband and infrastructure to support healthcare, economic opportunity and education.
Richardson said during the forum his top priority is addressing veterans’ healthcare. Richardson served in the Marine Corps and lost his father, a veteran, to suicide after he was unable to get mental health resources at the VA hospital.
Harris said he wants to focus on restricting acess to abortions and said he would not raise taxes for Alabamians. Harris previously criticized Marques for his vote to increase the gas tax through the Rebuild Alabama Act of 2019. Prior to the vote, the gas tax had not been raised in the state since 1992, and the Business Council of Alabama and other organizations supported the measure to provide improvements to Alabama’s infrastructure. The bill passed by comfortable margins, with Democratic and Republican support. 
McKee said during the forum’s spur of the moment question and answer segment that he wanted to invest in communities to keep them sustainable.
Matthews, a former Trump appointee in the U.S. Department of Agriculture, said in an interview after the forum people should vote for him because he knows how D.C. policy works.
“Very rarely do people have the opportunity to elect somebody who understands how the executive branch works at a granular level,” he said. “I’ve dealt with infrastructure problems, and I’ve dealt with healthcare and housing and economic and business development, and I understand an aspect of governance that most people never get exposed to because usually people get elected into the legislative branch, and the way that they learn about the executive branch is through a superficial means.”
The winner of the primary will face U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Mobile, in the November general election. No other Democratic candidate qualified for the election.
2nd Congressional District: Marques has raised $1.3 million and spent $1.1 million; McKee has raised $521,000 and spent nearly $525,000; Harris has raised $246,000 and spent $82,000; Matthews has raised 48,000 and spent $36,000 and Richardson has raised $7,700 and spent $7,600. Horn has not reported any filings as of Friday afternoon.
Alabama’s 6th Congressional District
The 6th Congressional District in the southern Birmingham suburbs and central Alabama is the only district where both parties have contested primaries. The seat is solidly Republican. 
Republican voters will choose between U.S. Rep. Gary Palmer, R-Hoover, and challenger Case Dixon. Democratic voters will choose between Jacob Bouma-Sims, Ashtyn Kennedy, Maurice Mercer and Keith Pilkington.
Palmer, the 12-year incumbent for the district, said on his campaign website that he believes in religious freedom and supports repealing the Affordable Care Act in favor of a healthcare program that will “free-market, patient-centered solutions that increase competition, expand choice, and put individuals back in control of their health care decisions.”
Dixon, Palmer’s only GOP challenger and a first-time candidate, told the Reflector last month he wants to reduce the cost of living and address affordability.
Longtime U.S. Rep. Gary Palmer faces first-time candidate in August special primary

Pilkington initially qualified for the 6th Congressional District seat in January as the only Democratic candidate on the ballot. He said last month he qualified for the special election because of persisting issues with affordability and immigration. Pilkington said he would focus on creating affordable housing options.
Ashtyn Kennedy, a social media content creator, said she wanted to create a data center moratorium in Alabama and would support a federal data center moratorium bill sponsored by U.S. Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-New York, and Bernie Sanders, I-Vermont.
Mercer, a former Pelham City Councilman Maurice, said in a recent interview he wants to stop the current war in Iran.
“Whether that is working to see both sides peacefully stop the war, or just pulling the USA out. We have our sons and daughters over there, and right now, I think the American people still don’t know 100% why,” he said.
Bouma-Sims wants to address issues with Alabama Power by making an federal alternative program through a plan he calls the “Cahaba River Corporation.”
“It’s not a takeover of Alabama Power, it’s not abolishing Alabama Power with the swipe of a pen, it’s an alternative,” he said to the Reflector last month.
Four Democrats vie for central Alabama congressional seat in special primary election

Dixon and Mercer accused Palmer of breaking his term limit campaign promise. According to a 2023 report from Al.com, when Palmer initially ran for office, he pledged to only serve 10 years but changed his mind when he decided to seek reelection in 2024, saying God told him to run for another term.
The winners will move on to the November general election. 
Campaign finances: Dixon has raised $25,200 and spent $25,000; Palmer has raised $1 million and spent $946,000; Kennedy has raised nearly $10,000 and spent $9,300 and Mercer has raised $6,500 and spent $4,700. Pilkington and Bouma-Sims had not reported any filings as of Friday afternoon.
Alabama’s 7th Congressional District
Two Republican candidates, Ammie Akin and David Perry, are running to represent west Alabama in the 7th Congressional District.
Akin told the Reflector last month that she wanted to address crime and affordability in the district and create educational opportunities.
Two Republicans vie for 7th congressional district nomination in special August primary

“You can’t create opportunity without education. This is why I love education, because education opens the door for everything,” she said. 
Perry also said he wants to prioritize public safety in the district. According to a report from the Tuscaloosa Police Department, violent crime decreased from 2024 to 2025. 
The winner of the election will face Democratic nominee and current U.S. Rep. Terri Sewell, D-Birmingham, in November. No other Democratic candidate qualified for the election.
Campaign finances: Akin has raised $151,000 and spent $35,000. Perry had not reported any filings as of Friday afternoon.
When do polls open?
Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Tuesday.
Where do I find my polling place?
The Alabama Secretary of State’s website allows you to check voter registration and the location of your polling place. You can find it here.
What do I need to vote?
Voters must present a valid photo ID before voting. Valid forms of ID include: 

Alabama driver’s license (not expired or expired less than 60 days)
Alabama Law Enforcement Agency digital driver’s license
Alabama Non-Driver ID (not expired or expired less than 60 days)
Alabama Photo Voter ID card
State-issued ID (Alabama or any other state)
Federal-issued ID
U.S. Passport
Employee ID from the federal government; state of Alabama; county; municipality, board or other entity of Alabama
Student or employee ID from a public or private post-secondary educational institution in Alabama or other states (including colleges, universities, postgraduate technical and professional schools)
Digital student or employee ID from a public or private post-secondary educational institution in Alabama or other states (including colleges, universities, postgraduate technical and professional schools)
Military ID
Tribal ID

What happens after Tuesday?
Each nominee will face their counterpart in the general election on Nov. 3. Independent candidates have until election day to qualify.
When will we know the results?
When polling locations close at 7 p.m., local election offices will begin counting ballots and reporting results to their county probate offices. The Alabama Secretary of State’s office will post results as they become available Tuesday night.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Local governments in Colorado enact moratoriums on data center development
description: Amid a nationwide race to develop large data centers to drive the artificial intelligence boom, some local Colorado governments hit pause by enacting moratoriums to research what local regulations make sense. Public criticism concerns the environmental and health effects of data centers, especially hyperscale sites that provide massive computing power for co[...]
text:
Construction on a data center expansion at the QTS site in Aurora, Colorado is pictured on Aug. 6, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Amid a nationwide race to develop large data centers to drive the artificial intelligence boom, some local Colorado governments hit pause by enacting moratoriums to research what local regulations make sense.
Public criticism concerns the environmental and health effects of data centers, especially hyperscale sites that provide massive computing power for companies like Google and Amazon, and inaction from the state government.
“The pushback against data centers is only growing right now,” state Sen. Cathy Kipp, a Fort Collins Democrat who sponsored a data center regulatory bill this year, said.
“There is a place for data science in the world because we do so much online and we do so much with electronics and data,” she said. “But people are failing to recognize the environmental concerns and … how the whole massive expansion of the hyperscale (centers) seems to be being built in a financially unsustainable way. I don’t know if we can solve the problem before the bubble bursts.”
Data centers can range from a single room in a company’s office to millions of square feet. They house servers and data storage infrastructure and have been used for decades to keep websites online, process digital payments and enable streaming, among many other uses. Recently, data centers increasingly are built to train and run AI and cloud storage, a workload that requires a bigger footprint and significantly more energy and water. One federally-funded study found that data centers accounted for 4.4% of the country’s energy usage in 2023 and could triple by 2028. The seemingly-unchecked proliferation is causing concern across the country.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A recent Gallup poll found that about 70% of Americans oppose data center construction in their town. Respondents were concerned about centers’ energy and water use, which they fear could lead to higher utility bills. They also cited worries about diesel exhaust from generators and noise pollution, as the humming of cooling systems, generators and fans at some data centers can sometimes be heard for hundreds of feet.
Supporters and those in the data center industry contend that development creates short-term construction jobs and property tax revenue, and can set a city up as a technological hub.
The Colorado Legislature considered two bills during its regular session this year on data center regulations but did not pass either one. One would have required so-called large load data centers — with a peak electricity need greater than 30 megawatts — to seek renewable energy for its power consumption, as Colorado pursues its clean energy and environmental goals. A competing bill backed by industry would have offered sales tax exemptions for data centers, and also had a more permissive renewable energy component. Both bills died in the final days of session after negotiations for a compromise bill failed.
One hyperscale data center
New York is the only state to enact a broad data center moratorium. Tax incentives are much more common, with 38 states offering some kind of benefit to attract data center construction.
The sponsors of the Colorado bill that would have required renewable energy sources, Kipp and Democratic Rep. Kyle Brown, plan to bring data center legislation forward in 2027, but they aren’t yet sure what the provisions will be.
“I certainly respect each and every community to be able to determine what they think is best on this particular issue,” Brown said of Colorado cities enacting moratoriums. “I think what it also highlights is the need for some kind of floor from the state, right? Moratoriums only exist for a finite period of time, and then what do we do afterward?”
About a week after the legislative session wrapped up, Denver City Council voted unanimously, with strong community support, on a one-year moratorium on new data center development. Leaders said it was an opportunity to figure out what new regulations and zoning policies make sense for the city eventually to adopt.
“We aren’t the only council in the country that’s addressing this, but we are early among councils that are looking at what this means for communities across the country,” Council member Diana Romero Campbell said during a May 18 meeting. “I’m also grateful that we are not waiting for the state to decide what happens in Denver. We need to be able to decide how and what we want our community to look like.”



Quotation







This moratorium will allow us to think of equitable regulations that put our communities first.


– Serena Gonzales-Gutierrez, member of Denver City Council 


The ordinance created a working group to study variables like noise levels, air pollution, energy use and zoning. It did not stop any current data center operations or permitted construction, including the controversial new CoreSite multi-tenant project in the Globeville Elyria-Swansea neighborhood. About 50 data centers operate in Denver, Council member Serena Gonzales-Gutierrez said during the May 18 meeting. There are about 60 in the whole state.
“This moratorium will allow us to think of equitable regulations that put our communities first,” she said. “We are hopeful that our future regulations will preserve our water and energy resources, address climate concerns and protect our neighbors from any potential consequences that arise from the construction and use of data centers.”
A day later, Jefferson County extended its moratorium until March. County commissioners noted that “data center” does not have a clear definition in county zoning policy, and the closest definition is from almost 50 years ago. Like Denver, the county sees a moratorium as a way to allow time to develop and debate regulations.
“We know that there’s a lot of interest and demand right now, but I am glad we are taking the time to fully consider some of the significant impacts to both our public and private infrastructure, looking at what those demands would be on our electrical power, on our water supply, on our telecommunications networks and even on our transportation systems,” Commissioner Rachel Zenzinger said during that May 19 meeting.
Larimer County decided to extend its existing data center moratorium to February, and Boulder County enacted a six-month moratorium at the beginning of June. In July, Broomfield passed an 18-month moratorium on data centers that use 10 megawatts of power or more. Woodland Park and Monument, two cities in conservative counties, also voted for 18-month and six-month pauses, respectively.
“There’s a lot of information out there and there’s a lot of different definitions of data centers. We need to be thoughtful in how we do this so we don’t create an ordinance that limits businesses like the city or Walmart or Safeway from having a server room,” Woodland Park Council member Catharine Nakai said during a July 16 meeting.
In Longmont, the City Council specifically targeted hyperscale data centers, voting in June to cap data center energy usage at 5% of the region’s grid, or 100 megawatts. Hyperscale data centers are the enormous campuses typically used by tech giants to deliver AI and cloud services on a large scale. They have an enormous power draw. QTS, the largest data center operator in the world, has a hyperscale location in Aurora south of the Denver International Airport. It is the only hyperscale site in Colorado.
And in Lochbuie, a small town on the border of Adams and Weld counties near Brighton, leaders passed a moratorium that at five years is the longest in the state.
“Why not set a precedent across the state of Colorado that this is not something we’ll rush into, that we want to be thoughtful, that we want to give all of our residents time to let their voices be heard?” Mayor Jamie Jeffery said during a July 21 meeting.
Role in Colorado’s growing economy
Other areas of Colorado are allowing data centers, but with varying levels of regulation. In April, Weld County updated its zoning code to allow data centers with a power draw of less than 50 megawatts in industrial areas in unincorporated parts of the county. County commissioners a special review process that requires a public hearing. Windsor is also weighing code changes but the City Council has not voted on a proposal yet.
And in Colorado Springs, a data center for a California-based AI company is set for a final vote from the City Council after a tumultuous journey through preliminary approval and an appeal from opponents.
In a statement, Dan Diorio, the vice president of state policy for the Data Center Coalition, said the industry “plays a significant role in enabling Colorado’s growing 21st-century economy” by paying taxes and supporting “stable, high-paying careers.”
“Rather than enacting moratoriums which will discourage investment and send a signal to the industry that the locality is closed for business, the community and its local leaders should work with the industry and all stakeholders to establish reasonable regulatory frameworks that meet the needs of the area without deterring the industry and the benefits it can bring,” he said. “The data center industry will continue to work with Colorado residents, communities, and policymakers to support the responsible development of this critical infrastructure and ensure Colorado remains competitive in the modern economy.”

text:
This photo was generated using AI on August 9.
The University of Delaware Fightin’ Blue Hens kick-off their 2026-2027 season on September 3. Their first four games of the season will feature first-time matchups against non-conference opponents.
 
The start of August signifies the beginning of the end to another summer of fun and sun, but it also means the beginning of the College Football season is fast approaching. The Blue Hens will start their second Football Bowl Subdivision (FBS) season on September 3, against four non-conference opponents.
Here’s a look at what awaits the Fightin’ Blue Hens through the first four games of the season: 
Blue Hens vs Merrimack College, Sept. 3 @ Delaware Stadium, 7:00 p.m.
The Blue Hens’ begin their season with a matchup against the Merrimack Warriors of the Football Championship Subdivision (FCS). This is the first time the two programs will face-off. 
The Warriors finished last season with a 4-8 overall record and lost to both FBS opponents they played (Kent State and Kennesaw State). Merrimack’s four wins were all won at home and half of them were decided by less than a field goal.  
Junior quarterback Ayden Pereira led the team in rushing and passing last season, but departed the program in the winter deciding to transfer to Georgia State and join the FBS level. The program returns their third leading rusher from last season, DeMarcus McElroy, and their third leading receiver, Austin Palmer.
This is Merrimack’s ninth season as an FCS school. The Warriors moved up from Division II before the 2019 season and were in the same subdivision of collegiate football as the Blue Hens before Delaware made the jump from FCS to FBS before last season.
Blue Hens at Vanderbilt University, Sept. 12 @ FirstBank Stadium, 4:15 p.m. 
The Blue Hens will play their first of seven nationally televised games in the second week of their season taking on the Vanderbilt Commodores. 
The Commodores finished last season tied for the fifth spot in the Southeastern Conference (SEC) standings with a conference record of 6-2 and an overall record of 10-3. The offense ranked ninth in FBS in total yards per game and the defense was 47th in scoring defense. The team finished just outside the College Football Playoff picture and was the 15th ranked team in the final AP Top 25 poll. 
Their dynamic offense was led by Heisman runner-up Diego Pavia. Pavia finished the season with 3,539 passing yards, 862 rushing yards and 39 total touchdowns. Pavia departed for the NFL signing as undrafted free agent with the Baltimore Ravens following the 2026 NFL Draft. Pavia was one of eight Commodores to sign as undrafted free agents following the 2026 NFL Draft. Tight end Eli Stowers was the only Vanderbilt player drafted. He was selected in the second round by the Philadelphia Eagles. 
This season the Commodores will attempt to continue their success with a new man under center. Head coach Clark Lea hasn’t named the team’s starting quarterback yet, though the team returns veterans Blaze Berlowitz and Whit Muschamp who each appeared for the team last season. Both are competing with the program’s highest ranked commit, five-star freshman quarterback Jared Curtis, for the team’s starting position according to ESPN.
This is the first meeting between the two programs.
Blue Hens vs Coastal Carolina University, Sept. 19 @ Delaware Stadium at 11:30 a.m.
The Blue Hens are no stranger to the Coastal Carolina program despite having never played the Chanticleers throughout the program’s history. 
The Blue Hens welcomed two transfers from the Coastal Carolina program this offseason — tight end Josh Humes and wide receiver Bryson Graves — a year after bringing in a pair of Coastal Carolina players for the 2025-2026 season. Last season, wide receiver Kyre Duplessis and defensive back Keontae Jenkins helped the Blue Hens to a 7-6 record and a bowl game victory after transferring from Coastal Carolina. Duplessis was second on the team in catches and receiving yards.
(To read about some of the other UD transfer players joining the program this season click here.)
Coastal Carolina enters the season with a new look roster and new head coach after finishing last season with a 6-7 record. The Chanticleers hired former Missouri State head coach Ryan Beard during the winter and in his first recruiting class, Beard brought in over 50 new players to the Chanticleer roster, according to the team’s website. Beard’s Missouri State team ranked fourth in Conference USA for yards allowed and first in offensive passing efficiency in the program’s first FBS season last year.  
The Blue Hens and the Coastal Carolina Chanticleers will face off on the football field for the first time in either school’s history on September 19.
Blue Hens at University of Virginia, Sept. 26 @ Scott Stadium (No time announced)
Delaware’s final non-conference game requires a trip to Charlottesville, Virginia, for a matchup with the Atlantic Coast Conference (ACC) runner-ups from a year ago. 
Virginia enters this season following a record setting 2025-2026 season that ended with a 13-7 victory over Missouri in the TaxSlayer Gator Bowl. The Cavaliers finished with a program high 11 wins and finished regular season conference play in sole possession of first place for the first time in program history. Virginia finished the season 29th in the country in total offense and 20th in total defense.
The team added to their core of returning players with over 20 transfers, including former Missouri quarterback Beau Pribula. Pribula threw for over 1,900 yards and ran for 297 more in ten games for Missouri last season and will most likely be the Cavaliers’ starting quarterback following the graduation of 2025-2026 starter Chandler Morris.
This is the first matchup between the two programs.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: At CoreCivic, immigration crackdowns are good for business
description: Revenue grew more than 27% for private prison operator CoreCivic as the Tennessee company profited from contracts with Immigration and Customs Enforcement that support the Trump administration’s mass detention and deportation agenda, according to a shareholders’ report released last week.  Revenue from ICE, alone, increased more than 50% compared to the same[...]
text:
Brentwood, Tenn.-based CoreCivic reported a 27% revenue jump tied to contacts with Immigration and Customs Enforcement to operate detention facilities. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Revenue grew more than 27% for private prison operator CoreCivic as the Tennessee company profited from contracts with Immigration and Customs Enforcement that support the Trump administration’s mass detention and deportation agenda, according to a shareholders’ report released last week. 
Revenue from ICE, alone, increased more than 50% compared to the same three-month period last year as the company housed more immigrants and negotiated higher daily fees for detaining them at facilities across the country.  CoreCivic also contracts with states to operate prisons across the nation, including four in Tennessee.
CoreCivic’s profits are also linked to several lucrative real estate deals with the Department of Homeland Security to expand the federal government’s detention capacity. Since July the company has sold four lockups in California, Minnesota and Kansas to the federal government to house immigrant detainees. In total, it earned $2.2 billion from the sales. CoreCivic will continue to operate the same four detention facilities under new managment contracts with ICE. 
Among the immigrant detention centers CoreCivic operates is one in Mason, Tennessee. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
In last week’s earnings call, CEO Patrick Swindle expressed optimism about future deals with ICE. The company’s immigrant detainee population is on pace to rise – it has grown by nearly 18% since April. Swindle said the company is in negotiations to potentially sell more of its detention centers to the federal government. 
“The solutions we provide to our federal customers, including primarily ICE and the U.S Marshals Service continue to be a significant component of our business,” Swindle said. The company contracts with the U.S. Marshals Service to house federal prisoners.
CoreCivic is a longtime ICE contractor, but the size and scope of its contracts with federal immigration enforcement quickly ballooned after Congress last year approved of a $75 billion budget boost for ICE and a $64 billion increase for Customs and Border Patrol over the next four years. 
The Tennessee companies profiting from the Trump administration’s immigration agenda

The federal contracts are now responsible for more than half of the company’s overall revenue. 
The amped-up immigration detention and deportation policies of the Trump administration, which have controversially included detaining individuals with no criminal records in detention facilities far from home without access to bond hearings, has drawn condemnation from human rights groups.
“Private prison corporations have long profited off the harm and death of Black and brown bodies across the country,” said Lisa Sherman Luna, executive director of the Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition.
“Now, Trump’s mass detention and deportation machine is driving record profits into the pockets of billionaires while families are separated and Tennesseans struggle to put food on the table. Most Americans agree that the attacks on immigrants go too far,” she said.
Swindle, speaking on a public earning call last week, did not address those criticisms directly, but characterized the company’s detention operations as humane and efficient.
“We remain confident that the corrections and detention beds that we provide are the most humane, most efficient logistically, most compliant, most secure, readily available and provide the best value to the government,” Swindle told investors.
CoreCivic is not alone among Tennessee companies reaping windfalls from a federal immigration spending spree.
Tennessee companies have entered contracts to supply materials for a wall at the nation’s southern border, parkas for ICE agents, mylar blankets and underwear for immigrant detainees and tactical breaching equipment for ICE officers. 
With three months remaining until a new fiscal year begins Oct. 1, the total value of contracts between Tennessee companies and the federal immigration enforcement agencies is approaching $1.7 billion, a figure that does not include CoreCivic’s property transactions. In 2024, the total value of those contracts stood at $255 million, according to https://www.usaspending.gov/, a public repository of federal government contract information.

title: Medicaid Work Rule Leaves Homeless People in the Cold
description: MISSOULA, Mont. — Tywon Pugh has seizures that make it hard to find and keep a job. “They called me a ‘liability to the job site,’” Pugh said, recalling the words of his manager when a seizure cost him his last job at a fast-food restaurant in this western Montana city. text:
Izzy Kadrmas, a medical assistant at a clinic for people without stable housing in Missoula, Montana, tests Tywon Pugh’s blood oxygen saturation. Pugh has recurring seizures that make it hard to find a job, which worries him as Montana implements Medicaid work requirements. (Photo by Katheryn Houghton/KFF Health News)MISSOULA, Mont. — Tywon Pugh has seizures that make it hard to find and keep a job.
“They called me a ‘liability to the job site,’” Pugh said, recalling the words of his manager when a seizure cost him his last job at a fast-food restaurant in this western Montana city.
When the 46-year-old lost work in the past, his wife of 10 years covered their rent and he tended to their home until he found another job. But his wife died last year. Soon after, Pugh became homeless. His problem with alcohol became worse, which made managing his seizures more difficult.
“When she died, my whole base was depleted,” Pugh said.
Medicaid pays for the prescriptions that keep Pugh’s seizures at bay. The government-subsidized health coverage would also pay for an addiction treatment program that Pugh said he has tried to get into, but he was told there’s a waitlist.
Pugh’s goal has been to get healthy enough to work again. But he’s worried about being able to keep the Medicaid coverage he needs to get to that point.
Early embrace of new rules
In the spring, the federal government finalized regulations requiring millions of people who receive Medicaid benefits to prove they’re working, volunteering, or going to school to keep their coverage. States have until January to begin those checks. Montana, Arkansas, and Nebraska have already started implementing them.
The Trump administration’s federal work requirements exempt certain groups of people: those with disabilities, those older than 64, pregnant people and Native Americans, among others. To receive an exemption, anyone without a clear-cut qualification — such as through their age or disability status — will have to prove they’re too sick to work.
But the administration decided that being homeless isn’t a medical condition and can’t count as an automatic out from having to meet the new requirements. Many conservative policymakers support work requirements, and some states have attempted to implement such rules for years. At least four states — Montana, Arizona, Kentucky, and Utah — previously proposed policies that included homelessness as an exemption.
But federal officials have said that’s not allowed. In an email to KFF Health News, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services declined to provide a comment on the record. But the agency confirmed that states must stick to the federal government’s list of exemptions. Homelessness in the U.S. increased by 27% from 2013 to 2025, according to data from the Department of Housing and Urban Development. Last year, about 746,000 people were homeless.
Many, like Pugh, qualified for Medicaid, though the number of enrollees who are homeless is difficult to measure. In 2023, 55% of patients who received medical or behavioral health services through one of the nation’s roughly 300 Health Care for the Homeless programs were enrolled in Medicaid.
Jennifer Tolbert, deputy director of KFF’s Program on Medicaid and the Uninsured, said the federal regulations are a lot stricter than many states had expected, even those on board with work requirements. (KFF is a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News.)
“It took everyone by surprise,” Tolbert said.
“My Medicaid is still active, but when are they gonna cut that off from me? I can’t get employed,” says Tywon Pugh, who has recurring seizures and has been homeless in Missoula, Montana, since his wife’s death in 2025. The federal government does not exempt people who are homeless from Medicaid work requirements. (Katheryn Houghton/KFF Health News)
Mehmet Oz, who leads CMS, touted the regulations as a “path to prosperity” during a press conference in June.
“We need to get people to try to work,” Oz said. In June, 25 mostly Democratic-led states sued the Trump administration over the regulations, arguing the medical frailty standard would be too hard for enrollees to meet — and for states to assess. The work requirements are projected to increase the number of uninsured people nationwide by more than 5 million by 2034, according to the Congressional Budget Office.
Most states will begin to implement the Medicaid work requirements in January.
Montana plans to begin booting Medicaid enrollees from coverage this October if they can’t prove they’re in compliance with the work requirement.
“My Medicaid is still active, but when are they gonna cut that off from me?” Pugh said. “I can’t get employed. How am I supposed to survive?”
The differences between the states’ and federal government’s exemption lists don’t end with people who are homeless. In Montana, lawmakers also planned to excuse people fleeing domestic violence and caregivers of hospitalized family members — two other groups left off the federal exemption list.
“These are simply parties that, due to a number of conditions, cannot meet those requirements,” Republican state Rep. Ed Buttrey said in 2019 when the Montana Legislature passed its first Medicaid work requirement bill. Buttrey did not comment for this article.
Federal officials have said many people who are homeless could fall under another exemption, such as being too sick to work. But, like many states, Montana’s system to automatically conduct those checks through existing medical records isn’t ready, though health department spokesperson Jon Ebelt said it should be in place by October. Anyone not automatically exempted by the state would have 30 days to prove their case.
A possible exemption for health
Pugh might qualify for a pass due to his seizures. But getting to doctor appointments the past year has been hard for him.
The anniversary of his wife’s death just passed. Typically, Pugh has to find a new place to sleep outside each night. One night while camping, Pugh lost his wallet and important documents. And with the addiction treatment centers that accept Medicaid patients overbooked, Pugh has had to rely on willpower to avoid drinking.
Izzy Kadrmas, a medical assistant at Partnership Health Center’s Watershed Clinic in Missoula, Montana, prepares to take Tywon Pugh’s blood for testing. Partnership Health Center is one of roughly 1,400 health centers nationwide that receive federal funding to serve patients based on what they can afford. (Katheryn Houghton/KFF Health News)
“I’m taking it one day at a time,” he said.
A little over two hours north, in Kalispell, Dustin Goss, a case manager at a homeless shelter called Samaritan House, said Pugh’s experience reflects why he’s worried that people who qualify for an exemption will get tangled in bureaucratic tape.
“You can’t really worry about getting paperwork done when you don’t know where you’re eating today,” Goss said.
Cassidy Kipp, who heads Samaritan House, said once people find shelter and start to stabilize, they typically find work. But even then, meeting the new requirements can be challenging. Clients often start with temporary and informal jobs — such as cleaning out a storage unit — that don’t come with a pay stub, Kipp said.
Kaitlyn Bosshardt, a social worker at Partnership Health Center, a health clinic in Missoula, has seen more people priced out of longtime rentals as housing costs outpace people’s paychecks. Meanwhile, affordable housing and rental aid are limited.
Partnership Health is one of roughly 1,400 health centers nationwide that receive federal funding to serve patients based on what they can afford — meaning even those who lose Medicaid can receive care. But organizations representing health centers have said if too many patients lose the coverage, some clinics won’t be able to fill the financial hole.
Arkansas has begun a ‘soft launch’ of Medicaid work requirements. What does that mean?

The other problem is that these clinics generally don’t provide specialty care.
One day in June, as temperatures hovered around 90,  Pugh visited Watershed Navigation Center, a refuge run by Partnership for people without steady housing to have a meal or see a doctor. His doctor, Atarah Sidey, told Pugh that the neurology clinic that managed his seizures had dismissed him from their care after he missed three appointments.
She referred Pugh to the other neurologist in town and talked about trying to find treatment for his addiction.
“It’s just that if I don’t make the effort at changing, it ain’t gonna happen and I’m gonna end up found on the side of the road somewhere,” Pugh told Sidey.
“You got this, though, Tywon,” she responded as Pugh nodded his head. “You can do this.”
Pugh has connected with a social worker for help keeping his Medicaid. By late July, he was waiting for space to open at a Missoula addiction treatment center and waiting on responses from two job applications.
In the hard moments, Pugh imagines his wife telling him to stay calm, that things will get better.
“I just don’t wanna lose hope in the meantime,” he said.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Fertilizer from coal a key part of North Dakota critical minerals processing plans
description: North Dakota’s abundant supply of lignite coal has been touted as a domestic source for critical minerals needed in magnets and electronics. But research at the University of North Dakota shows the potential for another lignite byproduct — fertilizer.  UND has secured a contract with the U.S. Department of Energy to expand its critical mineral […]
text:
Dan Laudal, executive director and research professor with the University of North Dakota College of Engineering and Mines, provides a tour of the critical minerals research facility in Grand Forks on May 26, 2026, to Sen. Kevin Cramer, center, and Department of Defense official Michael Duffey. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor) North Dakota’s abundant supply of lignite coal has been touted as a domestic source for critical minerals needed in magnets and electronics. But research at the University of North Dakota shows the potential for another lignite byproduct — fertilizer. 
UND has secured a contract with the U.S. Department of Energy to expand its critical mineral refining to the first commercial-scale test site at the Falkirk coal mine near Underwood. 
Dan Laudal, executive director and research professor with the UND College of Engineering and Mines, in a presentation last month to legislators, said a key to making the pilot project work is its ability to make enough money so that it can survive beyond the five-year Department of Energy contract. 
Laudal said the $100 million project is estimated to have about $13 million a year in operating costs and potential for $14 million in revenue. About 87% of the revenue would come from fertilizer, according to his presentation. 
The fertilizer made while refining for critical minerals would be different from the nitrogen fertilizer made at Basin Electric Power Cooperative’s coal gasification plant near Beulah. 
University of North Dakota seeks to scale up critical mineral refining

The fertilizer made at Underwood would be made from the organic material in coal, extracting what is known as humic acid. It would be similar to extracting humic acid from leonardite, which is already being done in North Dakota and a handful of other sites around the United States. 
“There’s nothing new that we need to invent,” Laudal said. 
Leonardite Products in Williston is one of the places that makes humic acid.
Cherie Harms, president of Leonardite Products, describes leonardite as lignite that was exposed to water from glaciers thousands of years ago, creating a substance that has little value as a fuel but is rich in organic matter. 
She said the humic acid that comes from leonardite doesn’t really act as a fertilizer, but when mixed with other fertilizer products, those products are more effective. 
Her company digs up leonardite near Williston, refines it and sells the humic acid to fertilizer companies. She said it is especially valuable in areas where there is little existing organic fertilizer in the soil. 
“Farmers may not even know they are using a fertilizer with humates,” Harms said. 
Rep. Mike Brandenburg, R-Edgeley, took notice when Laudal mentioned fertilizer. Farmers like Brandenburg have seen fertilizer prices shoot up in recent years because of conflicts in other areas of the globe that supply fertilizer to the U.S. The U.S. war with Iran and the closing of the Strait of Hormuz has driven up costs this year. 
Brandenburg said North Dakota farmers pay a premium price for fertilizer compared to other states and needs in-state fertilizer production. 
“We’ve got to get it done,” Brandenburg said. 
Harms, who also is one of the founders of the Humic Products Trade Association, said the rising prices have driven up demand for humates from fertilizer suppliers in the U.S. 
It will be a few years before the Underwood site is able to help meet that demand. 
Laudal said the design phase would take about 15 months followed by two years of construction. 
Rare earth minerals seen as a rare opportunity in North Dakota

The Underwood pilot site would be about 10% the size of a full-scale facility. It would be owned by a company called Ore Spring Materials, created through a partnership with UND, North American Coal and others. 
Laudal said it would allow UND to test processes developed in Grand Forks at a scale large enough to prove it can work at a full-size facility.
UND has been working to finalize the contraction with the Department of Energy, but Laudal said he expects the contract to take effect in January.
Laudal in May provided a tour of UND’s critical minerals research facility in Grand Forks for U.S. Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., a Department of Defense official and others. 
That tour focused on the process UND has developed for removing critical minerals and rare earth elements from lignite coal before the coal is burned. The process yields high-value minerals in small quantities and a cleaner burning coal. 
Laudal said the many minerals found embedded with lignite coal are critical because of their importance to the economy and because they are at high risk to supply chair disruptions, with most of the refining done in other countries, primarily China. 
With the fertilizer product providing much of the revenue in the short term, it would help research and developments of the critical minerals aspect of the operation. 
He said developing an industry that can take advantage of North Dakota’s critical minerals is where the real value lies. 
“North Dakota has an opportunity to become a national leader in critical and strategic materials production and value-added manufacturing,” Laudal said.
Reach North Dakota Monitor deputy editor Jeff Beach at jbeach@northdakotamonitor.com

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas librarians grapple with enforcing book restriction law after court ruling
description: Arkansas library directors said they have several unanswered questions about how a 2023 state law restricting access to library materials will be enforced after a federal appeals court ruled that it can go into effect. The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals lifted the injunction on two sections of Act 372 on July 30 but […]
text:
(Catherine McQueen/Getty Images)Arkansas library directors said they have several unanswered questions about how a 2023 state law restricting access to library materials will be enforced after a federal appeals court ruled that it can go into effect.
The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals lifted the injunction on two sections of Act 372 on July 30 but the formal order for the ruling to take effect hasn’t been issued yet. 
The two sections create criminal liability for librarians who distribute content that some consider “obscene” or “harmful to minors,” and give city and county governing bodies the final say over library content.
Adam Webb, executive director of the Garland County Library and president of the Arkansas Library Association, said he hopes the appeals court’s mandate comes with clarity on how to enforce language that a lower court deemed unconstitutionally vague.
One section of Act 372 states that anyone who “furnishes, presents, provides, [or] makes available” an item that is “harmful to minors” can be charged with a Class A misdemeanor, punishable by a maximum prison sentence of one year. 
Appeals court allows Arkansas to enforce law restricting library materials

U.S. District Judge Timothy Brooks wrote in December 2024 that the law’s lack of specificity for terms like “furnishing” and “harmful” would create “burdens on public access to speech” that violate the First Amendment.
“We’re trying to figure out exactly what ‘harmful to minors’ would mean in the context of books when an 8-year-old can read a book, but we’re not sure if they understand all the concepts that could be in an adult fiction book,” said Webb, one of the 18 plaintiffs that challenged Act 372.
The plaintiffs’ lead attorney, John Adams, said in July that the legal team is “evaluating all available legal options, including further review by the courts.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Preemptive measures

The Independence County Library in Batesville announced July 31 via Facebook that it would no longer allow patrons under 18 to check out manga content — comic books and graphic novels that originate from Japan — and adult-oriented graphic novels.
Library staff are combing through the restricted materials to find ones without any sexually explicit images and allow anyone to check them out, library director Carlene Morrison said Wednesday. 
Parents can check out restricted materials for their children, but the library treats those materials “like an R-rated movie” now, Morrison said.
Morrison said Batesville library staff have been “putting stickers on” books with sexually explicit prose as a warning that minors can only access those books with parental permission.
The Independence County Library’s new policy is one of three options libraries face, said Nate Coulter, executive director of the Central Arkansas Library System and another plaintiff challenging Act 372. The other options are removing books from the library entirely or risking prosecution, he said.
Before Act 372 became law, Crawford County’s five library branches in 2023 placed LGBTQ+ children’s books in “social sections” in response to outcry from local conservatives. The “social sections” included green stickers marking the books as separate from the rest of the collection.

Crawford County libraries return segregated LGBTQ+ books to original sections after judge’s order

 

The plaintiffs against Act 372 claim that the approach by Crawford County, which is also a defendant in the case, “is exactly what will happen everywhere” under Act 372, Coulter said.
Crawford County lost a separate federal lawsuit in 2024 after three parents alleged that isolating LGBTQ+ books violated the First Amendment. A federal judge ordered the county library system to return the books to their original sections.
Morrison said she and her colleagues consider Act 372 “ridiculous” and have told concerned patrons the library would not restrict access to books without the law.
“I hope they overturn it [in court] again and we don’t have to jump through these hoops,” she said.
 Other potential impacts

Because Act 372 does not define how libraries “make available” their materials, Webb said requiring parental consent for minors to access books with adult content puts librarians in an awkward position.
“If a parent checks that book out and gives it to their minor child, do we as librarians have a duty to report that parent as having violated the law because the parent has made the material available to the child?” Webb said.
The law also applies to “anybody, even in your private home, who might want to give somebody else a book,” said Faulkner-Van Buren Regional Library executive director John McGraw.
Webb and McGraw said they are concerned about the impact on their library systems’ “little free libraries,” to which anyone can contribute. Since libraries are “providing the venue,” one could argue that they make materials available even if they’re stocked by members of the public, Webb said.
Coulter noted that the law could impede libraries’ ability to host story time for young children or civics classes for middle or high school students because they might be in the vicinity of books with sexual content. Civics classes help students get community service hours required under the LEARNS Act of 2023, one of Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders’ signature laws.
“What do I tell the parents who are happy that their kids will get some service credit hours to graduate by coming to the library?” Coulter said.
Arkansas Explained: Proposal aimed at restricting access to ‘sexually explicit’ library books

 Proposed library funding rules

The removal of the injunction on Act 372 comes as the Arkansas Department of Education has been considering new rules that hinge public libraries’ funding on ensuring patrons age 16 or younger cannot check out materials that depict or describe sexual contact and behavior.
The Arkansas State Library Board will meet Friday to consider sending the rules to a legislative panel for further approval. Sanders appointed all six board members.
Dozens of Arkansans told the education department in June that they oppose the draft rules. Library directors have said some libraries are too small, with many having only one room, to relocate certain materials so children can’t reach them.
Public libraries already had content challenge policies before Act 372. McGraw said any removal or relocation of a book should happen only “by policy and not because of hysteria.”
Coulter said he finds it frustrating that the state’s attempts to police library content imply that libraries and librarians are unsafe for children.
“Public librarians are not in the group that you should lie awake at night worrying about your kids [being around], and to raise up teachers and librarians as a threat to your children is a mind-boggling thing,” he said.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV Department of Human Services using $8M in TANF money to pay for broken online database
description: West Virginia is using nearly $8 million in federal anti-poverty dollars to pay for its long-troubled and broken online database system.
text:
The West Virginia Department of Human Services operates the PATH system, an online management system for programs in the state, including Medicaid and foster care. (Source: wvpath.wv.gov)West Virginia is using nearly $8 million in federal anti-poverty dollars to pay for its long-troubled and broken online database system.
It’s the same pot of federal funding — Temporary Assistance for Needy Families money — that Gov. Patrick Morrisey said is running out, prompting an abrupt closure in July of the school clothing allowance application window for low-income kids.
Del. Evan Worrell, R-Cabell. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
“I think the important question is not simply where TANF dollars are being spent, but whether those dollars are being used in a way that actually serves the families and children they were intended to help,” said Del. Evan Worrell, R-Cabell, who serves as House Health Chair.
“If funding that could support school clothing assistance is instead being directed to PATH, or there is a structural deficit in part, due to spending on PATH, that deserves a clear explanation,” he told West Virginia Watch.
The PATH system is a massive online management system used by the state Department of Human Services to manage critical programs, like Medicaid and the foster care system. It’s also how West Virginia residents apply for Medicaid and welfare programs and can report possible child abuse. 
The system, launched under Gov. Jim Justice, has cost the state nearly $400 million and still isn’t functioning properly, experiencing regular outages and hiccups processing needed data. The state is still investing new money into PATH, including TANF dollars, due to its necessity. Lawmakers recently allocated $7.4 million in the FY 2027 state budget for continued operation of the PATH system. 
West Virginia Department of Human Services Deputy Secretary Christina Mullins. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Speaking before lawmakers on Sunday, DoHS Deputy Secretary Christina Mullins couldn’t say how much the expected spend is on PATH this year. She declined to comment on TANF spending for PATH, saying that new DoHS Secretary Carl Ayers would answer those questions for lawmakers in a public meeting scheduled for Tuesday afternoon. 
Sen. Ben Queen, R-Harrison
“We have legislators here who are just frustrated, and I just hope that the department is willing to work with the Legislature and let us open up the hood to understand exactly where we’re where we’re missing the boat,” said Senate Majority Whip Ben Queen, R-Harrison.
PATH is used to process applications for the school clothing allowance program, which provides $200 to needy families to use for kids’ clothes. 
Morrisey has faced scrutiny after the program launched later than expected in July then closed its application in seven days due to running out of funding.
Mullins clarified to lawmakers that the agency received 52,000 applications but hasn’t yet processed all of those; the total number of children to receive the clothing allowance is unknown at this time.
Last year, 57,000 children received the school clothing voucher, costing the state around $11 million. 
West Virginia pays for the school clothing allowance program with TANF funding.
Morrisey has been reviewing the state’s use of those federal dollars after he announced a looming multi-million deficit in those funds. The review was linked to the delayed start of the school clothing allowance program. 
The state’s spending of TANF dollars has risen under Morrisey by his own documentation, though he has said increased use of those funds during the COVID-era led to projected funding shortfalls.
Morrisey recently shifted his focus to potential fraud in the school clothing voucher program, saying that some money is untraceable since parents can withdraw school clothing funds from an ATM machine. He has signaled possible changes to that program. 
DoHS looking to overhaul PATH, find new vendor 
The state contracted with Optum in 2017 for more than $300 million to build a new Integrated Eligibility System to manage its programs. A portion of the project was paid by federal dollars. The state’s contract with Optum goes through 2027.
“It really probably isn’t feasible to replace PATH … So, rather than pursuing full high-risk system replacement, DoHS views targeted system enhancements as the most practical path forward,”  Mullins said. 
DoHS is seeking a vendor on a $39 million, nine-year contract to take over the massive online system, but it won’t be an easy transition process.
“While a meaningful reduction in annual operating costs compared to the current name frame baseline is anticipated, specific cost figures and pricing structures will be finalized only after the competitive vendor bids are received and evaluated,” Mullins said. 
The state will not be able to move the information to a cloud storage system before the 2027 Optum contract expires, according to Mullins. A new contract is expected to be finalized by early next year.
The state has to currently spend more than $9 million for necessary improvements to PATH in order to implement the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” which will impact the online database. The federal bill mandates changes to several programs intertwined with PATH, including the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and Medicaid.
“We’re all frustrated. It’s not working for us, but we’re spending to the tune of $9 million dollars for modifications and enhancements on something we know isn’t working,” Worrell said. “I’m trying to understand why we would continue to invest and enhance something that isn’t working for us … I think we need to continue going down this path, pun intended, to try to understand what we’re spending.”
Mullins said that, in her opinion, fixing PATH should be the agency’s biggest priority.
“I crave data to be able to make better decisions,” Mullins said. “I think that what we can do and what we can realize, not just in money savings, but improving outcomes for kids and families, is really in that data.”
In recent audits, the Morrisey administration estimated the state could save $7.2 million by fixing the PATH system. The work to fix the system is expected to take one to five years, according to the DoHS audit.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: ‘Not too reassured’: WV lawmakers unimpressed by Flock rep’s answers to privacy concerns, more
description: As localities across West Virginia move forward with purchasing controversial surveillance equipment meant to assist law enforcement agencies, a representative for Flock Safety — the major contractor behind several of these agreements — presented to state lawmakers on Sunday in an attempt to answer questions about the company and its products.
text:
Kevin Kane, the director of Government Affairs for Flock Safety, presents to the Joint Standing Committee on Government Organization in House chambers on Sunday, Aug. 9, 2026 in Charleston, West Virginia. Lawmakers on the committee spent over an hour seeking clear information on how Flock — which is entering into contracts with localities and businesses across the state — functions. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)As localities across West Virginia move forward with purchasing controversial surveillance equipment meant to assist law enforcement agencies, a representative for Flock Safety — the major contractor behind several of these agreements — presented to state lawmakers on Sunday in an attempt to answer questions about the company and its products.
Overall, some lawmakers on the Joint Standing Committee on Government Organization were unimpressed with the few answers they received from Kevin Kane, the director of Government Affairs for Flock Safety. For over an hour, legislators asked Kane about how Flock functions — they wanted more insight into how the data collected by Flock technology is stored, who owns and has access to it, what security measures exist to protect it and how bad actors who misuse it are found, among numerous other things.
Del. Tristan Leavitt, R-Kanahwa
“To me, where the rubber meets the road on this is getting answers to specific questions about what the safeguards are,” said Del. Tristan Leavitt, R-Kanawha. “Based on the reporting that’s out there, there are a lot of questions and I was not too reassured about the answers we got today.”
Leavitt — along with more than 10 other legislators from the joint committee — grilled Kane on recent controversies circulating around Flock. They referred to investigations revealing that police across the country have misused the technology to stalk people unrelated to criminal investigations and a December incident where 60 Flock cameras in California were compromised, leaving public livestreams available for anyone to access and download from a 30 day period. They attempted to get clear answers on who actually owns the information collected by Flock’s system and what data exists to support the company’s assertions over the software’s accuracy.
Several of the questions were met with contradicting information and promises from Kane that he would follow up with their offices in private.
Sen. Patricia Rucker, R-Jefferson
“I’m glad they were willing to answer any and all questions, but I’m not totally certain that the answers were direct. There was definitely some talking around the direct answers,” said Sen. Patricia Rucker, R-Jefferson. “There was a little bit of skating around the questions instead of actually wanting to address directly what our concerns were.”
Kane asserted that Flock has “never been hacked” and the incident in Bakersfield, California, was due to “a bug” with the internet service provider. 
He said that Flock has implemented more protections, like an internal audit program, to flag questionable queries into collected data. 
Kane said that automatic license plate readers, or ALPRs, from the company only capture license plate numbers, and that the system operated with “about 99.99%” accuracy for flagging plates that are already on law enforcement’s radar due to information collected in investigations, like AMBER alerts or stolen vehicles. 
But that data — and several other assertions made by Kane — are only provable through internal surveys performed by Flock, not an independent source. In 2024, a police department in Roseville, California performed its own audit of Flock’s ALPR accuracy. They found that the Flock technology misread license plates in 71% of the alerts it sent to police.
Kane also said — numerous times — that “all of the data” collected by Flock’s systems are “100% owned” by the customers they serve, like law enforcement agencies, private businesses and home owners associations. But that data, he also said, is accessible to Flock corporate and pulled to help train the company’s AI models, as well as for any other use the company may have.
Del. Ryan Browning, R-Wayne
“Under your agreements, it grants Flock non‑exclusive, worldwide, perpetual, royalty‑free right and license during and after the term thereof to disclose the agency’s data, inclusive of any footage, to enable law enforcement monitoring against law enforcement,” said Del. Ryan Browning, R-Wayne. “I don’t think that sounds like it’s the citizens’ data when you have a perpetual right to access this data at any time.”
Kane, in response, said he understood this to be “quite standard language” for services like those provided by Flock.
That language, Browning said, is included in the contract that Huntington City Council recently entered into to install a $2.1 million Flock surveillance system, which will include ALPRs along with audio detection, live video cameras and drone services.
The five-year contract for the devices will cost Huntington $394,785 the first year and $438,220 per year thereafter, according to a resolution. The city will pay another $77,560 for two years for professional services with Flock. 
After Huntington faced backlash, leaders of some cities in the area have spoken out against the cameras, or reconsidered their agreements with the company. The Putnam County Commission reportedly purchased eight of the Flock cameras last year, but officials there said they wouldn’t be turned on. 
Community organizers in Huntington are collecting signatures in an effort to pass a city ordinance prohibiting mass surveillance systems that would require the city to void the contracts with Flock. 
West Virginia arm of the American Civil Liberties Union is suing Huntington in Cabell County Circuit Court, alleging the city neglected key procedural matters in awarding the Flock contract.
And while Sunday’s meeting — which also included a presentation from Alasdair Whitney, legislative counsel for the Institute for Justice, a libertarian legal group that has sued Flock and other surveillance companies over alleged civil liberty violations — was focused on ALPRs specifically, lawmakers said there is much more at stake.
“We know there are more than license plate readers being purchased — we’re seeing it (in West Virginia) already. There are cameras, drones, voice recorders, more. These things are all connected, and they’re all being marketed here,” Rucker said. “We can’t pretend that (ALPRs) are the only technology in front of us, and we need to be aware of the potential risks that all of these tools can bring when used together.”
Leavitt said limiting the conversation was a disservice to both lawmakers and the public.
“Giving only information about their license plate readers when people are asking about facial recognition — that’s not very helpful to policymakers who are trying to craft a policy that applies in every way,” Leavitt said. 
Rucker said she had concerns about how the technology sold and operated by Flock could violate residents’ rights under the Fourth Amendment. If a police officer needs a warrant to survey someone suspected of committing a crime, she posed, how is it constitutional for a camera or other technology — including automatic license plate readers, or ALPRs — to survey without that barrier?
Kane said that Flock “strongly encourages” governing bodies to implement “robust guardrails” to mitigate adverse outcomes of using the technology, including against people who may abuse access to it. He urged lawmakers to “not just rely on the practices” set forth by vendors like Flock.
And while Kane framed the services offered by Flock as a tool to improve “precision policing,” Whitney urged lawmakers to exercise caution regarding the use of the technology. Several courts are considering cases that could define how extensive evidence collected from Flock and other surveillance companies can be used. 
Whitney said that lawmakers in West Virginia and beyond, however, should not wait on the courts to implement their own “technology-neutral” safeguards to ensure that whatever surveillance technology is used, runs both ethically and legally.
He said that the Institute for Justice has created model legislation to help put these protections in place. That legislation would include language clarifying that a warrant is required, with limited exceptions, before law enforcement use ALPR data to track citizens. The legislation would also lock down data‑sharing across jurisdictions, letting West Virginia agencies refuse out‑of‑state or federal requests unless there’s a warrant or a clearly defined exception, and layer in basic auditing and transparency rules so lawmakers and the public can see how often and why the system is searched. 
Whitney stressed that his proposal doesn’t ban Flock’s cameras or other surveillance tools; it’s designed to set a floor of protections around “location information” before the technology spreads to “every street corner.”
Rucker, speaking after Sunday’s meeting, said that the Legislature’s discussions over Flock and other surveillance technology is just beginning. She said she understands that the technology offered by Flock can help law enforcement agencies — some of which are severely understaffed and overburdened — but there is a necessary balance that must be struck to ensure that residents don’t have their privacy violated.
“We can only use these things in good conscience if all the safeguards are in place and with the understanding that a search warrant is still necessary to track a citizen,” Rucker said
Leavitt said he looked forward to hearing more from Flock regarding the numerous questions he posed that Kane was unable to answer, but he also understands that Flock is a private company attempting to sell a product to governments of all sizes across the country.
“These are questions that have also been asked before other legislatures, and some other legislatures have been very unhappy with the candor they received … So now I think it’s very important to follow up, but at the end of the day, large companies pay government relations people a lot of money to do the job that they do, to provide information in a smooth way,” Leavitt said. “We could craft the best policy on earth, but without knowing the specifics of how their technology works, it would be irrelevant.”
Lori Kersey contributed to this report.
