Trahan said he’s worked with both Dunlap and LePage in Augusta. 
While in the state Legislature, Dunlap was the chair of the Inland Fisheries and Wildlife Committee, and Trahan said Dunlap was consistently strong on outdoor and firearm protections. 
And as governor, LePage was a “backstop” on Second Amendment issues, Trahan said. 
But the partisan nature of the issue will follow both candidates on the campaign trail. 
“For LePage, that makes it easy when your party is so strong on the Second Amendment,” Trahan said. “But for Matt Dunlap, it makes it far more difficult. I believe he’ll be strong on the Second Amendment, but I think, like Jared Golden, he’ll get beat up by his party.” 
Similar positions on both sides 
John Commerford, chair of the NRA Political Victory Fund, said Thursday that LePage has a strong record of opposing gun control measures. 
“And we need leaders in Congress who know what the Second Amendment is about and respect it,” he said. “They respect our true constitutional freedoms.”
LePage has held few media events and speeches so far in this race, and declined to speak directly with the Portland Press Herald last month for a Q&A on the race. But Thursday he made it clear that gun rights are a central issue of his campaign, and said the NRA endorsement is one of the most important endorsements he expects to receive.
LePage thanked the NRA for advocating for firearms, criticizing Democratic lawmakers for “putting out some silly laws every time we have a disaster,” like Maine’s red flag law, adding that “law enforcement is telling us it’s not a good idea, it’s not a good law, and but no one listens.”
“So we need to be vigilant, we need to have our guns,” he said. “I know this sounds crazy, but every year that Obama was president I bought a gun, I bought another gun, and I’m one that has a lot of guns. They’ve never been out of their kits.” 
Republican Paul LePage speaks at an Aug. 6 press conference at Maine Military Supply in Holden, where the NRA’s political arm announced its endorsement of the former governor in the race to replace Democratic U.S. Rep. Jared Golden. (Photo by Andrew Clark/ Maine Morning Star)
Both LePage and Commerford highlighted actions taken during his two terms as governor.
While in office, LePage vetoed several gun control bills, including a red flag proposal and a background check expansion. He also supported a 2018 measure that allowed Maine residents over 21 to carry concealed weapons without a permit. 
Commerford also emphasized that gun rights are about safety.  
“The Second Amendment is about that two a.m. glass break and providing for security of yourself, your family,” Commerford said. “It’s your personal safety. It’s your responsibility first. It’s about providing a hard check on our freedoms and restoring those.”
Two March reports from the U.S. Bureau of Justice Statistics found that crime continued to fall in 2024, according to crime data, which often lags months or years behind. 
The Bureau’s “Crime Known to Law Enforcement, 2024” report found that Maine’s rate of violent offense was significantly lower than the national average and had the lowest violent offense rate of any state that met the report’s statistical criteria. 
And preliminary data from the FBI in May reported that violent crime nationwide fell sharply in 2025. 
LePage acknowledged that Maine is “still a very safe, safe state” but said in the rural 2nd District, it can often take a long time for law enforcement to arrive, and in that window, access to guns is crucial.
But a May report from the nonprofit think tank Council on Criminal Justice found that Americans’ views on crime often don’t match reality, and those perceptions are instead shaped by personal experiences and economic conditions. 
The report draws on decades of Gallup survey data to examine how people perceive crime and what drives those beliefs, and found that even during periods when crime declined, people continued to believe it was rising. 
Dunlap has similarly said he is a longtime supporter of the Second Amendment and, if elected, would work to protect those rights in Congress. 
“It’s not surprising that a partisan group like the NRA endorsed a partisan like Paul LePage,” Dunlap campaign spokesperson Harry Burke said. “If Paul LePage ever wants to join Matt for a skeetshooting contest, we’d be happy to see who’s a better shot.”
And while Dunlap doesn’t seem to differ from LePage on the issue, he is quick to pivot to other issues. 
When asked about gun policy at a May primary debate, Dunlap said that most people in the 2nd District own guns and use them responsibly before turning to other reasons for violence.
“The guns haven’t changed, and they haven’t gotten easier to get, but we need to look at it’s causing people to snap and take something that was unthinkable and now it’s become almost inevitable,” Dunlap said. “We need to get to the origins of violence, and that’s going to take some work and some study.”
Even in that same short video reshared Thursday, Dunlap doesn’t dwell long on gun policy. 
“But also this fall we have a lot of other things to worry about — the cost of healthcare is skyrocketing, heating oil is almost doubled and we’re coming into another heating season soon,” Dunlap said. “And we have a Congress that doesn’t seem to think that is a very big deal. And that’s why I’m running for Congress, because I think we can do better than that.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: As Democrats elsewhere squabble among themselves, Kansas voters just want to win
description: For Kansas Democrats, winning isn’t everything. It’s the only thing. That’s the key to unlocking the results of Tuesday’s primary election, and it explains why Democrats in the Sunflower State have resisted the siren song of socialist and leftist candidates heard elsewhere across the nation this midterm cycle. Indeed, an out-and-proud communist candidate in[...]
text:
Adam Hamilton, pastor of the largest United Methodist Church in the country, announces his candidacy for U.S. Senate on April 30, 2026, in Prairie Village, Kansas. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)For Kansas Democrats, winning isn’t everything. It’s the only thing.
That’s the key to unlocking the results of Tuesday’s primary election, and it explains why Democrats in the Sunflower State have resisted the siren song of socialist and leftist candidates heard elsewhere across the nation this midterm cycle.
Indeed, an out-and-proud communist candidate in Lawrence lost his bid to unseat incumbent Democratic state Rep. Susan Wikle. She won 78%-22%. Sarah Preu challenged incumbent U.S. Rep. Sharice Davids over taking money from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee and funding U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement but was crushed in that primary, winning only 17% of the vote.
Democrats elsewhere might be consumed with anger at the party establishment and want to fight back at all costs.
Here in Kansas, they just want a shot at winning elections.


 Kansas Reflector video
Putting the judicial selection amendment aside, the two biggest races Tuesday were for governor and U.S. Senate respectively. In each case, Kansas Democrats prioritized electability. (I’ll pause for a moment here while Gov. Laura Kelly’s staff calms down.)
State Sen. Cindy Holscher prevailed over fellow state Sen. Ethan Corson not because of any great difference in political experience or ideology. Indeed, painting her as anything like the Democratic Socialists of America-affiliated candidates romping elsewhere in the country is laughably absurd. She’s a moderate Johnson County Democrat, just like Corson — and just like the third Democrat in the race, Overland Park Mayor Curt Skoog.
Yes, Senate President and GOP gubernatorial candidate Ty Masterson calls her extreme. He would have done the same to Corson or Skoog.
No, it came down to juice. I wrote about this about this in June, and Holscher simply ran a better race than Corson. I know both lawmakers from my time at the Statehouse, and both seem dedicated to their constituents. But Holscher branded herself as populist fighter, and that stance has broad appeal to Kansas Democrats, who have been dramatically outnumbered since the state began.
Over on the Senate side, you could witness more ruthless pragmatism. Adam Hamilton, the Methodist megachurch pastor, won the primary over 10 other Democrats. Many were exceptionally well qualified, and personable. One of them, Christy Davis, even wrote a couple of columns for Kansas Reflector before entering the political fray.
Hamilton proved himself a prodigious fundraiser and polished public presence. Given the bevy of opportunities that Democrats are pursuing across the nation this year, it seems unlikely that a Kansas Senate contest will warrant a lot of official party funds. That means financing falls to the candidate and associated groups.
Democrats picked him, based on all of the above. Subsequent race appraisals by professional prognosticators suggest that the party has put itself in a stronger position.
As has so often been the case in past decades, Kansas has set an example for the nation in this primary.
Popular, competent candidates who speak to genuine concerns of voters matter. Nothing else.
Forget the disputes between socialists and liberals and centrists. Forget the clawing for power between Democrats who once held power and those who want to hold power in the future.
This narrative entrances national political writers and opinion columnists. They will write hundreds of thousands of words on the subject, and because our great nation sees thousands of elections every year, they will find support for whatever take they plan to share. Or, like departing New York Times conservative columnist Ross Douthat, they will fling their arms in the air in confused exasperation.
He haughtily proclaims: “I find that I’ve lost my sense of which contemporary worldview is most in need of criticism or opposition, where the good guys and bad guys are. Each major faction seems potentially dangerous, tempted toward the dark side in some unique way, contested or cross-pressured to a degree that makes me uncertain where the side of the angels really lies.”
On the ground, at the state level, I can’t imagine anyone having such a challenge. Neither Democrats nor Republicans in Kansas seem critically “dangerous” to me right now. Not more or less than they ever were, at least. Each party has members with good ideas and bad ones, which can be implemented in good or bad ways.
And if you think that any side of politics gives safe haven to angels, try covering a campaign.
National Democrats will soon face a choice. Donald Trump will inevitably depart, and they will have to engage with a new coalition of supporters with a new generation of leaders. Those leaders may be leftists or liberals or centrists. Perhaps they will even be ever so slightly right of center. But to win popular votes in general elections, they must be sensible, levelheaded and willing to avoid the temptation of saying ludicrous things they will have to walk back in five to 10 years.
That doesn’t mean they have to be boring or cookie cutter. It does mean accepting the United States is a diverse country, both in population and beliefs. It does mean accepting the value of persuasion, rather than calling out or preaching. 
It ultimately accepting that the most direct way to achieve political change — left, right and center — is to win elections. 
Kansas Democrats have shown that they value people who can do so. Will other Democrats notice?
Clay Wirestone is Kansas Reflector opinion editor. His first book, “Opinionated: Kansas Journalists Who Proved Why Commentary Matters — Then and Now,” comes out Sept. 29 from the University Press of Kansas. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: As Madison grapples with police shooting, a dispute over who is in charge
description: While Madison attempts to respond to the police killing of Corey Ruiz on July 22, a dispute has emerged within city government over the authority of the city’s independent police monitor to subpoena materials related to the incident from the police department and the Wisconsin Department of Justice.  In the weeks since Ruiz was killed, […]
text:
Madison's east side responded to the police shooting of Corey Ruiz with a vigil Thursday evening. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)While Madison attempts to respond to the police killing of Corey Ruiz on July 22, a dispute has emerged within city government over the authority of the city’s independent police monitor to subpoena materials related to the incident from the police department and the Wisconsin Department of Justice. 
In the weeks since Ruiz was killed, the city has seen the occupation of a major intersection, standoffs with police as the city moved to reclaim the occupied area, a marathon common council meeting and continued tensions between elected officials and the people they’ve empowered to oversee the city’s cops. 
Aeiramique Glass, the city’s independent police monitor, has drawn criticism for getting into an altercation with police officers while they worked to clear the intersection of Williamson and South Baldwin Streets early Tuesday morning and later saying in a now-deleted video posted to social media that she would “burn this city down.” 
Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said “it’s disturbing anytime a city employee is calling for violence,” while reiterating the independence of Glass’ office. William Sulton, a Milwaukee-based civil rights attorney hired by Glass to represent the office, said she was making a “figurative, idiomatic expression.”
Glass’ position was established by the common council in 2020 as part of the city’s response to the widespread police reform protests that summer. The Office of the Independent Monitor and the Police Civilian Oversight Board were established and given independence from the mayor’s office and council. 
Madison is the only city in the state with such a civilian oversight system, and this is the first time the system has had to respond to a police killing, meaning that as the board and office work to investigate Ruiz’s death, they’re testing the limits of the ordinance granting them those powers for the first time. 
Within the ordinance establishing the OIM, the city gave the office complete access to MPD documents and the authority to issue subpoenas — so long as those provisions don’t conflict with other laws. 
“The OIM shall, to the extent permitted by law, have unfettered access to all MPD records, policies, Standard Operating Procedures, data, computer databases, and other information necessary to fulfill the duties of the OIM,” the ordinance states. “The Monitor may, to the extent permitted by law, issue subpoenas for the purpose of compelling testimony or receiving documents necessary to fulfill the duties of the OIM.”
Soon after Ruiz was killed, Glass opened her own investigation and issued a subpoena to the police department demanding all records related to the shooting be handed over to her office by July 31. 
However, under state law, when a police officer kills someone, the investigation must be conducted by an outside agency. In this case, the Wisconsin Department of Justice’s Division of Criminal Investigation is handling the review. DCI’s investigative report will be turned over to Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne, who will determine if the officer who killed Ruiz should be charged with a crime. 
Glass, members of the oversight board and activists in the community have argued that the ordinance establishing OIM granting “unfettered access” to police department materials and subpoena authority means that the department should hand over its materials related to the shooting — including dash cam videos, 911 call recordings, a list of officers on duty and communications with the chief of police. 
“We have a mandate and an ordinance that says we are to have unfettered access to all of MPD’s records, databases, video footage, everything,” Glass told the Examiner. “There’s no limit to what we are able to and should have access to.”
But the city attorney’s office, MPD and city officials say that limits on the office’s subpoena authority are set under state law. Once the independent investigation started, all of those materials, initially under the purview of the department, are now controlled by DOJ and state law prevents the release of evidence and materials pertaining to an open criminal investigation. 
Because DOJ is investigating a government employee, state law also prevents the release of “information relating to the current investigation of a possible criminal offense or possible misconduct connected with employment by an employee prior to disposition of the investigation.”
“I think the case is clearly made [that] we can’t interfere with a criminal investigation,” Madison Alder Tag Evers told the Examiner. “The concern is the release of that information could compromise the ongoing investigation and if it’s determined prosecution is warranted, complicate or interfere with the prosecution of a crime.”
DOJ’s work in these cases can often be slow and clash with the public’s demands for answers. The Examiner has previously reported on the flaws of the independent investigation system. 
 A spokesperson for DOJ did not respond to a request for comment.
The argument over the limits of the Madison independent monitor’s subpoena power have resulted in dueling FAQ pages on the city’s website in which the mayor’s office says it is limited in what can be released and Glass accuses the city attorney and mayor of helping the police department obstruct her investigation. 
This dispute was explicitly predicted when the common council drafted the ordinance in 2020. In a pair of memos to the council, City Attorney Michael Haas wrote that giving the independent monitor  subpoena power without explicitly outlining its limits could lead to legal challenges. 
“It is the opinion of our Office that the Council may enact an ordinance providing subpoena authority to the Independent Monitor,” the memo states. “Where there is no contrary statutory provision or contractual right, we would expect such subpoenas to be enforceable.  It is less clear that a subpoena issued in the course of an investigation, or in a case which could lead to a disciplinary decision by the Police Chief or PFC, would be held to be enforceable if challenged.” 
Haas’ memo also directly addresses the question of officer-involved shooting investigations. 
“It may also be useful to note that, under [the statute], all officer-involved shooting deaths are investigated in the first instance by an outside law enforcement agency rather than by MPD, and that the Monitor would not be entitled to participate in such investigations,” the memo states. 
At a meeting of the Police Civilian Oversight Board Executive Subcommittee on Wednesday, Haas and board members continued to debate the issue.
“People cannot deny that the words ‘to the extent permitted by law,’ are in the ordinances, and I think that has been consistently overlooked when people simply talk about unfettered access and subpoena authority,” said Haas, whose office is working to release an official opinion on the issue. “Those words were intentionally put in the ordinances, and that means we have to look to existing Wisconsin law.”
But members of the board and independent monitor staff suggested that Haas’ office should seek outside legal opinions on the matter and charged that the city attorney’s office has a conflict of interest in the matter. Glass has asserted several times that the ordinance’s grant of independence to her office means that the city attorney doesn’t represent the office — a claim that city officials also dispute. 
“There’s an inherent structural conflict of interest between city attorney offices and police oversight agencies,” the independent monitor’s data analyst Greg Gelembiuk said at the Wednesday meeting. “You can see this play out again and again and again across cities in the U.S. City attorney’s offices are very enmeshed with police departments, and of course, the mayor’s office. They have a primary role of risk management. Police oversight agencies have a primary role of investigating police, exposing the truth. Those roles are in conflict, and because of that, you have a universal pattern where you cannot rely on the opinions of the city attorney’s office to be accurate and valid.” 
Glass has hired an outside attorney, Milwaukee-based William Sulton, to represent the office, telling the Examiner that she has “the ability to take full legal action that is available to us.” Sulton did not respond to a request for comment. 
Glass has previously threatened to sue the city over the limits of her authority, a legal action that itself is in dispute because even though the ordinance grants the office independence, it is still a city department and a city can’t sue itself. 
“The basic law in Wisconsin is that one city agency cannot sue another city agency. City agencies are all part of the same organization and one arm cannot sue another arm,” Haas told the Madison alternative newspaper Isthmus during the previous episode. “City agencies have the authority delegated to them in the ordinances and cannot file lawsuits independent of the city.”

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: More data center proposals keep coming to Pennsylvania. So does the outcry.
description: The influx of users to the Facebook group reflects the surging discourse about data centers across the state, seen in grassroots social media groups, internet search traffic, and the flurry of bills sponsored by state lawmakers. It’s all in response to souring public opinion as new projects are proposed across the state.
text:
A sign opposing a data center project proposed for East Whiteland Township in Chester County on Saturday, May 9, 2026. (Photo by Peter Hall/Capital-Star)Ethan Young is a summer intern for the Pennsylvania Legislative Correspondents Association, and a rising senior at the University of Pennsylvania. 
In January, as her curiosity about data centers grew, longtime Pennsylvania environmental activist Karen Feridun turned to Facebook to create a group she hoped would allow those who felt similar to ask questions, too. 
Two months later, the group surpassed 500 members. And in the weeks that followed, the numbers continued to grow. During some weeks, more than 1,000 new people signed up. 
Today, the Pennsylvania Data Center Resistance Facebook group has more than 41,000 members. 
“It really took off in ways that shocked me,” Feridun said. “It’s clearly of interest to people in a way that I’ve never seen an issue be of interest.”
The influx of users to the Facebook group reflects the surging discourse about data centers across the state, seen in grassroots social media groups, internet search traffic, and the flurry of bills sponsored by state lawmakers. It’s all in response to souring public opinion as new projects are proposed across the state.
The Pennsylvania Data Center Resistance Facebook group. (Screenshot)
A Quinnipiac University poll of 895 Pennsylvania voters conducted last month found that 74% opposed having a data center built in their community while 16% said they supported it. Three-quarters of respondents said they were following news about AI data centers either very or somewhat closely. 
“The issue’s salience to Pennsylvania voters has seen a rapid increase over the last year,” said Chris Borick, a political science professor at Lehigh University. “Not only is it an issue that Pennsylvanians increasingly said is important to them, it’s an issue that they’re incredibly concerned about in terms of the impact on their lives.”  
That “meteoric” increase, as Borick noted, has altered the political landscape in the state. There’s no comparable environmental — or even general political issue — has transcended party lines like this, he added. 
The Pennsylvania Data Center Resistance Facebook group began to rapidly grow this past spring. Gov. Josh Shapiro announced Amazon’s $20 billion investment to build AI data center infrastructure across Pennsylvania in June. Around that same time, Pennsylvanians began searching for information about data centers more often. 
Google users from the commonwealth showed a growing interest in the search terms “data center” and “AI data center,” throughout 2025 until last month, according to data from Google Trends. It measures search interest relative to a term’s greatest popularity. The relative interest in both terms peaked in May.



Sarah Jackson, a professor of communications at the University of Pennsylvania, said she suspects more people are organizing around the issue not necessarily as a result of shifting public opinion, but because they are directly impacted.

“For many people they seemed a far away thing if they knew they existed at all. But the combined economic and political power of the tech and energy industries has increasingly expanded into people’s communities,” she wrote in a statement. 
Calls and messages to state legislators from constituents regarding data centers have also ballooned in recent months. 
Sen. Katie Muth, (D-Berks), said it’s the number one issue her office is hearing about. Her staff said the office has received 504 emails about data centers so far this year. An additional 182 emails referenced high electricity bills as a concern relating to data centers. 
And of the 807 calls her office has answered — encompassing 193 legislative issues — 72 have been about data centers. 
Sen. Katie Muth (D-Montgomery) pushes for a three-year moratorium on data centers on June 23, 2026. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Beth Rementer, a spokesperson for the House Democratic caucus, said that while the feedback expressed to different members varies, data center development has been among the top issues constituents contacted lawmakers about over the last six months. 

“Overall, people are strongly opposed to letting data centers operate without any regulation,” she added. 
Kate Flessner, a spokesperson for Senate Republicans said in a statement the perspectives of constituents are greatly beneficial to the work of the caucus. 

“The issue of data centers is certainly evolving and regional perspectives throughout the Commonwealth are differing and warrant careful examination,” she said.
Borick, the political science professor, said the number of data center bills introduced by lawmakers in recent months is a clear sign they are “absolutely following opinion and concerns.”
“I think in Pennsylvania among other places, legislators in many ways were caught off-guard on how the public would respond to the proliferation of data centers and data center proposals,” he added. 
During the current session of the General Assembly — which began in January 2025 and runs until November — lawmakers have introduced at least 30 bills aimed at regulating, or in some cases accelerating, data center development, according to a keyword search of the LegisScan database. 



Amid budget negotiations, lawmakers introduced eight proposals on the issue in May and eight more in June.
The legislation introduced encompassed a wide range of proposals, from a three-year statewide moratorium, sponsored by Muth to a bill sponsored by Sen. Greg Rothman (R-Cumberland) that, in its original form, would have expedited permitting and created a “regulatory sandbox” for data centers.
Information about the Pennsylvania Data Center Resistance Facebook group as of Aug. 7. 2026. (Screenshot)
Several data center regulation bills were advanced by the Democratic-controlled House — including the plan backed by Shapiro — and nearly every lawmaker supported efforts to repeal an existing sales and use tax exemption for data center equipment. 
Despite that consensus, the final $50.8 billion budget deal reached by lawmakers in July only included language requiring data centers with electric outputs larger than 10 megawatts to submit information annually about their energy and water usage.
“It’s hard for me to find an easy comparison point in terms of how it’s reordered things in the state in lots of ways — and so quickly,” Borick said of the politics surrounding data centers.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio U.S. Senate candidates offer contrasting visions for data centers
description: As data centers continue to grow both in numbers and unpopularity, the candidates in Ohio’s U.S. Senate race are calling for more oversight. While they offer contrasting visions for data centers, neither has embraced a full halt in construction desired by advocates. Incumbent Republican Ohio U.S. Sen. Jon Husted played a pivotal role in bringing […]
text:
Former U.S. Senator Sherrod Brown, left, and U.S. Senator Jon Husted, right. (Photos from WEWS)As data centers continue to grow both in numbers and unpopularity, the candidates in Ohio’s U.S. Senate race are calling for more oversight. While they offer contrasting visions for data centers, neither has embraced a full halt in construction desired by advocates.
Incumbent Republican Ohio U.S. Sen. Jon Husted played a pivotal role in bringing several billion-dollar data center projects to Ohio as lieutenant governor from 2019 to 2025. He backed tens of millions of dollars in tax breaks for past projects and consistently defends new data center development, arguing that they create construction jobs and broaden the tax base for rural communities.
“If you’re connected to a wire, you’re using the data center,” Husted said in a July 22 appearance on a conservative podcast. “So, understand that when we look in the mirror, we are the problem.”
Serious concerns raised over proliferation of Ohio data centers

Democratic nominee Sherrod Brown slammed Husted’s record of supporting tax breaks for data center developers in two July ads. In a third ad, he promised to make data centers pay the full cost of their electricity use.
He has also said companies should safely process water used to run data systems and that local communities deserve more transparency when making decisions about new projects. Brown has strong support from construction unions, including many that support data center projects because of the jobs they provide. Brown has called to end the data center tax breaks and says that local communities should have a say on whether to allow data center construction.
“Ohioans shouldn’t be forced to subsidize these costs and Ohioans — not Jon Husted and his billionaire friends — should get to decide if data centers are built in their community,” Brown said in a statement for this story.
Husted did not respond when asked to comment for this story.
One day after Brown’s ad was released, Husted introduced the Ratepayer Protection Act, a U.S. Senate bill that would ask states to consider measures to make data centers pay for their electricity usage. Husted has otherwise said the federal government should not get involved, calling data centers a “local issue.”
Husted and Brown are part of a laundry list of politicians — including President Donald Trump, Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, and both parties’ nominees to replace him — who have expressed support for “ratepayer protection” policies. The proposals are also backed by a major data center lobbying group and tech companies like Microsoft that own data centers.
Multiple experts said most of the power to lower utility bills lies with regional brokers and state commissions, and federal legislation would do little to move the needle. Even so, Case Western Reserve University energy policy professor Joshua Basseches said the symbolic unity on the issue is encouraging.
Ohio proposed constitutional amendment to ban data centers will not be on this year’s ballot

“There’s so much partisanship in this country right now that if this could be a bipartisan issue, I think that would be great,” he said.
A full 71% of Ohioans are in favor of a temporary ban, also known as a moratorium, on new data center construction, according to a Bowling Green State University poll.
The Libertarian candidate for governor, Don Kissick, has called for a moratorium. Republican governor candidate Vivek Ramaswamy said this week that if elected he wants to halt new projects until lawmakers require data centers to offer free electricity to nearby residents. Last month, Democratic candidate Dr. Amy Acton announced her support for a conditional moratorium on data centers if requirements on costs, union labor, transparency, environmental standards, community benefit agreements, and development are not met.
Austin Baurichter is a lawyer and volunteer for anti-data center advocacy group Conserve Ohio, which is gathering signatures to put a moratorium on data centers on the 2027 ballot. He compared Brown and Husted’s promises to regulate data centers to a politician handing an umbrella to someone drowning in a flood.
“Anything less than a full, 12-month moratorium on any advancement of any kind of a data center development falls short of what the people of this state are asking for,” he said.
Husted’s record on data centers
One month into Husted’s tenure as lieutenant governor, Google announced its first major data center in Ohio: a $600 million project in New Albany.
“Google investing in Ohio to open a new data center is great news for our state,” Husted said in a press release at the time. “Ohio is establishing itself as a premier destination for technology investment, and it further strengthens our case that Ohio is becoming the tech capital of the Midwest.”


The deal came with a reported 15-year, $43.5 million sales tax break from the state. Amazon got $81 million in state tax incentives for a data center in Hilliard in 2014, and Meta’s first data center in New Albany came with a 40-year, $37 million tax break in 2017.
The exemption on new equipment for large data centers flew under the radar when it was passed by the Ohio legislature in 2011.
Hyperscale data centers, or facilities that use more than 40 to 50 megawatts of power, were a small percentage of total data center electricity use at that time, according to an environmental advocacy group. Total electricity consumption across the U.S. grew at a slow 0.1% per year from 2005 to 2020.
A June 2023 press release by Husted touting a $7.8 billion investment by Amazon in the state cited a new use for data centers’ computing power: artificial intelligence.
The number of hyperscale data centers doubled worldwide between 2019 and 2024. Data centers could rise from accounting for 4% of total U.S. electricity consumption right now to 9% by 2030, according to projections by the Electric Power Research Institute.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Tech companies poured tens of billions of dollars into Ohio to build new data centers and expand existing campuses. That $600 million Google data center in 2019 has since ballooned into a project spanning sites in New Albany, Columbus, and Lancaster.
“Data centers are essential to our digital lives, and Google’s additional multibillion-dollar investment further establishes central Ohio as an important tech hub in America,” Husted said in June 2024 as Google announced another $2.3 billion investment in central Ohio.
His time as lieutenant governor ended when he was appointed to the U.S. Senate in January 2025, reducing his public appearances at data center groundbreakings and his say in Ohio’s tax code.
“If Ohio wants to be a leader, a leading edge tech state in the Midwest, having those kinds of investments in the state is important,” he said in an interview with Signal Ohio in 2025.
Signal Ohio later reported that the state lost out on $1.6 billion in taxes from data centers in 2025, more than 11 times what they expected. Gov. Mike DeWine has since paused applications for new tax exemptions for data centers.
Meanwhile, U.S. electricity consumption rose 1.7% per year from 2020 to 2026. The average Ohio electricity bill grew by more than 53% from June 2021 to June 2026, far more than the national average, according to the Electricity Price Hub from Heatmap and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
More Ohioans are getting their power shut off as energy costs surge

Brown’s record on data centers
Brown’s record on data centers started before Ohio had a sales tax exemption for them. As a first-term U.S. senator in 2010, Brown secured $2.8 million in funding for a Dayton-area research center to develop water cooling technology for large data centers.
Today, water cooling systems make large data centers more energy efficient, but they created another problem: A large data center can use up to five million gallons of water per day, according to a 2025 report by the Environmental and Energy Study Institute.
That water must be cooled before it is put back in the environment, Case Western Reserve University environmental law professor Victor Flatt explained, or it can affect local wildlife.
Brown acknowledged this in a June interview with Spectrum News, saying, “They’ve got to make sure that they process the water right and recirculate it.”
Brown did not specify any stance on environmental regulations for data centers in a statement for this story. As a congressman from 1993 to 2025, his only public statement on data centers was a press release welcoming Amazon Web Services to New Albany in 2015.
On the campaign trail 11 years later, Brown has repeatedly criticized the “out-of-control” tax breaks under Husted’s watch and labeled him “the face of data centers” in ads.
Would the Ratepayer Protection Act protect ratepayers?
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Both candidates promise to make data centers pay the full cost of their electricity usage.
The White House’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge, which asks data center developers to pay for their utility usage, received commitments from about 200 entities and endorsements from several sitting governors, including Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine.
A companion bill to Husted’s Ratepayer Protection Act passed out of the U.S. House Committee on Energy and Commerce by a unanimous vote in July.
Even so, experts say relief from the federal government in the near future is unlikely.
Public utilities are generally regulated by state commissions like the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio, consultant David M. Klaus said. Klaus worked in the U.S. Department of Energy under three Democratic administrations and wrote a report about the limits of federal action to regulate data centers’ utility bills.
Case Western energy policy professor Basseches said that this is why Congressional legislation like Husted’s Ratepayer Protection Act is narrow in scope.
“The federal government has never been involved in this way, certainly not in a legislative capacity,” Basseches said. “If this thing were to ever cross the finish line and become law, I expect there would be a lot of legal challenges and a lot of fights over authority between different states and the feds.”
PUCO allowed major utility provider AEP Ohio to treat data centers differently in 2025, but a June bill in the state legislature that would have extended the practice across the state didn’t reach the finish line before the legislature’s summer recess.
AEP Ohio says new data center tariff is working, critics aren’t buying it

Other concerns about data centers: the environment and transparency
More power demand from data centers means more power plants, Flatt said. PJM Interconnection, a regional broker that makes sure there is enough power supply to meet demand in Ohio and 12 other states, came up 6.8 gigawatts short in its most recent auction. It warned that data centers may face involuntary outages as a result.
Flatt said new plants in Ohio are likely to be powered by fossil fuels. A 10-gigawatt data center project in Piketon — expected to be the largest data center in the world — will be powered by a new $33.3 billion natural gas plant.
Husted has expressed support for fossil fuels and nuclear energy to power data centers since 2023. He has also criticized wind and solar energy, saying they are “inadequate” to meet increased demand.
In most places, Flatt said solar energy with battery power backup is the cheapest, easiest, fastest form of energy production to build and permit.
“But some states like Ohio and the federal government have put some roadblocks in front of developing solar and certainly in front of developing wind, which would be the second-cheapest,” he added. “That’s going to lead to increased air pollution.”
Chevron donated $200,000 to a super PAC supporting Husted’s election bid in June, and a super PAC that backs nuclear energy spent almost $75,000 on ads supporting him in the second quarter. He also has deep ties to Ohio’s utility lobby.
While Brown has not directly addressed the intersection of data centers and energy production, he consistently supported clean energy initiatives while in the Senate.
Both candidates have otherwise said they see data centers as a local issue. At a July 11 stop in Ironton, Brown said the approval process should be “a local decision with everyone knowing what is at stake.”
The failed June bill included a provision stating that public records requests can supersede nondisclosure agreements, a common tactic used by data center developers to keep plans secret.
While Husted backs data centers, Brown is silent on the prospect of a moratorium
Hyperscale data centers bring jobs to local communities, leading many prominent Ohio labor unions to support them.
Dorsey Hager, the executive secretary-treasurer of the Columbus-Central Ohio Building and Construction Trades Council, estimated in May that data centers make up at least 40% of work hours by union members.
The Ohio Building and Construction Trades Council endorsed Brown in March. The president of the Ohio AFL-CIO, another large union backing Brown’s election campaign, also defended data centers because of the jobs they create.
Democratic nominee for Ohio governor Amy Acton said she would not allow data centers into the state if they do not meet several requirements, including stipulations on union labor, environmental standards, and more. Brown did not respond to a question for this story asking for his reaction to the policy.
Andrew Gula, a volunteer who gathers signatures for Conserve Ohio’s proposed data center moratorium, said he hears a variety of opinions from people who work on building and powering AI data centers. Some have told him they feel like they’re helping automate others’ jobs, and for others, “it is what it is,” he said.
Baurichter, another volunteer for Conserve Ohio, lives in Higginsport, a small village on the Ohio River. He said support for data centers because of the jobs they create in rural Ohio reflects a “corporate-centric” mindset that puts people second.
The lack of support among top Ohio politicians for a moratorium has made him increasingly disillusioned with the political system, he said, adding that Conserve Ohio aims to “take things into our own hands” by collecting signatures for its 2027 ballot initiative.
Baurichter estimated that around 65% of Conserve Ohio’s members are conservative or voted for Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election. In Ohio’s U.S. Senate election this November, he said “any reasonable person” opposed to data centers would vote for the “lesser of two evils.”
“But that misses altogether that this is nothing but a perpetuation of the same dysfunction that this government has exhibited for decades, that people are waking up to,” he said.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Lawmakers say data loss is keeping hurricane-harmed Georgia farmers from insurance payments
description: Nearly two years after Hurricane Helene unleashed flooding and fierce winds across the South, some Georgia farmers say they still haven’t received compensation for damages, despite efforts from both sides of the political aisle. Newman Pryor remembers the night the storm hit. He runs Pryor farms, growing pecans and row crops across four east Georgia […]
text:
A tree-damaged house near Evans, Georgia as seen shortly after Hurricane Helene damaged the area in 2024. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderNearly two years after Hurricane Helene unleashed flooding and fierce winds across the South, some Georgia farmers say they still haven’t received compensation for damages, despite efforts from both sides of the political aisle.
Newman Pryor. Photo courtesy of Pryor Farms
Newman Pryor remembers the night the storm hit. He runs Pryor farms, growing pecans and row crops across four east Georgia counties: Screven, Effingham, Bulloch and Jenkins.
“It was much scarier than we anticipated it to be because they predicted it to go more to the west,” he said. “They were saying it was going to go to Atlanta, which would be well to the west of us, and it wasn’t going to be all that bad. I knew we were going to get some wind from it, but I didn’t think it was going to be nearly what we ended up with.”
Pryor said his operation, particularly his pecan trees, took heavy wind damage.
“It just destroyed the trees, tore them up, put a bunch of limbs on the ground, knocked down power lines and stuff like that,” he said. “We were not even able to process our pecans that year because it destroyed our electric infrastructure, so we couldn’t even process the pecans.We had to outsource that.”
Pryor Farms wasn’t unique. The hurricane created at least $5.5 billion in agricultural and timber losses, according to the University of Georgia.
But Pryor said he expected help from a type of federal hurricane insurance for wind damage to crops. It’s available for farmers to purchase from the U.S. Department of Agriculture on top of their underlying crop insurance policy. Farmers can get it in regions that experience hurricanes, including all of Georgia.
It’s supposed to be paid out if a farm’s county or an adjacent county is within the area of sustained hurricane-force winds – and not just wind gusts – from a named hurricane, based on data published by the National Hurricane Center.
“Our agent said, ‘Don’t worry, it’s coming.Your claim is good,’” Pryor said. “It never did.”
U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff’s office estimates up to 85 farmers could have missed out on indemnity payments they should have been eligible for.
Taylor Sills, executive director of the Georgia Cotton Commission, said the total unpaid amount could be as high as $10 million.
“There’s a lot of these rural communities and farms that are a long way from getting back, especially in some of these communities where that insurance product did not trigger a payment. We have been working on this issue from a lot of different angles and have unfortunately not been able to fix that quite yet,” he said.
‘We continue to work on it’
U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins speaks at NG Turf in Whitesburg, Georgia. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Speaking to reporters at a recent event on a North Georgia farm, U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said her agency is working on helping the farmers, but amending the program will ultimately require an act of Congress.
“I myself have been in probably half a dozen meetings on this trying to figure out how to, at least in the short term, make some changes, not to go against the current law, but is there anything we can do to help those farmers that were not able to access that particular program?” she said.
Rollins estimates up to two dozen Georgia farmers are facing this problem. She said she’s met with leaders from the National Ocean and Atmospheric Administration, which oversees the National Hurricane Center, and with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who oversees NOAA.
“We continue to work on it,” she said.
Bipartisan trio of Georgia lawmakers seek to change data source
Republican Congressman Buddy Carter at a Georgia Chamber event in Athens, Aug. 5, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Congressman Buddy Carter, a Pooler Republican, has introduced a resolution he hopes will protect farmers after future storms, but time is running short for the measure to move forward this year.
Co-sponsored by Georgia Congressmen Rick Allen, an Augusta Republican, and Sanford Bishop, an Albany Democrat, it seeks to allow the agriculture secretary to create an alternate dataset for insurance determinations if the standard one is incomplete.
Citing reports that Helene damaged some of NOAA’s systems, Carter said he blames damage from the storm for causing inaccurate wind data and leaving farmers in the lurch.
One NOAA document indicated that “widespread power outages caused nearly all automated observation sites to stop reporting so it is quite likely that the strongest winds that occurred were not recorded by any observation platforms.”
“The equipment was damaged during the storm, and that is still the information that came from that equipment that they have to use,” Carter said in an interview last week. “It shows the path of the hurricane going up through middle Georgia when we know it was more toward east Georgia. Those counties were impacted more, and they didn’t get the relief that they needed.”
The resolution has been referred to committee but it hasn’t seen any further action. Carter is not running for re-election following an unsuccessful bid for the U.S. Senate. His term ends Jan. 3, and so does the congressional term. The House is in recess until the end of August, and is scheduled to be out for much of the rest of the year.
Despite the short runway, Carter expressed confidence his bill would take off.
“It needs to get through,” he said. “We’re going to do everything we can. We’re going to sprint to the finish line, work as hard as we can to get it passed, and I’m very optimistic we’ve still got a good opportunity to get it passed.”
Ossoff presses for information
U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff at a rally for him and former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, who is running for governor, in Atlanta on May 31, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Ossoff, a Democrat who is up for re-election this year in a nationally watched race, has sought to pressure the USDA to re-examine the eligibility of farmers in 11 counties.
In a June letter to the agency, Ossoff cited a National Hurricane Center report describing wind gusts above the hurricane force threshold of 74 miles per hour in at least three counties – Towns, Chatham and Echols – and asked the agency to take another look at the data.
“Ensuring that our farmers receive the support they planned for and invested in is the very least USDA can do,” Ossoff wrote.
But in a July 20 response, USDA Under Secretary Richard Fordyce told Ossoff there was nothing the agency could do.
Fordyce wrote that the agency “acknowledges that gusts can be just as damaging as sustained winds,” but added that hurricanes, and the insurance policy, are defined by sustained winds and not gusts.
At the time, wind was considered “sustained” if it lasted for two minutes.
“I appreciate and understand the concerns of you and your constituents,” Fordyce added. “(The agency) went to great lengths to ensure all available data was incorporated into our review of the counties listed in your letter. Based on our review, producers in all counties eligible for payment under the HIP-WI endorsement have been paid.”
Last week, Ossoff followed up with the National Ocean and Atmospheric Administration and requested confirmation that all weather data was ultimately recovered and if there was data loss, how it was accounted for in determining wind speeds.
‘Just one more kick’
But until Congress changes the rules or a flaw in the data is revealed, the farmers will remain in limbo, and Pryor said people are beyond frustrated.
“It is an insurance policy that we bought and paid for, and then we’re denied for some bogus reason,” he said. “And there’s no reason why any person couldn’t see exactly where the hurricane went. You can see pictures from space where it took out the lighting, and it’s right on us. It’s obvious as anything that we got the hurricane.”
Pryor said it feels impossible to generate profit in the current economy, and the lack of hurricane payments feels like being kicked when you’re already down.
“We’re all slowly selling our farms right now. The farm economy is the worst I’ve ever seen,” he said. “This is just one more kick. It would really help if we could get it because of all the other things that we have going against us.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: New partnership brings college and career resources to Detroit neighborhoods
description: A new partnership in Detroit will provide middle schoolers through adult learners with access to resources designed to help residents enter and complete college, with hubs expected to open on the city’s east and west sides this fall. Graduate 313, a partnership between the Jamie and Denise Jacob Family Foundation and Detroit College Access Network, […]
text:
Kendra Agee, program Director, and LaTonia Gee, program manager for Graduate 313, assist students with college access support during Detroit Onsite Admissions Day. Photo by Lance Knight.A new partnership in Detroit will provide middle schoolers through adult learners with access to resources designed to help residents enter and complete college, with hubs expected to open on the city’s east and west sides this fall.
Graduate 313, a partnership between the Jamie and Denise Jacob Family Foundation and Detroit College Access Network, aims to expand educational opportunities for Detroiters in what organizers describe as a first-of-its-kind, neighborhood-based college and career success initiative backed by a $3.5 million investment.
After exhausting the model of supporting what most organizations refer to as a “college coach” that walks program participants through the college experience, the Jacob Family Foundation is supporting DCAN, which has worked to ensure equitable access to postsecondary education for Detroiters since 2012, as it launches Graduate 313.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The new model will deliver college and career resources directly within Detroit neighborhoods, Jacob Family Foundation Executive Director Megan Fenkell said, funding an initial three-year investment with additional help from partners including the General Motors Foundation and Rocket Community Fund.
“We wondered what would happen if there was a place in Detroit that students all the way from middle school to adult learners could go where they could get the support to get to and through college (or) return to college,” Fenkell said. “DCAN is the intermediary, and quite frankly, the leader in Detroit when it comes to all things college-going. So, it just seemed like the natural fit for us.”
Graduate 313 will launch this fall with a flagship office for Graduate 313 and DCAN programming on the city’s west side in a building located near the intersection of Plymouth and Evergreen roads. 
Graduate 313 will launch its programming in two physical locations this fall with a flagship office for Graduate 313 and DCANprogramming on the city’s west side in a building located near the intersection of Plymouth and Evergreen roads. (Submitted photo)
On the east side of the city, Graduate 313 will occupy space in the former Winans Academy of Performing Arts building as an “impact partner” within Anchor Detroit, a community hub developed by Life Remodeled.
After a year of advising, the initiative is now fully-staffed and will begin offering services inside physical buildings. Services will include one-on-one-advising, emergency grants, wraparound services and college field trips that will either allow Graduate 313 to connect with a school, nonprofit or out-of-school time partner to take students to college campuses in the area or bring colleges to their physical locations.
Along with resources, DCAN Senior Director of Community Hubs Jasmine Brooks said Graduate 313 is modeled to provide locations that are accessible by walking, car or city bus routes based on “asset mapping” that determined locations that would be most beneficial to Detroiters.
“As a native Detroiter, you don’t necessarily operate in silos, but residents that live on the west side, that’s where they kind of stay put,” she said. “Those that live on the east side or southwest Detroit usually stick to the neighborhood in the area where you’re most comfortable in.
“We want to change that trajectory by having these neighborhood hubs across the city, so that no matter where you live, you have somewhere in your neighborhood — in your backyard — where you’re able to go and access college access resources and an opportunity to then also persist and actually complete those credentials.”
Graduate 313 was launched with the intention of improving the City of Detroit’s access to and completion of college degrees. According to the U.S. Census Bureau, 18% of Detroit residents age 25 and older hold a bachelor’s degree. The initiative is aligned with helping boost that number toward Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s “Sixty by 30” goal of having 60% of working-age adults earn a postsecondary college degree or skill certificate by 2030.
MiSean Washington, program manager for Graduate 313, advises a student on next steps after applying to college during Detroit College Onsite Day. Photo by Lance Knight.
Graduate 313 will help address the challenges city residents young and old face by bringing resources closer to the communities that need them most, creating clearer pathways to college, career training and economic mobility, Brooks said.
Graduate 313 plans to measure success by tracking who’s coming through its doors, setting a goal of reaching 5,000 Detroit residents in its first year, Brooks said, with the intention of increasing that number year-over-year. This will be done by collecting data on who takes advantage of its services while assigning participants in the program to one of six advisors for high school, college and adult learners.
“We’re not only trying to connect them to credentialing and postsecondary planning, but we’re also trying to connect them to the resources that are preventing the barriers that they have right now,” Brooks said. “We want to help eliminate that. 
“So I think it’s a unique position to be in, where we’re not just concerned necessarily just with our numbers — like we’ve got to hit a certain amount of people — but we really want to make sure that we’re touching people so that they spread the word that, ‘Here’s genuinely a staff of people that are going to connect me across the city of Detroit to people in places that I may not have had access to if I had not been connected through Graduate 313 and the Detroit College Access Network.’”
While the Jacob Family Foundation is on board for a three-year funding commitment, Fenkell said the foundation and DCAN also are actively fundraising to continue the effort past the three-year grant.
The foundation believes giving residents access to support that will help them get to “day one” of college in a setting that isn’t intimidating with help from people who are embedded in the community will help remove the barriers that could be the deciding factor in whether they decide to continue toward the completion of a degree, she said.
“We know that the student counselor ratio at the high schools is extremely off balance,” she said. “It’s just challenging to get the support easily. (Graduate 313 provides) a wide range of support that you’re not necessarily able to easily seek out on all college campuses.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio’s 9th Congressional district race: The candidates’ records on data centers
description: The race for Ohio’s 9th U.S. Congressional district is one of the state’s most closely contested, and the candidates have contrasting records and positions when it comes to data center development. Derek Merrin, the Republican nominee and former state representative who is facing long-time Ohio Democratic U.S. Rep. Marcy Kaptur in the November election, vote[...]
text:
COLUMBUS, OH — JANUARY 03: Rep. Derek Merrin (R-Moclova Township) (center) during the Pledge of Allegiance at the opening day ceremonies of the 135th General Assembly of the State of Ohio, January 3, 2023, in the House Chamber at the Ohio Statehouse in Columbus, Ohio. (Photo by Graham Stokes for Ohio Capital Journal)The race for Ohio’s 9th U.S. Congressional district is one of the state’s most closely contested, and the candidates have contrasting records and positions when it comes to data center development.
Derek Merrin, the Republican nominee and former state representative who is facing long-time Ohio Democratic U.S. Rep. Marcy Kaptur in the November election, voted for Ohio’s data center tax breaks when he was an Ohio state representative in 2017. Kaptur has spoken out against data centers for draining power and water from local communities, saying the companies should pay for that, not the citizens.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Ohio’s data centers have received $2.5 billion in state and local tax incentives between 2017 and 2024, according to a 2025 report by SRC EvalMetrics on behalf of the Ohio Chamber of Commerce. 
Merrin, who served four terms as an Ohio state representative for the Toledo district from 2016 to 2024, did not respond to the Ohio Capital Journal’s questions for this story.
Merrin received a $1,000 political donation from the American Electric Power Ohio Committee for Responsible Government in 2021. AEP had received more than $6 million in data center tax breaks in Ohio as of September 2024, according to Policy Matters Ohio. 
Merrin received a $500 political donation from Windstream Holdings’ PAC in 2022. That same year, Windstream Holdings listed eight “key data center locations” in Ohio. 
One of the data center locations was operated by Cologix, which received more than $6 million in data center tax breaks as of September 2024, according to Policy Matters Ohio. 
Another one of Windstream’s Ohio data centers location was operated by CyrusOne, which received more than $5 million in data center break breaks as of September 2024, according to Policy Matters Ohio. 
Ohio has more than 200 data centers, the sixth-highest state in the country, according to Pew Research Center. Most of the data centers are in central Ohio. Cincinnati has 26 and Cleveland has 22, according to the Data Center Map. 
Ohioans are seeing increased electric bills. The average Ohio residential utility bills are projected to be about $800 for the summer — a 17% increase compared to last summer, according to a report by Third Way. 
Merrin lost a close race to Kaptur during the 2024 election and the Cook Political Report says Ohio’s 9th Congressional District race is a toss-up.
Kaptur raised concerns over data centers at the end of last year.
“How much more will our citizens be forced to pay for power and water?” Kaptur asked, speaking on the U.S. House floor. 
“They have a right to know. Will our building trades be true partners in economic growth or just temporary labor while facing higher utility bills at home? And how many permanent jobs will these largely opaque facilities actually provide? … The American people deserve to know how AI data centers will affect their communities.”
When the Ohio Capital Journal asked if Kaptur supports bringing more data centers to Ohio’s 9th Congressional District, Kaptur’s campaign spokesperson Kylie Blitzer responded.
U.S. Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-OH) (2nd L) speaks as Rep.-elect Andy Levin (D-MI) (L) and Rep. Tim Ryan (D-OH) (R) listen during a news conference on Capitol Hill in Washington, DC. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)
“Economic development should strengthen our communities, not drain their resources, and put added burdens on our people.
“If data center companies want to do business here, they should pay their fair share — not force hardworking people and local municipalities to subsidize billions in tax breaks for wealthy CEOs and shareholders who can easily afford to pay their own way,” Blitzer said in an email. 
Ohio Democratic candidate for governor Amy Acton recently announced she supports a conditional moratorium on data centers “if requirements on costs, union labor, transparency, environmental standards, community benefit agreements, and development are not met,” she said in a statement.
Ohio Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy’s data center plan is three-fold.
“If a data center is built in your community, then (1) you will no longer have to pay for your home’s electricity, (2) you will pay lower property taxes, and (3) the data center will be required to abide by all air and water quality standards without exception, and we will take the necessary steps to protect Ohio’s fertile farmland,” he said in a statement.
Neither candidate has laid out exactly how they intend to accomplish their promises, whether that be using the limited powers of the governor’s office or some combination of working with the legislature, data center operators, utilities, or utility regulators.
Lawmakers at the Ohio Statehouse have yet to pass any data center legislation. 
Conserve Ohio, the grassroots organization behind a proposed constitutional amendment to ban new data centers, are collecting signatures to make the 2027 ballot.

title: Launching the Somaliland Ohio Association: Building a stronger, more engaged community in Ohio
description: On July 18, 2026, Somaliland community members across Ohio gathered in Columbus to officially launch the Somaliland Ohio Association, marking a new chapter for a community that has spent years building connections, supporting families, and contributing to the state they call home. While the Association is newly established, the community behind it is not. Fo[...]
text:
Members of the Somaliland Ohio Association. (Photo provided.)On July 18, 2026, Somaliland community members across Ohio gathered in Columbus to officially launch the Somaliland Ohio Association, marking a new chapter for a community that has spent years building connections, supporting families, and contributing to the state they call home.
While the Association is newly established, the community behind it is not. For years, Somalilanders in Ohio have organized cultural events, supported families, celebrated heritage, encouraged youth, and created networks to help community members succeed. 
The launch creates a formal platform to expand that work and address the opportunities and challenges facing a growing community in Ohio.
As Ohio continues to grow and become more diverse, community-led organizations play an important role in helping families navigate the systems that impact their daily lives. 
The Somaliland Ohio Association aims to support community members in areas such as education, workforce development, entrepreneurship, civic participation, and access to resources.
Education remains one of the community’s most important priorities. Many immigrant families face challenges understanding school systems, accessing educational opportunities, and finding resources that help children succeed. 
By creating stronger networks between families, educators, and community leaders, the Association can help ensure that young people have the support they need to reach their full potential.
Small businesses are another important part of the Somaliland community’s contribution to Ohio. Like many immigrant communities, Somalilanders have built businesses, created jobs, and contributed to local economies. 
The Association can help aspiring entrepreneurs by connecting them with information about business resources, financial literacy, licensing requirements, and opportunities available throughout Ohio.
Workforce integration is also an important part of building stronger communities. Many Somalilanders in Ohio work in essential industries, pursue professional careers, and contribute to the state’s economy. 
Community organizations can help newcomers and established residents alike by providing connections, mentorship, and guidance that allow people to fully participate in Ohio’s workforce.
The launch of the Somaliland Ohio Association also represents an opportunity for greater civic engagement. A strong democracy depends on communities understanding how local and state government works and having a voice in decisions that affect their families. 
The Association aims to encourage community members to become more engaged with schools, local government, and civic institutions throughout Ohio.
The Somaliland community’s story is part of the larger American story of immigrants building stronger communities while preserving their heritage. 
Somalilanders have established communities in the United States for decades, contributing as professionals, entrepreneurs, workers, and citizens. In Ohio, they have become part of the state’s diverse fabric.
The official launch event brought together Somaliland elders, women, youth, community leaders, and guests from different backgrounds. 
The presence of community partners, including Columbus City Council Member Mark Sigrist, reflected the importance of collaboration between local institutions and the diverse communities that make Ohio stronger.
The Association’s leadership team — President Faysal M. Suubane, Vice President Mohamed Fu.ad, Chief External Relations Officer Ibraahim Mohammad, and Treasurer Abdisalam Burale — represents a commitment to service and creating opportunities for future generations.
The Somaliland Ohio Association is not only about preserving culture. It is about building pathways to opportunity, strengthening civic participation, and ensuring that every member of Ohio’s growing communities has the resources and support needed to succeed.
Ohio’s future depends on communities working together. When immigrant communities are empowered to participate fully in education, business, civic life, and public conversations, the entire state benefits.
