title: Trump announces $180M for mining education as administration recommits to coal
text: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump said Friday the federal government will fund $180 million in grants for mining schools across the county as part of his administration’s goal of rebuilding the U.S. coal industry. The grants will include $100 million from the Department of Energy spread across the 14 accredited mining schools in the U.S., while the Department of Defense will dedicate just over $80 million for three major schools of mining and metallurgy: the Colorado School of Mines, the South Dakota School of Mines and Johns Hopkins University. The Johns Hopkins University grant will help to create a new “multi-material recycling innovation hub,” while the South Dakota School of Mines’ funding will go toward establishing a consortium of workforce development programs alongside the University of Kentucky and Missouri S&T University.Trump framed the announcement as part of his ongoing effort to rebuild the U.S. coal industry and reopen mines, a central pillar of his energy policy. He has previously sought to shorten the regulation process for new mines and limit the impact of environmental regulations. Trump stressed the national importance of funding mining programs, given that other countries, such as China, graduate students at a far higher rate. Accredited mining programs at U.S. educational institutions graduate less than 170 mining engineers each year, he said, while China graduates more than 3,000 annually. “We're not doing you favors,” Trump told a crowd, including miners and many of the schools’ representatives, at a ceremony at the State Department building in Washington. “We're doing ourselves favors. We need your industry.”Half of the U.S. mining workforce is set to retire within the next three years, he added. “That's why my administration is making an unprecedented financial commitment to our nation's mining schools,” Trump said. “It's going to keep us nice and young and vibrant.”In addition to increasing support for mining education, Trump announced more than $2 billion worth of new mining contracts and projects. Those investments include $150 million for Minnesota-based Niron Magnetics to develop rare-earth-free magnets that are domestically produced to support the defense industrial base and $1.4 billion for Sila Nanotechnologies, a California-based firm, to “expand production of silicon-carbon battery anodes and build out a lithium-ion battery cell manufacturing facility to strengthen the supply chains of satellite operations, unmanned aerial systems, and munitions,” according to a White House fact sheet.Several of the speakers during the ceremony Friday, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, highlighted the national security benefits of increasing U.S. mine production. “At the core of this is our industrial strength,” Rubio said. “But also our national sovereignty — that we never depend on other countries for things we need to prosper and to defend ourselves as a people.”

text:
Democratic nominee Dan Ahlers, left, will face Republican nominee Gov. Larry Rhoden in the Nov. 3 general election. (South Dakota Searchlight photos by Joshua Haiar and Makenzie Huber)Two debates between South Dakota’s candidates for governor will take place in September.
The first will be at the South Dakota State Fair in Huron during the fair Sept. 2-7, with the time and date of the debate yet to be confirmed. 
The second is scheduled for 8 p.m. Central, 7 p.m. Mountain on Sept. 28, and will take place at the South Dakota Public Broadcasting studio in Sioux Falls, in partnership with South Dakota News Watch.
Podcast: Rhoden’s victory, a quote that doomed Doeden, and a Democrat’s ‘uphill battle’

Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden won the nomination to be his party’s candidate after finishing second in a four-way primary on June 2, and then defeating Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden in a July 28 runoff.
The general election will take place on Nov. 3. 
Rhoden is seeking to be elected governor for the first time. The former lieutenant governor assumed the governorship in January of 2025, when then-Gov. Kristi Noem took a job with President Donald Trump’s administration. 
Rhoden is running with his lieutenant governor, Tony Venhuizen. 
Democrat Dan Ahlers, a former lawmaker from Dell Rapids, has yet to announce a running mate, but told South Dakota Searchlight on Friday he expects to reveal his pick “very shortly.”
In a press release announcing Rhoden’s intention to participate in the two debates, Venhuizen preemptively challenged Ahlers’ running mate to a debate.
Ahlers, who said he’d accepted the invitations for the two debates, said his running mate is prepared to debate Venhuizen.

title: UTA proposes an increase to a $3 base fare. But first, it wants to hear from Utahns
description: After 13 years of paying $2.50 to ride a local Utah Transit Authority bus or train, commuters may see a fare increase to $3 next year. But first, UTA officials say they want to  hear their feedback. “This would help offset the increased costs that have happened over 13 years,” said Gavin Gustafson, senior public […]
text:
A UTA Trax train travels through Salt Lake City on Thursday, April 18, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)After 13 years of paying $2.50 to ride a local Utah Transit Authority bus or train, commuters may see a fare increase to $3 next year. But first, UTA officials say they want to  hear their feedback.
“This would help offset the increased costs that have happened over 13 years,” said Gavin Gustafson, senior public information officer at UTA. “I can’t think of anything that hasn’t gone up over the past 13 years, and so it helps to offset the cost of, say, operating maintenance and expanding the transit service as well.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The fare increase is something the authority has held off for as long as possible, Gustafson said. However, the costs to keep the service running has gone substantially up in the last decade.
Fare revenue represents about 4% of UTA’s $1 billion 2026 budget. Most of its funding comes from sales taxes.
“It’s not terribly significant,” Gustafson said. “It does help with the day-to-day cost, but we’ve built out quite an expansive system over the past 10 to 15 years, and so there’s a significant amount of debt, of course, that comes with that.”
In addition to the fare increase, UTA is proposing other service changes for 2027, including an expansion to the S-Line that connects to Sugar House and a tool to make contactless payments easier for occasional riders. These proposals aren’t final yet, and Utahns are invited to voice their opinion during a public comment period from Aug. 10 through Sept. 9.



Let us know what you think...


 


The authority is also constructing a new station at Highland Drive and Simpson Avenue, as well as another one in the Sugar House business district, near the University of Utah health center. 
While a contactless form of payment is already available with FAREPAY cards, UTA is also studying allowing a tap-to-pay system for regular credit and debit cards.
The authority hasn’t set a specific date in which these changes may take place. However, they are penciled in for next year, Gustafson said.
“We encourage everyone to review the proposed changes and share their feedback through the proper channels,” he said. “As valuable as it is to receive feedback online and through Facebook comments, for example, it doesn’t go into the official public record. Those kinds of things are not necessarily tracked and categorized and logged.”
UTA will host a virtual public meeting on Aug. 26 at 5:30 p.m. to present an overview of the proposed updates and to answer some questions. Registration is available at this link. 
Comments may also be submitted online through UTA’s public comment website, by email at hearingofficer@rideuta.com, by phone at 801-287-3888, or by mail to the Utah Authority.
Public comments must be received, postmarked or submitted electronically by 5 p.m. on Sept. 9 to be included in the official public comment record.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Heat-related illnesses on rise in New Mexico amid record-high temperatures
description: Already this summer, 770 New Mexicans have visited statewide emergency rooms for heat-related illnesses. That’s more than all of last summer, according to the state Health Department, with more than a month remaining in the season.
text:
Volunteer Ernie Montoya stands at the Roswell cooling center Aug. 7, 2026, which the New Mexico Office of Housing helped fund amid a statewide heat wave. (Photo courtesy Ernie Montoya) Already this summer, 770 New Mexicans have visited statewide emergency rooms for heat-related illnesses. That’s more than all of last summer, according to the state Health Department, with more than a month remaining in the season. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The spike in heat-related emergencies comes amid a statewide record heat wave. In the first week of August, Albuquerque and Farmington have broken six high temperature records, with temperatures hovering above 100 degrees each day this month, National Weather Service meteorologist Randall Hergert told Source NM on Friday. 
The service has also issued multiple heat advisories throughout August, including one in effect through Saturday evening for those cities as well as northern New Mexico between Los Alamos and Taos. 
Hergert said much of the state has endured a “dry patch” without adequate afternoon monsoons to offset heat and decrease overnight low temperatures. But he said forecasts call for a respite beginning early next week, with more moisture and temperatures finally decreasing below triple digits. 
State health officials, in a news release Thursday, urged the public, particularly elderly and young children, to stay hydrated and avoid the sun if possible. 
“Anyone can be affected, but children, adults over 65, outdoor workers and people with chronic conditions are more susceptible and should take extra care when it’s hot,” Chelsea Langer, chief of the department’s Health Epidemiology Bureau, said in a statement.
For those without air conditions, the state’s new Office of Housing has spent some of its legislative funding to help set up five cooling centers in southern New Mexico, where temperatures have regularly exceeded 100 degrees Fahrenheit all summer. 
Already this summer, heat-related emergency room visits have exceeded last summer’s, according to an Aug. 6, 2026, announcement from the New Mexico Department of Health. Pictured above: A map of the areas National Weather Service has issued a heat advisory for, highlighted above in orange, ahead of the weekend beginning Aug. 8, 2026. (Courtesy NWS)
The cooling centers opened with the help of $20,000 grants the office provided to the town of Tatum, City of Hobbs and Eastern Regional Housing Authority of Roswell, department spokesperson Stacy Johnston told Source NM in an email. During a cold snap this January, the office also provided about $820,000 for warming centers to entities across the state. 
One of the Roswell cooling centers is housed in a Presbyterian church on the outskirts of the city. Ernie Montoya, a volunteer with the church and Food Not Bombs Roswell, told Source NM on Thursday that the center has already served nearly 2,000 people, most of them unhoused, along with 300 of their pets. The center has also served as a hub to offer people showers, haircuts and other services. 
“The impact is huge. We are changing people’s lives tremendously, even if it’s just a haircut,” he said. “They feel like they’re being forgotten. We don’t have to be the hand that pushes them down. We can be the hand that lifts them up.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Board sides with doctor who cited ‘stand your ground’ law after striking combative patient
description: The Iowa Board of Medicine has dismissed disciplinary charges against a physician who argued Iowa’s “stand your ground” law protected him from sanctions for physically striking a handcuffed, combative patient. State records indicate Dr. Curtis Waite, who practices emergency medicine, was working in the emergency room at Mary Greeley Hospital in Ames the nigh[...]
text:
The Iowa Board of Medicine regulates the state's medical profession as part of the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing. (Photo by Getty Images, board seal courtesy the State of Iowa) The Iowa Board of Medicine has dismissed disciplinary charges against a physician who argued Iowa’s “stand your ground” law protected him from sanctions for physically striking a handcuffed, combative patient.
State records indicate Dr. Curtis Waite, who practices emergency medicine, was working in the emergency room at Mary Greeley Hospital in Ames the night of Nov. 14, 2023, when police brought in a suspect, who appeared to be experiencing some form of psychosis, for treatment of head lacerations.
The patient had allegedly assaulted several people, then attempted to take a police officer’s gun, and then threatened a paramedic who had to pin the man against the wall at the hospital using a wheelchair, according to the board.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
State records indicate that shortly after Waite entered the treatment room where the patient was lying in bed with his hands cuffed behind his back, the patient spit blood in Waite’s face and then kicked him in the head. The Board of Medicine says that according to the “several” police officers who were in the room at the time, Waite responded to the attack by striking the patient in the head three or four times.
The Board of Medicine quotes Waite explaining his actions by stating, “I was stunned, saw stars and instructively  reacted.”
Waite left the room and the patient was treated by other hospital staff before being charged by police with assaulting Waite. According to the board, Mary Greeley Hospital placed Waite on leave after the incident, but he eventually returned to work with the understanding that he’d undergo an evaluation and submit to a monitoring program.
In July 2025, the Board of Medicine charged Waite with one count of unprofessional conduct. Waite then sought a dismissal of the charge, arguing Iowa’s “stand your ground” law allows individuals to use reasonable force against others to defend themselves against the use of unlawful force.



Quotation







A physician is not required to stand by and accept serious injury or death to avoid touching the patient that is actively assaulting him.


– Iowa Board of Medicine


Lawyers for the state argued the law could not be used to redefine the standard of care that’s expected of physicians dealing with combative and unruly patients. Waite could have stepped back, the state argued, and his failure to do so amounted to an ethical decision that warranted some form of sanction.
If Waite was unable to control himself in a heated situation in which he was being assaulted, he might not have the capacity to work in emergency medicine, the state argued.
In deciding to dismiss the charge against Waite, the board noted that it was not going to address the question of whether the stand-your-ground law applied to the case at hand. Instead, the board said, it was going to examine the underlying question of whether Waite’s actions violated the professional standards to which Iowa physicians are held.
“Dr. Waite had been subject to (the patient) spitting in his mouth and Dr. Waite had just been kicked in the head with some force,” the board stated in its decision. “It is reasonable to believe Dr. Waite was facing further imminent harm from (the patient) whose legs remained unrestrained … Given Dr. Waite’s location in a corner between the bed and a chair, he could not have withdrawn without risking further strikes by (the patient). The board finds a physician is not required to stand by and accept serious injury or death to avoid touching the patient that is actively assaulting him.”
The board noted that it appeared the patient was not injured by Waite’s punches as they were delivered with limited force. “In other words, these were not proverbial ‘haymaker’ punches,” the board stated.
While physically striking a patient is “not normally considered within the bounds of professional behavior, given the totality of the circumstances here, Dr. Waite’s actions do not rise to the level of unprofessional conduct,” the board ruled.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Waite or his attorney for comment on the case.

name: Mississippi Today
title: FAITH scholarship funding scare fuels push for state lawmakers to step up
description: My'Kayla Gaines Cochnauer at her Natchez home with items she will take to Mississippi State, where she will be studying psychology at the Starkville university, Friday, July 31, 2026.
text:
My’Kayla Gaines Cochnauer was delivering DoorDash orders Wednesday when a text from her adoptive mother ended days of uncertainty over how she would pay for her first semester at Mississippi State University.
The message shared a screenshot of an email telling the 18-year-old from Natchez that her Fostering Access and Inspiring True Hope, or FAITH, Scholarship had been restored — a week after the state Office of Student Financial Aid told applicants the awards would not be funded.
Her family had been scrambling to figure out how to cover roughly $5,000 in college costs before she was supposed to move into her dorm and begin studying psychology in mid-August. 
My’Kayla Gaines Cochnauer at her Natchez home on Friday, July 31, 2026. She is looking forward to studying psychology at Mississippi State University in Starkville. Credit: Vickie D. King/ Mississippi Today
“I am really happy that I and other kids can now go to college without having to worry about work or where my next dollars will come from,” Cochnauer said. “But I wonder why it took all this media attention to fix this problem?” 
Cochnauer is among 170 former foster youths whose scholarships will now be covered for their first semester of college after the Woodward Hines Education Foundation pledged $800,000 to help fill a funding gap in the state aid program. The foundation is also soliciting donations to help cover the scholarships..
The foundation’s contribution is a one-time fix. Mississippi’s financial aid office still faces a $7.3 million shortfall that could reduce aid for nearly 27,000 students, such as those receiving the Mississippi Tuition Assistance Grant (MTAG), Mississippi Eminent Scholars Grant (MESG) and the Higher Education Legislative Plan (HELP). The shortage could affect programs serving low-income students and teachers as well as the FAITH scholarship recipients.
Woodward Hines President and CEO Jim McHale learned about the FAITH  scholarship funding issue on Monday. The foundation’s board met Tuesday and unanimously approved a plan to cover eligible students’ first college semester. Officials at state universities and college foundations have also pledged to support FAITH scholarship students.  
But private donations can’t solve Mississippi’s broader financial aid funding crisis, McHale said. 
“If legislators say they want a strong, educated population and economic workforce then it’s imperative that they invest in the aid that covers tuition of young students and adults looking to boost their careers or education,” he said. 
READ MORE: FAITH Scholarships get $800K boost from Woodward Hines foundation
Earlier this year, state financial aid office officials requested $6.5 million from the Legislature for FAITH scholarships and the Winter-Reed Teacher Loan Repayment Program, which helps eligible teachers repay student loans. Lawmakers appropriated $3 million for both programs. The financial aid office applied the full appropriation to the FAITH scholarships, leaving the loan repayment program unfunded for the first time since it was created in 2021.
Jim McHale, president and CEO of the Woodward Hines Education Foundation, speaks about the FAITH Scholarship during a news conference at the Capitol in Jackson on Wednesday, Aug. 5, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Senate Appropriations Chairman Briggs Hopson, a Republican from Vicksburg, did not respond to a request for comment before publication. 
Some colleges and universities, including Delta State and Mississippi Christian University — formerly Mississippi College — have committed to financially supporting FAITH recipients, said Sen. Nicole Boyd, a Republican from Oxford who is chair of the Senate Universities and Colleges Committee.
The state financial aid office prioritized new FAITH applicants on a first-come, first-served basis, said Jennifer Rogers, the agency’s executive director. The $3 million was enough to cover scholarship renewals for 159 students and first-time awards for 23 new applicants, she said. 
With the Woodward Hines foundation’s support, about 170 new applicants will get scholarships, too.
Most of those students, 95 of them, plan to attend community colleges, Boyd said.
On Wednesday, officials notified the new applicants that the scholarships would be funded after all.
At least that’s true for this year.
Demand for state financial aid has grown, Rogers said. In 2025, the financial aid office distributed more than $51 million to 22,377 students. Changes to the Free Application for Federal Student Aid, known as FAFSA, and state eligibility requirements have expanded the pool of students who are now eligible for aid, she said. Rogers also said  a reduction in the number of credit hours required to qualify as a full-time student and changes to the HELP grant made another 4,520 students eligible for state-funded grants.
State lawmakers need to prevent another funding shortfall, said Rep. Bill Kinkade, a Republican from Byhalia, who sponsored the legislation that created the FAITH scholarship in 2022. The scholarship also has special meaning for Kinkade, who spent part of his childhood in a group home in Jackson. 
“We made a promise to these students and we will try to honor them by funding those scholarships next year,” Kinkade said.
Rep. Bill Kinkade speaks about the Bill Kinkade Fostering Access and Inspiring True Hope, or FAITH, Scholarship during a news conference at the Capitol in Jackson on Wednesday, Aug. 5, 2026. He spent part of his childhood living in a group home in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Kinkade said he plans to work with lawmakers before the legislative session starts in January to address anticipated funding needs for the state financial aid office.
Kell Smith, executive director of Mississippi’s Community College Board, said he was grateful for the recent work to ensure FAITH scholarship students have the opportunity to attend college. 
“The FAITH scholarship is integral to a population like first-generation students that oftentimes need help navigating higher education and processes,” Smith said. “This is just an opportunity for us to continue to provide those training and educational opportunities that are so beneficial to our students and to our families and to the state.” 
Tammy Cochnauer, My’Kayla’s adoptive mother, said she wants the Legislature to establish rules requiring earlier notification whenever scholarship funding is in jeopardy. The funding crisis erects burdens for students who are determined to get an education, she said. 
“The state should be encouraging students like My’Kayla to stay in Mississippi to pursue a  higher education, and eventually give back to our communities,” Tammy Cochnauer said. 
For My’Kayla, the immediate uncertainty is over. She plans to move into her Creswell dorm room at Mississippi State on Aug. 14 
As grateful as she is for the financial support, she worries about scholarships disappearing again. 
“It’s good and all that we got it returned back,” My’Kayla Gaines Cochnauer said. “But 170 kids were left to figure out what would come next. It doesn’t erase what happened, and it doesn’t erase the feeling of being abandoned by the system.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: Bodnar vows to stay in Montana Senate race despite ‘speculation, silliness’
description: With 80 hours to go before the deadline for candidates to drop out of November’s election, independent U.S. Senate candidate Seth Bodnar said his campaign is about sending someone to D.C. who works for Montana, not political parties, and he is in the race regardless of who else is — or isn’t. [should be timing […]
text:
With 80 hours to go before the deadline for candidates to drop out of November’s election, independent U.S. Senate candidate Seth Bodnar said his campaign is about sending someone to D.C. who works for Montana, not political parties, and he is in the race regardless of who else is — or isn’t. [should be timing in lede not location speaking 72 hours … ]
“I believe that Montana voters deserve the freedom to send a message to Washington that they reject a broken political system, that they deserve leadership that’s focused on bringing us together to solve problems rather than just tearing us apart to win elections,” Bodnar said.
Bodnar’s press conference, held in Billings, came as rumors and speculation about whether someone might leave the race have flown around Montana’s political sphere as Monday’s deadline to drop out nears. A growing coalition of organizations and political figures has called for the winner of the Democratic primary, Alani Bankhead, to drop out and allow support to coalesce against Republican Kurt Alme, while Republicans have amplified rumors Bodnar might blink first, or Democrats might run former Gov. Steve Bullock.
A state Democratic party spokesperson said the rumor about Bullock had no substance.
On Wednesday, Montana voters did gain an additional option, as the Secretary of State’s Office confirmed Jami Woodman, a volunteer with Democratic candidate Reilly Neill’s primary race, filed as a write-in candidate. Woodman said in a video she “bought a line” for voters because the Senate race “is a mess.” With her declaration, a blank line will appear on ballots, but only votes for Woodman will be tallied. 
Bankhead has been firm in her stance, even as her campaign has been unable to show the same level of support and fundraising as either Bodnar or Alme — she’s raised less than $60,000 compared to millions for each opponent. 
She isn’t fazed by those shortcomings, saying her focus is on “the 48,772 votes cast for me by the people of Montana and the remaining population whom I’ll be representing.”
“Bodnar’s sphere of elites have used their money and power to manipulate and bully donors and leaders throughout the party and Montana,” Bankhead said in a text message on Friday.
She said she is the only candidate not beholden to big donors and that she “will never stop fighting for Montanans, and I will never quit.”
She told Politico that as a woman of faith, it would take a “lightning bolt from God,” for her to drop out of the race.
Bodnar, the former University of Montana president, launched his campaign with the backing of former Democratic U.S. Sen. Jon Tester, has a cross-partisan coalition of Montana’s elected officials backing him, and has earned endorsements from nearly every center-left aligned political organization in the state, including environmental and union groups. 
Alme, meanwhile, was a last-minute addition to the field of candidates in March when incumbent Sen. Steve Daines decided to withdraw his candidacy at the literal last minute, clearing the way for Alme to file without drawing stronger Democratic opponents. 
As an independent candidate, Bodnar was required to meet a signature threshold to get on the November ballot, which he says shows the support and appetite of Montanans for his campaign. 
“Nearly 30,000 Montanans from 52 different counties across the state signed their own personal Declaration of Independence earlier this year to get me on the ballot in November, but I think they were saying something much bigger than just put Seth Bodnar on the ballot,” Bodnar said. “I think they were saying, ‘Give us another choice because let’s lift our eyes above politics for him, because something much bigger is happening right now in this country.’”
Bankhead, an Air Force special operations veteran and life coach, was unknown prior to her primary candidacy. 
An outside political action committee spent more than $2.5 million on boosting her profile over former legislator Neill. Bankhead won by more than 12,000 votes, but the PAC quickly withdrew from Montana politics, saying Bankhead had no path to victory. 
Calls for Bankhead to end her campaign have come from organizations that have endorsed Bodnar and political actions committees like Montana Freedom PAC, which has put up signs around Helena, where she lives. 
Signs around Helena advocate for Democrat Alani Bankhead to drop out of the U.S. Senate race. (Micah Drew/ Daily Montanan)
Whether Bankhead could actually withdraw has also been a question, as state law says a party must replace a candidate that withdraws. 
But lawyers have argued the Montana Democratic Party would have the option to select no candidate as a replacement, and the party’s executive board was briefed on the legal argument of such actions at a meeting last week, according to the Montana Free Press. 
The state party, meanwhile, is still publicly supporting Bankhead as its nominee. 
“Alani won the primary. We had something like 48,000 voters who participated in that primary,” Montana Democratic Party spokesperson Sofia Perez told the Daily Montanna. “What does it say to them if she leaves? It’s a form of voter suppression. If someone wins a primary, that should be it.”
But some of those primary voters have expressed their support for Bankhead only extended through the primary. 
Erika McMillin, a board member of the Montana Federation of Public Employees, the state’s largest union, said she voted for Bankhead in the primary as the best option, but now backs Bodnar. 
“Following our union’s endorsement process, I believe Seth is the only candidate with a legitimate path to victory who still shares our members’ values,” McMillin said in a statement announcing the union’s endorsement of Bodnar. 
At an event Bankhead held in Townsend on Thursday, several attendees of the public asked her to drop out, leading to the organizers to cut the event off early, according to the Montana State StateNews Bureau. 
During his press conference, Bodnar said he had never personally asked Bankhead to drop out, but that she had made the request of him. 
He also said he was not collaborating with any political action committees running ads and messaging asking her to drop out. 
Comparing himself to his main opponents — Libertarian Kyle Austin is also running — Bodnar said he believes Alme would be beholden to the party and not break with Trump on key issues such as the Iran War. 
He also said he believes Bankhead is unvetted and pointed to concerning statements she’s made on podcasts and interviews, including a widely circulated quote where she says “if you’re poor right now, it’s because you decided you wanted to be poor.”
Bankhead told the Daily Montanan her podcast is related to her life-coaching business and aimed at high-achieving individuals, and the specific context of her statement was about some well-off clients of hers that did not practice good money management. 
There is a growing trend of Democratic candidates dropping out of races in reliably Republican states to allow head-to-head matchups between independents and Republicans, including in Idaho, Alaska, South Dakota, and Nebraska, where independent Dan Osborn is making his second run at unseating a sitting Republican. Osborn lost by just seven points in 2024, while the state voted for President Donald Trump by 21 points. 
Polling of Montana’s senate race shows Alme winning comfortably in any scenario that includes three or four candidates; but a two-way race with Bodnar is more competitive than one with Bankhead.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Public input planned as North Dakota lawmakers shape kratom plan
description: North Dakota lawmakers on Friday began talks about restricting kratom and related substances, part of a process the public will get to weigh in on next week. Lawmakers are preparing for a special session next month called by Republican Gov. Kelly Armstrong to consider prohibiting and regulating aspects of kratom products, including criminal penalties. Kratom[...]
text:
Sen. Michelle Axtman, left, and Rep. Pat Heinert, both R-Bismarck, listen during a meeting of the Legislature's Kratom Working Group on Aug. 7, 2026. (Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota lawmakers on Friday began talks about restricting kratom and related substances, part of a process the public will get to weigh in on next week.
Lawmakers are preparing for a special session next month called by Republican Gov. Kelly Armstrong to consider prohibiting and regulating aspects of kratom products, including criminal penalties. Kratom – temporarily banned statewide by Armstrong – is derived from a tropical tree in Southeast Asia that people use as an energy booster, for pain management and to cope with withdrawals from drugs such as fentanyl and heroin.
Two psychoactive ingredients known as mitragynine and 7-OH are found in kratom leaves. The latter is a frequent subject of officials’ concerns as an addictive, potent, synthetic product that until recently was available at gas stations and smoke shops. Armstrong linked overdoses and deaths to such items in banning kratom and related products by his executive order.
What to know about the ban on kratom in North Dakota

The Legislature’s five-member, all-Republican Kratom Working Group heard comments from fellow lawmakers about what issues they think are most important, such as prohibiting synthetic derivatives like 7-OH, allowing but restricting natural kratom products, considering what other states have done and weighing the science and effects of kratom.
Sen. Kristin Roers, R-Fargo, wondered whether the Legislature can adequately address kratom regulations within a three-day special session.
“If we’re going to do something in regulation, how do we possibly do that well enough in the short amount of time that we’re allowing ourselves, or do we continue the full ban until the full session and then have the regulation conversation then?” said Roers, a registered nurse.
The next regular legislative session begins in January.
Rep. SuAnn Olson, R-Baldwin, asked the panel to consider the extensive testimony from early last year on two kratom-related bills, in which many people detailed how natural kratom has helped them relieve pain. The testimony included multiple North Dakotans’ personal stories. 
“We can’t just discount what that did for them,” Olson said.
House Judiciary Chairman Larry Klemin, R-Bismarck, pointed out that the Legislature already weighed kratom issues in those two bills, a mitragynine ban defeated in the House, and an optional kratom study lawmakers later chose not to do.
“I just wanted to make sure you were aware that we’ve had this all discussed, and thoroughly, not too long ago,” Klemin told the panel.
Working Group Co-Chair Sen. Michelle Axtman, R-Bismarck, called the 2025 testimony “incredibly outdated,” missing perspectives from parents, physicians and law enforcement. The issue is no longer the same, she said.
“I think we can look back at the testimony. We also have to look at what has happened since that testimony has occurred,” Axtman said. 
Klemin recommended bills to prohibit synthetic versions of kratom and to allow but regulate the natural substance. He also suggested kratom could be merged into the state’s medical marijuana laws. 
Other lawmakers expressed concern for how to help people who might experience withdrawals from kratom products, substances that became illegal in just a matter of days in North Dakota this month. Officials have recommended people in crisis call FirstLink at 988, or seek out resources by calling FirstLink at 211 or the state’s Behavioral Health Division at 701-328-8908.
Rep. Eric Murphy, R-Grand Forks, suggested lawmakers read scientific papers on kratom and 7-OH and distinguish between the natural product and synthetic derivatives.
“I think what we have to guard against is adulterated product, which is quite common, apparently, and that’s where the problem lies,” said Murphy, who teaches biomedical sciences at the University of North Dakota School of Medicine and Health Sciences. 
In addition to his public health emergency executive order, Armstrong approved an emergency pharmaceutical rule to outlaw 7-OH as a controlled substance. He cited his actions to the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration’s move last month to temporarily classify 7-OH and other compounds as a controlled substance.
Growing concerns prompt calls to address kratom substances in North Dakota

The working group will meet at 10:30 a.m. Wednesday at the state Capitol. Invited medical professionals and scientists will appear. The public may offer comments with a time limit per person, Co-Chair Rep. Pat Heinert, R-Bismarck, said.
He said he would like to hear from parents who have lost children. In the last five years, North Dakota logged 23 deaths in which officials attributed kratom or related substances as a part of the primary cause.
“That’s what started this whole thing,” Heinert, a former sheriff, told reporters. “We have to react to that. That’s our responsibility. We’re here to create laws to protect the people of North Dakota.”
He said he hopes for a ban on synthetic products and guardrails on natural kratom. The 2027 Legislature is likely to deal further with kratom topics. One subject could be improving addiction services for adolescents, Axtman said.
“I think the crisis regarding withdrawals and usage of kratom has maybe highlighted that,” Axtman told reporters. 
In May, the North Dakota Public Health Association passed a resolution urging the Legislature to prohibit kratom and related products.
Association Vice President Mark Strand said he hopes lawmakers study kratom with a scientific approach and an empathetic eye.
“I think my ultimate concern is empathy for the users, because they’re not doing it to be bad actors,” said Strand, a professor in North Dakota State University’s Pharmacy Practice and Public Health Departments. “They’re doing it because of underlying issues that have led them there.”
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura can be reached at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Don Lemon challenges constitutionality of FACE Act in legal defense of church protest charges
description: Independent journalist Don Lemon is challenging the constitutionality of a law underlying federal charges against him stemming from a protest against an immigration official inside a St. Paul church. If Lemon prevails, the ruling could have far-reaching consequences for a law aimed at protecting access to abortion clinics and houses of worship. Lemon, a form[...]
text:
Independent journalist and former CNN anchor Don Lemon exits the Warren E. Burger Federal Building and U.S. Courthouse in St. Paul, Minn. on Friday, Feb. 13, 2026. Lemon pleaded not guilty to federal charges stemming from his coverage of a protest against a pastor and ICE official at a St. Paul church in January. (Photo by Alex Baumhardt/Minnesota Reformer)Independent journalist Don Lemon is challenging the constitutionality of a law underlying federal charges against him stemming from a protest against an immigration official inside a St. Paul church. If Lemon prevails, the ruling could have far-reaching consequences for a law aimed at protecting access to abortion clinics and houses of worship.
Lemon, a former CNN anchor who now has a YouTube show, was indicted along with three other journalists who covered a protest on Jan. 18 at Cities Church, where a pastor, David Easterwood is also a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement official. (Easterwood was not present at the service.)
The charges against journalists — pursued by the highest ranks of President Donald Trump’s Justice Department — represented a striking attack on the free press as the administration faced critical news coverage of the brutality of Operation Metro Surge, which had already led to the killing of an American citizen, Renee Good. (Minnesota Reformer joined a consortium of news organizations condemning the prosecution of journalists and filing a “friend-of-the-court” brief calling for dismissal based on First Amendment grounds.)
Prosecutors didn’t distinguish between protesters and journalists — including Lemon’s producer, Michael Beute, and Twin Cities independent journalist Georgia Fort — and leveled the same two felony charges against 39 people: conspiracy against the right of religious freedom at a place of worship and injuring, intimidating and interfering with the exercise of right of religious freedom at a place of worship.
The Justice Department’s response to Operation Metro Surge, including opening an investigation into Good’s wife, led to the resignations of career prosecutors — including former acting U.S. Attorney Joe Thompson, who is now representing Lemon along with prominent Washington D.C. defense attorney Abbe Lowell.
In three motions filed on Friday, Lemon’s attorneys argue the charges should be dismissed because his conduct is protected by the First Amendment, the federal government’s prosecution is “vindictive,” and because one of the laws cited is unconstitutional.
One charge comes from a 1994 law signed by President Bill Clinton called the Freedom of Access to Clinic Entrances Act — the FACE Act — which protects people’s right to freely access abortion clinics and places of worship.
The unusual pairing of abortion clinics and houses of worship is the product of unintentional bipartisanship. Democrats introduced the bill in response to a wave of militant protests and blockades of reproductive health clinics, and a Republican added protections to places of worship as a poison pill to doom its passage. But Democrats didn’t object.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Lemon’s attorneys focus their argument specifically on the provision concerning religious houses of worship. They argue the law oversteps Congress’ power because religious ceremonies are confined to private acts and don’t involve interstate commerce — unlike reproductive clinics, where patients, healthcare providers, and medical supplies travel across state lines for abortions. They also argue if the FACE Act is ruled unconstitutional, the other felony charge must be dismissed.
And yet, as Lemon’s constitutional challenge proceeds in court, it could expand beyond his attorney’s narrowly tailored arguments, said University of California, Davis law professor Mary Ziegler.
“(This argument) is taking a bigger shot at the statute than is necessary for him to get acquitted and one that could have unintended consequences,” Ziegler said, i.e., the reproductive health facility section of the law could also be ruled unconstitutional.
The law requires actual threats of violence or obstruction — locking the doors of the church or blocking entrances with a vehicle — and ample video evidence shows parishioners coming and going during the demonstration and Lemon interviewing the lead pastor, Jonathan Parnell.
Indeed, Fort’s attorneys did not challenge the constitutionality of the FACE Act in three motions for dismissal filed on Thursday, instead simply asserting her First Amendment rights and alleging vindictive prosecution.
Ziegler said, however, it’s the Trump administration that ultimately opened the door for challenges to the FACE Act by charging Lemon, saying that if his attorneys didn’t raise the issue another group likely would through a friend-of-the-court brief.
The FACE Act has seldom been used in prosecutions. Shortly after Trump began his second term, he pardoned activists who blocked abortion clinics, and the Justice Department announced it would curtail prosecutions of the offense.
The case has already been beset by a series of prosecutorial missteps, including mistakenly indicting a person who was never near the church, and falsely alleging a parishioner broke an arm in a search warrant.
U.S. Magistrate Judge Douglas Micko initially rejected charges against Lemon, and then-Chief Judge Patrick Schiltz and the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals declined the government’s appeals, leading prosecutors to pursue a series of legal maneuvers to secure grand jury indictments instead.

name: WyoFile
title: Trump uses the phone to boost Degenfelder’s bid for Wyoming governor
description:
The president called on Wyoming voters to back his Republican pick for Wyoming’s next governor. 
The post Trump uses the phone to boost Degenfelder’s bid for Wyoming governor appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
For the thousands of people who tuned into President Donald Trump’s telephone rally Thursday afternoon with Megan Degenfelder, his pick for Wyoming’s next governor, listeners heard an abbreviated, virtual version of what has become a core instrument of his political power. 
In place of the usual Trump rally mix of rock, pop and show tunes, the event featured a single anthem when it opened with Lee Greenwood’s “God Bless the U.S.A.” From there, the telerally lasted another 15 minutes as the president asked Wyoming — the state that gave him the widest margin of victory in 2024 — to back the Republican candidate he endorsed in January. 
“So get out and vote for Megan Degenfelder,” he said. “And you’re going to be happy. You’re going to say, ‘President Trump gave me a good idea.’ You’ll look back in the years and you’ll say, ‘That was a great, a great choice.’” 
Degenfelder, who now serves as Wyoming’s superintendent of public instruction, is vying for the Republican nomination against Sen. Eric Barlow of Gillette, Col. Brent Bien of Cody and Curt Blake of Centennial, who is running a “word-of-mouth” campaign. 
Barlow, Bien and Degenfelder each have their own edge in the race. While Trump endorsed Degenfelder before she even announced her campaign, the Wyoming Republican Party endorsed Bien in July. Barlow, meanwhile, released internal polling two weeks ago that shows him with a comfortable lead. 
The Republican nominee will face Democratic candidate Kenneth Casner of Casper and Constitution Party candidate Rebecca Bextel of Jackson in November’s general election, though Bextel has said she is running as an “insurance policy” against Barlow and would drop out if he loses in the primary to either Degenfelder or Bien. 
“Campaigns have different priorities,” Barlow wrote in a statement. “Nearly 12 months ago, I committed to showing up, listening, and earning Wyomingites’ support, community by community. Last night, that meant knocking doors in Cheyenne and sharing root beer floats with neighbors at a local park. We’ll finish this campaign the same way we started it, by having respectful conversations with the people of Wyoming.”
Cheryl Aguiar, Bien’s campaign manager, wrote in a statement, “we didn’t even watch it,” referring to the telerally.
“Our focus is on the campaign and Brent’s plan to move Wyoming forward,” she wrote. “Brent and all of the thousands of supporters remain confident in Brent’s message and the support we are seeing across the state as we head towards the primary.” 
Over the years, Trump’s support for early voting has wavered — sometimes encouraging and criticizing the practice at the same event. Absentee voting, which accounts for both mail-in and early voting in Wyoming, is popular among residents. At least 45% of the state’s registered voters cast their ballots absentee in the most recent election. 
Trump encouraged it Thursday.
“Early voting is happening right now, and it ends on Monday, Aug. 17,” he said. “So you have just 11 days to go out and vote early, and you can also vote on Election Day.”
Degenfelder thanked the president for his support and told listeners what she sees as the stakes of the governor’s race. 
“We have a very important decision to make in this election. Will we go along to get along? Will we play nice and comfortably manage our decline? That’s what Colorado did, and look where they are now,” Degenfelder said. “Or will we stand up, push back, challenge the status quo, and fight for what we know is right, even when it’s unpopular?”
About 20,600 people tuned in Thursday, according to Degenfelder’s campaign, which is about twice as many as attended Trump’s 2022 in-person rally in Casper when he backed Harriet Hageman against Liz Cheney. It’s not clear how many at the telerally were registered Wyoming voters, but according to Degenfelder’s campaign, most who joined the rally answered a call inviting them to attend rather than dialing in.  
At the end of the call, listeners were asked to participate. 
“Can President Trump count on your vote in the primary election for governor for Meghan Degenfelder?” a moderator asked. “Press one for yes. Press two for no. Press three for undecided.”
Slightly more than three-fourths pressed one for yes, according to Degenfelder’s campaign, while 10% answered no and 14% said they were undecided. 
Trump hosted his first telerally in 2020 when the COVID-19 pandemic made holding large, in-person campaign rallies more difficult. His company applied to trademark “telerally,” which the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office ultimately rejected because the word is merely descriptive. Regardless, Trump’s telerallies have stuck around. This midterm election, he’s hosted telerallies in states like Georgia, Kansas, Alabama, South Carolina and Louisiana. Most of those candidates went on to win their primary elections, but a few lost their bids for nomination. 
A Trump endorsement is potent in Wyoming, but how potent during this election remains to be seen. What does the telerally and its timing indicate? Potentially several things, Jim King, a retired University of Wyoming political professor, told WyoFile on Friday.  
“The race may be close,” King said, adding that he’s not seen any independent polling and is unsure of where the candidates stand relative to one another. 
“We are also entering this stretch with just a couple more weeks left, and so candidates want to double down,” he said. “They want to make sure that they’re out there before the voters.”
A telerally may not generate the same spectacle as an in-person gathering, King said, but news outlets across the state are still writing about it. 
The primary election is Aug. 18. Early voting is already underway. 
For more information about candidates in Wyoming’s federal, state and legislative races, check out WyoFile’s 2026 Election Guide.

title: Nancy N. Thayer
description:
In her last six years, in Vermont, she made many friends and enjoyed attending concerts and theater, always being a supporter of the arts.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Nancy N. Thayer.
text:
Born: 05/13/1025
Evanston, Illinois
Died: 07/22/2026
South Burlington, Vermont
Details of service:
A memorial service will be held at The Residence at Quarry Hill, 435 Quarry Hill Rd., South Burlington on Friday, Aug. 28 at 3 p.m. A celebration of Life will be held at the First Congregational Church, Essex Junction, on Saturday, Aug. 29 at 4 p.m.

Nancy Noyes Thayer, 101, passed away peacefully on July 22, 2026.
Born on May 13, 1925, in Evanston, Illinois, to George Frederick Noyes and Dorothy Hall Noyes, Nancy grew up in Evanston and graduated from Evanston Township High School in 1943. She went on to attend Connecticut College, graduating in 1947.
Before starting her family, Nancy worked in banking in both New York City and Chicago, taking time in between for an adventurous six-week trip through Europe with three of her close high school friends. In later years, she commented about how welcoming Europeans were to have Americans visiting post-war Europe.
On April 14, 1950, Nancy married the love of her life, Bruce William Thayer. After spending a memorable week-long honeymoon in Vero Beach, Florida, the couple knew it was a place they wanted to return to. Decades later, they made that dream a reality, making Vero Beach their home from 1989 to 2010. Following Bruce’s passing, Nancy continued to enjoy her years in Vero Beach until 2020, when she relocated to The Residence at Quarry Hill in South Burlington to be closer to her family.
Nancy is survived by her three children: Elizabeth Hall Thayer of Burlington;  Robert Bruce Thayer of Egnar, Colorado; and Emily Thayer Guziak and her husband Tim of Essex. She is also survived by eight grandchildren: Jamie Hurd (Jeff) of Madras, Oregon. Robert Thayer of Denver, Colorado, Erin Thayer of Whitehall, Arkansas, Kristy Clough (Pras Pathmanathan) of Washington, D.C., Carrie Clough (Jimmy Bader) of Denver, Colorado, Kelsey Guziak (Alex Levin) of Jericho, Melissa Guziak (Andrew McAfee) of Grand Junction, Colorado, and Caleb Guziak of Salt Lake City, Utah, and six great grandchildren: Lucas, Jacob, Nolan, Livie, Ellie and Louisa.
Nancy was predeceased by her husband of nearly 60 years, Bruce; and her brothers George, Richard and Tom.  She is also survived by a sister-in-law, Virginia Noyes, of Wilmette, Illinois, and many nieces and nephews.
Nancy and Bruce spent many wonderful family summer vacations at Watervale Resort, in Arcadia, Michigan, where they made lifelong friends. Nancy always made friends wherever Bruce’s career took them: Chicago, Illinois, Battle Creek, Michigan, and Barrington, Illinois, through her love for entertaining, her volunteer work and love of people. In her last six years, in Vermont, she made many friends and enjoyed attending concerts and theater, always being a supporter of the arts.
She was a member of many Episcopal churches, most recently All Saints Episcopal Church, South Burlington. She loved to sing in church choirs. One of her favorite places to travel was London, England to hear the London Welsh Festival of Male Choirs, and to Paris, France where she loved to take her grandchildren.
Nancy celebrated her 100th birthday in Paris with 14 family members at her favorite restaurant, Chez Plumeau atop Montmarte.
A memorial service will be held at The Residence at Quarry Hill, 435 Quarry Hill Rd., South Burlington on Friday, Aug. 28 at 3 p.m. A Celebration of Life will be held at the First Congregational Church, Essex Junction, on Saturday, Aug. 29 at 4 p.m. Interment of ashes will take place at a later date at Blaine Township Cemetery, Arcadia, Michigan.  Memorials may be made to the Grand Traverse Regional Land Conservancy, 2846 N Three Mile Rd, Traverse City, Michigan 49686. www.gtrlc.org.

Idaho public health agencies have issued
public health advisories for North Idaho's Fernan Lake and the upper end of Hayden Lake. (Photos courtesy of the Panhandle Health District)Officials from the Panhandle Health District, alongside the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare and the Idaho Department of Environmental Quality, issued public health advisories Aug. 6 warning of harmful cyanobacteria bloom in Fernan Lake and the upper end of Hayden Lake.
Cyanobacteria, referred to as harmful algae bloom and normally a natural part of Idaho’s water bodies, can multiply and release toxic chemical compounds – known as cyanotoxins – in response to increases in temperature, according to the press release.
Recent water sampling indicates the presence of cyanobacteria, alsoknown as a harmful algae bloom, in the north end of Hayden Lake. (Map courtesy of the Panhandle Health District)
Officials recommend avoiding contact with discolored water, surface scums, or areas with visible green streaks or mats; and to keep pets and children away from affected water, as they are most at-risk of harmful exposure. The elderly and those with compromised immune systems should also avoid contact with affected water.
Symptoms of contact with cyanobacteria vary according to exposure time and may include: rashes, hives, diarrhea, vomiting, coughing and/or wheezing. 
If contact has been made with water containing cyanobacteria, officials recommend washing off with fresh water.
Drinking affected water can result in more severe symptoms impacting the liver and nervous system, according to the press release.
Officials warn those using the lake as a drinking source that cyanobacteria cannot be removed by boiling or filtering the water.
If choosing to eat fish from the lake, officials also recommend removing all fat, skin and organs before cooking, as toxins can accumulate in those tissues, the press release said.
If exhibiting the persistent presence of cyanotoxin-related symptoms, consult with your health care provider or veterinarian in case of pet exposure.
For more information, and a list of active Idaho harmful algae bloom advisories, visit: https://www.gethealthy.dhw.idaho.gov/recreational-water-health-advisories.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Historic site defaced, senator’s populist pitch and tourists abound: CT politics news
description: Murphy maps out his vision of ‘economic populism.’ State tourism had a big year. And a robbery at the Nathan Hale Homestead in Coventry.
text:
These news briefs are part of The Connecticut Mirror’s 2026 political coverage. For more news about the 2026 legislative session, campaigns, elections and more, sign up here for The Issue, the CT Mirror’s weekly politics newsletter.
Murphy maps out vision of ‘economic populism’
U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., has been vocally calling on his own party to figure out a path forward ever since President Donald Trump returned to office. He and three other Democratic senators are starting to sketch out what that could look like.
They argue Democrats can’t “simply oppose Trump and his billionaire friends,” but that they also need to take on corporate interests in data centers, Social Security, housing, farming and youth sports.
“If Democrats are going to be the party of working people, we have to prove that we can be trusted to unrig the system by confronting the elites who are doing the rigging,” the memo from the senators reads. 
— Lisa Hagen, Federal Policy Reporter
State tourism had a big year in 2025
Last year, visitors from outside Connecticut pumped some $12.3 billion in direct spending into the state economy according to an annual report.
The state’s latest tourism and marketing report highlights that more than 72 million people visited the state last year, a 3.1% increase from 2024. In a press release, the governor’s office also noted that this means Connecticut more than doubled the 2025 national tourism growth rate, which was 1.5%.
The success comes in the wake of the state’s Pizza Capital of the U.S campaign. The report notes tourism supported more than 125,000 jobs in the state. 
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter
Vandalism at historic site
Gov. Ned Lamont on Friday announced that he would ask state agencies to find money to repair damage at the Nathan Hale Homestead in Coventry after “an apparent act of vandalism.”
Police said a man broke in, stole cash and merchandise and damaged the property, including two of the barns. Anyone with information about the incident can contact the Coventry Police Department.
The homestead is the family home of Nathan Hale, Connecticut’s official state hero and an American Revolutionary War spy who was executed at age 21. Nonprofit organization Connecticut Landmarks runs the site as a museum. 
— Ginny Monk, Investigative Reporter

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ Attorney General launches investigation into embattled immigration detention center
description: State officials said the investigation will examine whether Geo Group employees violated detainees' civil rights.
text:
A detainee in the window of the Delaney Hall detention center in Newark on May 28, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Attorney General Jennifer Davenport announced Friday that the state has issued investigative subpoenas as part of a civil rights investigation into conditions at Delaney Hall, the embattled private immigration detention facility in Newark. 
The investigation will examine whether Geo Group employees violated detainees’ civil rights, following mounting reports of poor conditions inside the facility and a string of detainee deaths reported in the last eight months. 
“New Jersey has both a legal and a moral duty to stand up for the civil rights of people within our state,” Davenport said in a statement. “For people who are held involuntarily, including by a private corporation like Geo Group, those rights include the right to humane treatment and adequate medical care.”
The investigation comes less than a week after the death of Edwin Jovanny Lopez Cornejo, a 39-year-old Salvadorian who was held at Delaney Hall after he was arrested by federal immigration agents in June. His mother said in an interview that Cornejo was supposed to be taking daily medication for diabetes and high blood pressure, which he was not receiving at the jail. She noted that he complained of numbness in his face and hand when they last spoke. She learned of his death only when contacted by University Hospital to come identify his body on Aug. 1.
Officials with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement claim that Lopez Cornejo had received “proper medical care and was seen by medical professionals” while in custody. His official cause of death is pending.   
The state Department of Health also confirmed the death of a third detainee connected to the facility, but has declined to release more information, citing pending investigations. Jean Wilson Brutus was the first reported death of a detainee at the jail in December 2025. 
The 1,000-bed facility has drawn scrutiny since it opened in May 2025. Earlier this year, detainees said they launched a hunger and labor strike over conditions inside, which led to nightly clashes between federal agents and protesters along Doremus Avenue. Officials have also blocked the state from conducting a full health inspection inside. 
Gov. Mikie Sherrill, a Democrat, said the civil rights investigation was necessary because of the stonewalling officials face at every turn. 
“We’ve heard the reports of disturbing conditions and have been heartbroken by recent deaths of detainees at the facility. ICE and The Geo Group have continued to block our efforts for a full health inspection and there are now reports that visitations have been stopped,” she said in a statement. 
Sherill repeated her position that Delaney Hall should be closed, and said her administration “will not tolerate a facility that abdicates any transparency and accountability.” 
Spokespeople for Geo Group and the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond for comment. 
If the investigation finds violations, the Attorney General’s Office said it would pursue civil enforcement action under the state Civil Rights Act and Law Against Discrimination. Officials are asking anyone with relevant information to contact the Affirmative Enforcement Unit.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska State Board of Education postpones approval of North Omaha girls school
description: LINCOLN — Nebraska’s State Board of Education delayed a vote on approving a nonpublic girls school in North Omaha over concerns about references to “abolitionist framework” that were at one point posted on the school’s website. The board voted 6-2 Friday to postpone its vote until a virtual meeting Aug. 11 to give members time […]
text:
Nebraska State Board of Education member Kirk Penner of Aurora. Jan. 9, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Nebraska’s State Board of Education delayed a vote on approving a nonpublic girls school in North Omaha over concerns about references to “abolitionist framework” that were at one point posted on the school’s website.
The board voted 6-2 Friday to postpone its vote until a virtual meeting Aug. 11 to give members time to question the school’s founder and CEO, DérNecia Phillips, Ph.D.
Board member Deborah Neary objected to the delay, arguing that the school meets all of the board’s official criteria for approval. She called the timing of members’ concerns “disrespectful” as the school aims to open Aug. 19.
“By saying we’re going to postpone the vote, we, as a board, are saying we are going to put different criteria on this school catering to African American children than we put on any other school we have ever approved,” Neary said. “That doesn’t sound legal. It sounds disrespectful. It sounds racist, and I can’t believe we’re even considering this.”
Board President Elizabeth Tegtmeier, who voted in favor of the postponement, pushed back on Neary’s criticism, saying she doesn’t believe the concerns are “racially motivated” in any way.
The school, Identity Preparatory Academy, is looking to serve fourth through eighth grade students in North Omaha, starting with fourth and fifth grade in its first year and adding grades each year after. Its website says enrollment is closed for the 2026-27 school year.
Board member Kirk Penner asked to postpone the vote due to concerns with wording that was temporarily posted on the school’s website, including “abolitionist framework” and “liberatory practices.” He cited a book, “We Want to Do More Than Survive: Abolitionist Teaching and the Pursuit of Educational Freedom” by Bettina L. Love, as the root of his worries, calling it “The Bible” for abolitionist teachings.
Phillips attended Friday’s meeting and provided testimony before the board’s discussion about the concerns. She said the terms “abolitionist framework” and “liberatory practices” were “exploratory language” that was put on the website during its design phase, but after collaboration with community members, the language was changed.
Phillips said the words used were “misinterpreted,” which Penner denied, saying, “You can’t misinterpret that.”
Phillips also defended her background as a 21-year educator and noted that her parents are U.S. Air Force veterans.
“Any claim of anti-Americanism has nothing to do with me,” Phillips said.
Penner said the language change on the website was a more sudden switch than what Phillips implied, and he argued that was the reason further discussion was needed. Tegtmeier said she was the one who suggested postponing the vote to Penner after Phillips’ testimony, rather than Penner voting no on the approval, which Penner agreed to.
“I’m curious to see if one of you breaks from voting with Deb Neary for the first time, and ask for the postponement,” Penner told the board in response to Neary’s objection. “I think it’s worth the time.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Board member Sherry Jones said her concerns lay not in the potential curriculum used in the school, but whether using an abolitionist framework violated the board’s rules for approval of nonpublic schools. She said parts of the rules mention “obedience to law, desirable citizenry, etcetera,” which she claimed abolitionist framework doesn’t support.
Board member Kristin Christensen, who was one of the two no votes on postponement alongside Neary, pushed back on this, saying abolitionist education is not about “breaking the law and tearing down society.” She said she would like Jones to seek a deeper understanding of what abolitionist framework means.
Neary expressed frustration that none of these concerns were raised during the two months when the board’s planning and evaluation committee was considering the school’s application. She said the board has developed a habit of waiting until the 11th hour to have discussions and causing chaos to the schools involved in the votes.
Neary asked the board why no such concerns were raised during the committee process. When no one immediately responded, she directed her question specifically to Jones.
Jones’ response: “I would encourage board members to take a look within themselves when questioning the function or dysfunction of committee and board work.”
Liz Renner, the board’s vice president, shared support for Identity Preparatory Academy’s vision, calling it the “perfect U.S. civics lesson.” She said she was hesitant to support postponing the vote due to the short timeline before the school’s intended opening.
“I’m just thinking of all those girls with their backpacks, ready and eager to start their day,” Renner said.
Renner asked Penner to make a commitment that he would go into their meeting with Phillips open-minded, rather than aiming to criticize and make a case for why the board shouldn’t approve the school. Though Penner never gave such a verbal commitment, Renner voted yes on the postponement.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Rhode Island candidates look to TV ads to sell themselves to voters
description: Rhode Island’s airwaves are getting increasingly crowded as more candidates launch ad campaigns in a more-than-$3-million battle for voters’ attention ahead of the Sept. 9 primary. Barrington Rep. Jason Knight on Friday became the third Democrat running to be Rhode Island’s next attorney general to make his TV debut in the four-way race. The 30-second […]
text:
Jason Knight, a Democratic candidate running to be Rhode Island's next attorney general, debuted his first ad of the primary on Aug. 7, 2026 (Screenshot/Jason Knight for AG)Rhode Island’s airwaves are getting increasingly crowded as more candidates launch ad campaigns in a more-than-$3-million battle for voters’ attention ahead of the Sept. 9 primary.
Barrington Rep. Jason Knight on Friday became the third Democrat running to be Rhode Island’s next attorney general to make his TV debut in the four-way race. The 30-second spot begins with Knight recounting the moment he learned of a shooting in 1994 at the Planned Parenthood clinic in Brookline, Massachusetts, where his wife worked.
At the time, Knight was serving aboard a submarine in the Atlantic Ocean when he learned of the shooting. His wife was unharmed, but he noted that “others weren’t so lucky.” The experience, he said, motivated his work in the Rhode Island General Assembly to codify Roe v. Wade protections into state law and fight for the passage of a law banning the manufacture and sale of certain semi-automatic weapons.
“That tragedy changed us forever,” Knight says in a voiceover. “As your attorney general, I’ll never stop fighting to protect women’s rights and keep us safe.”
Knight’s campaign is spending over $128,000 for 706 ad broadcast airings through the primary election, according to filings made with the Federal Communications Commission (FCC).
The commercial will begin to air on WPRI along with The CW, myRITV, and Fox affiliate WNAC beginning Saturday.
Knight, a former prosecutor who has represented parts of Barrington and Warren in the House for the past decade, will have the top spot on the list of four Democrats appearing on the Sept. 9 ballot. Below him will be Keith Hoffmann, Rep. Joe Solomon, and Kim Ahern.
While first on the ballot, two of his Democratic opponents have already beaten Knight to the airwaves
Hoffmann, a former chief of policy and senior counsel at the AG’s office, was the first out with an ad, landing a spot in July as part of a $1 million media campaign. FCC filings show Hoffmann’s campaign has purchased over $412,000 worth of ads across Rhode Island’s broadcast and cable TV networks.
Ahern, the former prosecutor who headed the state’s Cannabis Control Commission, aired her debut ad the following week. FCC filings show Ahern’s campaign has spent over $104,000 on television commercials.
Solomon remains the only candidate without a record of ad purchases. Shastery Gonzalez Pena, a spokesperson for the Solomon campaign, said in an email Friday that TV ads would be airing statewide in the coming weeks.
Early voting begins Aug. 20 — the same week Xay Khamsyvoravong, a Newport city councilor and former mayor of the City by the Sea, will begin his ad blitz in the five-way Democratic race for lieutenant governor.
FCC filings show Khamsyvoravong’s campaign has reserved $119,890 for 377 commercials across Rhode Island’s major networks and cable.
But the former Newport mayor can’t say he’s the first in his contest to go on TV. Former state Sen. Cindy Coyne earned that honor after spending $500 for two commercial spots on WNAC during the July 31 debate hosted by WPRI-TV, which shares broadcast operations with the Providence Fox affiliate.
FCC filings show Coyne’s campaign has reserved $10,770 for 45 spots across WJAR and Coastal ABC between Aug. 13 and 19.
The governor’s race remains the biggest TV matchup, with incumbent Dan McKee and Helena Buonanno Foulkes accounting for nearly two-thirds of all broadcast and cable spending in Rhode Island as of Friday. 
Over 70% of that spending has come from Foulkes, whose campaign has committed over $1.5 million into TV commercials since late May, according to Rhode Island Current’s review of FCC forms. McKee, who was the first of any candidate to air an ad this year, has so far spent $621,673 across Rhode Island’s broadcast and cable networks.
Providence Mayor Brett Smiley remains the only local official on television. Filings show his campaign has spent over $469,000 on broadcast and cable ads. David Morales, his Democratic challenger, has said he has no intention of advertising on television.
